# Overview



**OpenMM** is a high-performance molecular dynamics (MD) simulation toolkit developed at Stanford University. It serves a dual purpose: as a **stand-alone application** for scientists who want to run simulations quickly, and as a **flexible library** that programmers can embed into their own software. OpenMM distinguishes itself through a combination of extreme customizability (custom forces and integrators defined via the Lepton expression engine), open-source licensing (MIT and LGPL), and exceptional GPU acceleration — making it one of the fastest MD engines available for biomolecular simulation today. The latest major release, OpenMM 8, also introduces support for machine learning potentials, reflecting the toolkit's continued evolution ([README.md](README.md#L1-L14)).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L14)

## Two-Layer Architecture

OpenMM is intentionally designed around a **two-layer architecture** that cleanly separates simulation infrastructure from end-user workflow. Understanding this separation is the single most important concept for navigating both the codebase and the documentation.

The **Library Layer** lives primarily in [`openmmapi/`](openmmapi/include/OpenMM.h#L1-L93) and [`olla/`](olla/src/Platform.cpp) directories. It provides the core C++ API — the `System`, `Context`, `Integrator`, and `Force` classes — along with the platform abstraction that routes computations to different hardware backends. This is the engine room: every simulation, regardless of how it's launched, ultimately executes through this layer.

The **Application Layer** lives in [`wrappers/python/openmm/app/`](wrappers/python/openmm/app/__init__.py) and provides a high-level Python API oriented around practical simulation workflows. This includes classes like `Simulation`, `ForceField`, `Modeller`, and file parsers for AMBER, CHARMM, GROMACS, PDB, and other formats. The application layer is what most users interact with directly — it translates human-readable inputs (force field XML files, structure files) into the low-level `System` objects the library layer expects ([docs-source/usersguide/introduction.rst](docs-source/usersguide/introduction.rst#L1-L10)).

Sources: [OpenMM.h](openmmapi/include/OpenMM.h#L1-L93), [introduction.rst](docs-source/usersguide/introduction.rst#L1-L10)

## High-Level Architecture

The following diagram illustrates how the major components of OpenMM relate to each other, from user-facing code down to hardware execution:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Application Layer (Python)"
        A[Simulation] --> B[ForceField]
        A --> C[Modeller / Topology]
        A --> D[File Parsers<br/>PDB, AMBER, CHARMM, GROMACS]
        A --> E[Reporters<br/>DCD, PDB, StateData]
    end

    subgraph "Library Layer (C++ API)"
        F[System] --> G[Force objects<br/>NonbondedForce, CustomForce, ...]
        F --> H[Integrator<br/>Langevin, Verlet, Custom, ...]
        I[Context] --> F
        I --> H
        I --> J[Platform]
    end

    subgraph "Platform Abstraction (olla)"
        J --> K[Kernel Registry]
        K --> L[Reference Platform]
        K --> M[CPU Platform]
        K --> N[CUDA Platform]
        K --> O[OpenCL Platform]
        K --> P[HIP Platform]
    end

    subgraph "Hardware"
        L --> Q[CPU]
        M --> Q
        N --> R[NVIDIA GPU]
        O --> S[AMD / Intel GPU]
        P --> T[AMD GPU ROCm]
    end

    A --> I
    B --> F
    D --> C
```

A user creates a `Simulation` object at the top, which internally assembles a `System` (particles + forces), binds it with an `Integrator` inside a `Context`, and the `Platform` dispatches computation to the fastest available hardware. This indirection means switching from CPU to GPU requires changing only one line of code.

Sources: [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L45-L80), [Kernel.h](olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h#L40-L60)

## Repository Structure

The repository is organized into clearly delineated directories, each serving a distinct role in the build and runtime architecture:

```
openmm/
├── openmmapi/          # Core C++ API (System, Context, Integrator, Force classes)
├── olla/               # Platform & Kernel abstraction layer (low-level plugin registry)
├── platforms/          # Hardware backend implementations
│   ├── reference/      #   Reference (debugging, correctness validation)
│   ├── cpu/            #   Optimized CPU (SIMD: SSE/AVX)
│   ├── cuda/           #   NVIDIA GPU (CUDA)
│   ├── opencl/         #   Cross-platform GPU (OpenCL)
│   └── hip/            #   AMD GPU (ROCm/HIP)
├── wrappers/python/    # SWIG-generated Python bindings + app layer
├── serialization/      # XML serialization for checkpointing
├── plugins/            # Optional force field plugins
│   ├── amoeba/         #   Amoeba polarizable force field
│   ├── drude/          #   Drude polarizable model
│   └── rpmd/           #   Ring-polymer molecular dynamics
├── libraries/          # Vendored third-party libraries (Lepton, vecmath, etc.)
├── tests/              # C++ test suite
├── examples/           # Python & C++ example simulations
└── docs-source/        # Sphinx documentation source
```

Sources: [Repository root](openmmapi/include/OpenMM.h), [olla](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h), [platforms](platforms/common/src/ComputeContext.cpp), [plugins](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi)

## Supported Platforms and Hardware

OpenMM's **platform system** is the architectural mechanism that enables hardware portability without code changes. A `Platform` acts as a registry of `Kernel` factories — each kernel implements a specific computation (e.g., "calculate nonbonded forces" or "integrate one time step") for a particular hardware target. When you create a `Context`, OpenMM automatically selects the fastest platform that supports all required kernels ([Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L45-L65)).

| Platform | Hardware Target | Precision | Best For |
|----------|----------------|-----------|----------|
| **Reference** | Any CPU | Double | Debugging, validation, correctness testing |
| **CPU** | x86 CPUs | Mixed (SP/DP) | Production runs without GPU; uses SSE/AVX SIMD |
| **CUDA** | NVIDIA GPUs | Mixed (configurable) | Highest performance on NVIDIA hardware |
| **OpenCL** | AMD, Intel, NVIDIA GPUs | Mixed (configurable) | Cross-vendor GPU portability |
| **HIP** | AMD GPUs (ROCm) | Mixed (configurable) | Native AMD GPU performance |

The Reference platform always returns a speed of `1.0`, while accelerated platforms return higher values proportional to their estimated throughput, allowing automatic platform selection to pick the fastest option ([Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L75-L80)).

> [!TIP]
> **Platform selection is automatic but overridable.** By default, `Context` picks the fastest available platform. You can override this with `Platform.getPlatformByName('CUDA')` or pass platform properties (like `'DeviceIndex'` or `'Precision'`) to control GPU selection and numerical precision.

Sources: [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L45-L100), [platforms/](platforms/common/src/ComputeContext.cpp)

## Core API Primitives

Three classes form the foundation of every OpenMM simulation:

**`System`** — the molecular system definition. A `System` holds the complete description of what to simulate: the number of particles, their masses, constraints, and a collection of `Force` objects that define interactions (bonded, nonbonded, implicit solvent, custom, etc.). Think of it as the static specification of your physical model ([openmmapi/include/openmm/System.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/System.h)).

**`Integrator`** — the time evolution engine. An `Integrator` advances the system through time by computing forces and updating positions/velocities. OpenMM ships with multiple integrators covering different simulation ensembles and algorithms. The `step(int steps)` method is the primary entry point for simulation ([Integrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Integrator.h#L40-L90)).

**`Context`** — the runtime binding. A `Context` binds a `System`, an `Integrator`, and a `Platform` together into a live simulation state. It holds positions, velocities, time, and provides methods like `getState()` to extract observables. Creating a `Context` is when GPU memory gets allocated and kernels get compiled ([Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h)).

Sources: [System.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/System.h), [Integrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Integrator.h#L40-L90), [Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h)

## Integrators and Forces

OpenMM provides a rich set of integrators covering the most common MD algorithms, alongside a uniquely powerful system of custom and standard forces:

| Category | Available Classes |
|----------|------------------|
| **Standard Integrators** | `VerletIntegrator`, `LangevinIntegrator`, `LangevinMiddleIntegrator`, `BrownianIntegrator`, `VariableLangevinIntegrator`, `VariableVerletIntegrator`, `NoseHooverIntegrator`, `CompoundIntegrator` |
| **Specialized Integrators** | `DPDIntegrator` (dissipative particle dynamics), `QTBIntegrator` (quantum thermal bath), `CustomIntegrator` (user-defined algorithms) |
| **Standard Forces** | `NonbondedForce`, `HarmonicBondForce`, `HarmonicAngleForce`, `PeriodicTorsionForce`, `RBTorsionForce`, `GBSAOBCForce`, `CMAPTorsionForce`, `CMMotionRemover` |
| **Thermostats & Barostats** | `AndersenThermostat`, `MonteCarloBarostat`, `MonteCarloAnisotropicBarostat`, `MonteCarloFlexibleBarostat`, `MonteCarloMembraneBarostat` |
| **Custom Forces** | `CustomBondForce`, `CustomAngleForce`, `CustomTorsionForce`, `CustomNonbondedForce`, `CustomGBForce`, `CustomExternalForce`, `CustomCVForce`, `CustomManyParticleForce`, `CustomHbondForce`, `CustomVolumeForce` |
| **Advanced Forces** | `ATMForce` (alchemical), `GayBerneForce`, `RMSDForce`, `RGForce`, `PythonForce` |

A `Force` object can add forces, contribute to potential energy, modify particle positions/velocities, define parameters, and even alter other forces' parameters at each time step ([Force.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Force.h#L40-L80)). Forces are organized into **force groups** (0–31) enabling multiple time step integration schemes where fast and slow forces are evaluated at different frequencies.

Sources: [OpenMM.h](openmmapi/include/OpenMM.h#L33-L91), [Force.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Force.h#L40-L80)

## Application Layer Highlights

The Python application layer, found in [`wrappers/python/openmm/app/`](wrappers/python/openmm/app/__init__.py), wraps the C++ API into a workflow-oriented interface. Its key components include:

- **`Simulation`** — the central orchestrator that combines topology, system, integrator, and platform into a single object with convenience methods like `minimizeEnergy()`, `step()`, and `saveCheckpoint()` ([simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L43-L58))
- **`ForceField`** — reads XML force field definition files (AMBER, CHARMM-compatible) and generates `System` objects from a `Topology`
- **`Modeller`** — provides tools for adding missing hydrogens, adding solvent boxes, and editing molecular structures
- **File parsers** — `PDBFile`, `AmberPrmtopFile`/`AmberInpcrdFile`, `CharmmPsfFile`/`CharmmParameterSet`, `GromacsTopFile`/`GromacsGroFile`, `TinkerFiles`, and more
- **Reporters** — `DCDReporter`, `PDBReporter`, `StateDataReporter`, `CheckpointReporter` for outputting trajectory and diagnostic data

A complete simulation can be expressed in as few as 15 lines of Python, as demonstrated in [`examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py`](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L1-L16).

Sources: [app/](wrappers/python/openmm/app/__init__.py), [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L43-L58), [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L1-L16)

## Plugin Ecosystem

OpenMM's plugin architecture extends core functionality without modifying the main library. Plugins are distributed independently and loaded at runtime, following the same platform abstraction pattern as the core. The repository includes four plugins in the [`plugins/`](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi) directory:

| Plugin | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| **Amoeba** | Polarizable multipole force field with AMOEBA potential, including GPU-accelerated platforms |
| **Drude** | Drude polarizable force field with classical Drude oscillators |
| **RPMD** | Ring-polymer molecular dynamics for nuclear quantum effects |
| **CPU PME** | Alternative CPU-optimized Particle Mesh Ewald implementation |

Each plugin mirrors the core structure: its own `openmmapi/`, `platforms/`, `serialization/`, and `wrappers/` subdirectories, demonstrating how the architecture is designed for extensibility.

Sources: [plugins/](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi), [library.rst](docs-source/usersguide/library.rst#L1-L22)

## Bundled Libraries

The [`libraries/`](libraries) directory contains vendored third-party libraries that OpenMM depends on. These are compiled as part of the OpenMM build rather than linked from the system, ensuring reproducibility across platforms. Key libraries include:

- **Lepton** — a compact expression parser and compiler used by `CustomForce` and `CustomIntegrator` to evaluate arbitrary mathematical expressions at runtime
- **vecmath** — SIMD-vectorized math operations (the performance backbone of the CPU platform)
- **pocketfft** — efficient FFT implementation used in Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) calculations
- **vkfft** — GPU-accelerated FFT library used by CUDA and OpenCL platforms for PME
- **sfmt** — SIMD-oriented fast Mersenne Twister pseudo-random number generator
- **asmjit** — JIT assembler used for dynamic code generation on CPU

Sources: [libraries/](libraries), [common/](platforms/common/src/ExpressionUtilities.cpp)

## A Minimal Working Example

The following Python script demonstrates the end-to-end workflow: load a structure, assign a force field, minimize energy, and run dynamics. This single file exercises all the major architectural layers described above ([simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L1-L16)):

```python
from openmm.app import *
from openmm import *
from openmm.unit import *

pdb = PDBFile('input.pdb')                                                    # Application layer: file parser
forcefield = ForceField('amber19-all.xml', 'amber19/tip3pfb.xml')             # Application layer: force field
system = forcefield.createSystem(pdb.topology, nonbondedMethod=PME,           # Library layer: System + Forces
                                  nonbondedCutoff=1*nanometer, constraints=HBonds)
integrator = LangevinMiddleIntegrator(300*kelvin, 1/picosecond,              # Library layer: Integrator
                                        0.004*picoseconds)
simulation = Simulation(pdb.topology, system, integrator)                      # Application layer: Simulation
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy()
simulation.reporters.append(StateDataReporter(stdout, 1000, step=True,
                                              potentialEnergy=True, temperature=True))
simulation.step(10000)
```

Sources: [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L1-L16)

# Quick Start



This guide walks you through running your first molecular dynamics simulation with OpenMM in under five minutes. By the end, you will understand the core simulation pipeline, execute a working example, and know where to find resources for deeper exploration. No prior molecular dynamics experience is required.

![OpenMM Architecture](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/blob/master/docs-source/images/ArchitectureLayers.jpg?raw=true)

## The Five-Minute Simulation Pipeline

Every OpenMM simulation follows a consistent, declarative pattern. You do not need to understand the underlying physics engine — you only need to supply the molecule, the force field that defines its interactions, an integrator that advances time, and a few simulation parameters. OpenMM handles everything else, including automatic GPU acceleration when available.

The pipeline has six stages, and the architecture reflects a clean separation of concerns across those stages:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Load Structure] --> B[Select Force Field]
    B --> C[Build System]
    C --> D[Create Integrator]
    D --> E[Initialize Simulation]
    E --> F[Minimize & Run]
    
    subgraph Input Layer
        A
        B
    end
    
    subgraph Core Engine
        C
        D
    end
    
    subgraph Execution Layer
        E
        F
    end
```

This three-tier architecture is the key mental model for working with OpenMM. The **Input Layer** reads your molecular structure and force field definitions. The **Core Engine** translates those into an internal `System` and `Integrator` that define the physics. The **Execution Layer** wraps everything into a `Simulation` object and drives the actual computation. Each layer communicates through well-defined Python objects, making the entire pipeline composable and testable.

Sources: [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L1-L16), [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L58-L115)

## Install OpenMM

OpenMM installs with a single command. The default installation includes CPU and Reference platforms. GPU support for NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (HIP), or Apple/Intel (OpenCL) is available through optional extras.

| Method | Command | GPU Support |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| **conda** (recommended) | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm` | Auto-detected CUDA |
| **pip** (CPU only) | `pip install openmm` | OpenCL, CPU, Reference |
| **pip** + CUDA 12 | `pip install openmm[cuda12]` | NVIDIA CUDA 12 |
| **pip** + HIP 6 | `pip install openmm[hip6]` | AMD ROCm/HIP 6 |

After installation, verify everything works correctly:

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

This command confirms the installation, checks for available GPU platforms (CUDA, OpenCL, HIP), and verifies that all platforms produce numerically consistent results against the Reference implementation. If GPU acceleration is available, you will see it listed — OpenMM will use it automatically with no additional configuration required.

> [!TIP]
> You do not need to choose a specific platform in your script. The `Simulation` class automatically selects the fastest available platform at runtime. If you have an NVIDIA GPU with proper drivers, CUDA acceleration is used transparently. This zero-configuration design is intentional — it lets the same script run optimally on laptops, workstations, and HPC clusters without modification.

Sources: [01_getting_started.rst](docs-source/usersguide/application/01_getting_started.rst#L36-L107)

## Your First Simulation Script

The following 16-line script is a complete, production-quality molecular dynamics simulation. It loads a PDB structure, parameterizes it with the Amber19 force field, energy-minimizes the system, runs 10,000 time steps, and saves both trajectory frames and progress reports.

```python
from openmm.app import *
from openmm import *
from openmm.unit import *
from sys import stdout

pdb = PDBFile('input.pdb')
forcefield = ForceField('amber19-all.xml', 'amber19/tip3pfb.xml')
system = forcefield.createSystem(pdb.topology, nonbondedMethod=PME,
        nonbondedCutoff=1*nanometer, constraints=HBonds)
integrator = LangevinMiddleIntegrator(300*kelvin, 1/picosecond, 0.004*picoseconds)
simulation = Simulation(pdb.topology, system, integrator)
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy()
simulation.reporters.append(DCDReporter('output.dcd', 1000))
simulation.reporters.append(StateDataReporter(stdout, 1000, step=True,
        potentialEnergy=True, temperature=True))
simulation.step(10000)
```

This script lives in the repository at `examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py`. Let us walk through every meaningful line and understand what it does.

Sources: [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L1-L16), [02_running_sims.rst](docs-source/usersguide/application/02_running_sims.rst#L10-L38)

## Line-by-Line Breakdown

### Imports

```python
from openmm.app import *
from openmm import *
from openmm.unit import *
from sys import stdout
```

These four imports pull in the entire application layer (`openmm.app`), the core engine (`openmm`), the physical units system (`openmm.unit`), and the standard output stream for console reporting. The application layer is the high-level API you will use for nearly all tasks. The core engine is only needed directly when working with low-level `System`, `Integrator`, or `Context` objects. Every script you write will start with these same imports.

Sources: [__init__.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/__init__.py#L1-L61)

### Loading a Molecular Structure

```python
pdb = PDBFile('input.pdb')
```

The `PDBFile` parser reads a standard PDB file and extracts two things: a **Topology** (the chemical connectivity — which atoms exist, what residues they belong to, how they are bonded) and **Positions** (the 3D coordinates of every atom). These two pieces of information are all OpenMM needs to build a simulation. The topology is accessed as `pdb.topology` and positions as `pdb.positions`.

Sources: [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L6), [__init__.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/__init__.py#L16)

### Selecting and Loading a Force Field

```python
forcefield = ForceField('amber19-all.xml', 'amber19/tip3pfb.xml')
```

The `ForceField` class accepts one or more XML files that define the physics of atomic interactions. Here we load two files: `amber19-all.xml` contains the complete Amber19 protein and nucleic acid parameters, and `amber19/tip3pfb.xml` specifies the TIP3P-FB water model. Multiple files are composited — the second file augments or overrides definitions from the first. The `ForceField` constructor searches for files in several locations in order: an absolute path, a path relative to the current working directory, and finally the bundled data directory at `openmm/app/data/`.

OpenMM ships with a comprehensive library of force fields across several major families:

| Force Field Family | Bundled Files | Water Models |
|---|---|---|
| **Amber19** | `amber19-all.xml`, `amber19/protein.ff19SB.xml`, `amber19/DNA.OL21.xml`, `amber19/lipid21.xml` | `tip3pfb.xml`, `tip4pfb.xml`, `opc.xml`, `opc3.xml`, `spce.xml` |
| **Amber14** | `amber14-all.xml`, `amber14/protein.ff14SB.xml`, `amber14/DNA.OL15.xml`, `amber14/RNA.OL3.xml`, `amber14/lipid17.xml` | `tip3pfb.xml`, `tip4pew.xml`, `opc.xml` |
| **CHARMM36** | `charmm36.xml`, `charmm36_2024.xml` | `tip3p-pme-b.xml`, `tip4p2005.xml`, `tip5p.xml` |
| **Amoeba** | `amoeba2018.xml`, `amoeba2013.xml` | `tip4pfb.xml` |
| **Implicit Solvent** | `implicit/gbn2.xml`, `implicit/obc2.xml` | — |

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L195-L220), [data directory](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data)

### Building the Physical System

```python
system = forcefield.createSystem(pdb.topology, nonbondedMethod=PME,
        nonbondedCutoff=1*nanometer, constraints=HBonds)
```

The `createSystem()` method is where the force field is applied to your specific molecule. It matches every residue in the topology against its template library, assigns atom types, computes bond connectivity, and generates all the force objects that govern interatomic interactions. The three parameters shown here are the most commonly used for simulations in explicit solvent:

- **`nonbondedMethod=PME`** — Particle Mesh Ewald, the gold-standard method for handling long-range electrostatic interactions in periodic systems
- **`nonbondedCutoff=1*nanometer`** — the real-space cutoff distance for nonbonded force calculations
- **`constraints=HBonds`** — constrains bonds involving hydrogen to their equilibrium lengths, enabling a larger 4 fs time step

Notice the explicit use of physical units: `1*nanometer`. OpenMM's unit system prevents silent unit errors — you cannot accidentally pass an angstrom where a nanometer is expected, because the types will not match.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1231-L1260), [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L8)

### Creating the Integrator

```python
integrator = LangevinMiddleIntegrator(300*kelvin, 1/picosecond, 0.004*picoseconds)
```

The integrator advances the simulation through time using a numerical algorithm. The `LangevinMiddleIntegrator` implements the BAOAB Langevin integrator (middle scheme), which provides excellent sampling and temperature control. Its three arguments define the thermodynamic ensemble: **temperature** (300 K), **friction coefficient** (1 ps⁻¹, controlling how strongly the system is coupled to the thermal bath), and **time step** (4 fs, the interval between force evaluations).

Sources: [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L9)

### Initializing and Running the Simulation

```python
simulation = Simulation(pdb.topology, system, integrator)
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy()
```

The `Simulation` class is the unified high-level interface that ties everything together. Its constructor accepts a topology, system, and integrator, then internally creates a `Context` — the low-level object that manages memory, platform selection, and computation. Setting positions loads the atomic coordinates into the simulation state. `minimizeEnergy()` performs a local energy minimization to remove any bad contacts or steric clashes that could cause the simulation to explode, using a default convergence tolerance of 10 kJ/mol/nm.

```python
simulation.reporters.append(DCDReporter('output.dcd', 1000))
simulation.reporters.append(StateDataReporter(stdout, 1000, step=True,
        potentialEnergy=True, temperature=True))
simulation.step(10000)
```

**Reporters** are how you extract data from a running simulation. The `DCDReporter` writes trajectory frames (atomic coordinates at each saved step) to a binary DCD file every 1,000 steps. The `StateDataReporter` prints a formatted line to the console with the step number, potential energy, and temperature, also every 1,000 steps. Finally, `simulation.step(10000)` runs the simulation for 10,000 time steps — at 4 fs per step, this is 40 picoseconds of simulated time.

> [!TIP]
> The `Simulation` object also provides `saveCheckpoint()` and `loadCheckpoint()` methods for long-running simulations. Call `simulation.saveCheckpoint('checkpoint.chk')` periodically (or use the `CheckpointReporter`) so you can resume from the exact simulation state if the process is interrupted. This is essential for production simulations that run for hours or days.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L58-L115), [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L125-L146), [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L283-L315)

## Supporting Multiple File Formats

OpenMM is not tied to PDB files or Amber force fields. The same simulation pattern works with all major biomolecular file formats. The table below shows how each format maps to the standard pipeline — only the first two lines (structure loading and system creation) change; everything else stays identical.

| Format | Loader Class | System Creation | Example File |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|-------------|
| **PDB** | `PDBFile('input.pdb')` | `ForceField(...).createSystem(pdb.topology, ...)` | [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py) |
| **Amber** | `AmberPrmtopFile('input.prmtop')` + `AmberInpcrdFile('input.inpcrd')` | `prmtop.createSystem(...)` | [simulateAmber.py](examples/python-examples/simulateAmber.py) |
| **GROMACS** | `GromacsTopFile('input.top')` + `GromacsGroFile('input.gro')` | `top.createSystem(...)` | [simulateGromacs.py](examples/python-examples/simulateGromacs.py) |
| **CHARMM** | `CharmmPsfFile('system.psf')` + `CharmmParameterSet(...)` | `psf.createSystem(params, ...)` | [simulateCharmm.py](examples/python-examples/simulateCharmm.py) |
| **Tinker/Amoeba** | `TinkerFiles('system.xyz', ['params.prm'])` | `tinker.createSystem(...)` | [simulateTinker.py](examples/python-examples/simulateTinker.py) |

For Amber, GROMACS, and CHARMM files, the force field parameters are embedded directly in the topology files, so you do not need to specify a separate `ForceField`. The `createSystem()` method on the loader class handles parameterization internally.

Sources: [simulateAmber.py](examples/python-examples/simulateAmber.py#L1-L16), [simulateGromacs.py](examples/python-examples/simulateGromacs.py#L1-L16), [simulateCharmm.py](examples/python-examples/simulateCharmm.py#L1-L34), [simulateTinker.py](examples/python-examples/simulateTinker.py#L1-L15)

## Where to Find Examples

All example scripts and their accompanying input files live in the `examples/python-examples/` directory of the repository. The directory structure is flat and self-contained — each example script and its required data files are in the same folder:

```
examples/python-examples/
├── simulatePdb.py          ← PDB + ForceField (Amber19)
├── simulateAmber.py        ← Amber PRMTOP + INPCRD
├── simulateGromacs.py      ← GROMACS TOP + GRO
├── simulateCharmm.py       ← CHARMM PSF + parameters
├── simulateTinker.py       ← Tinker XYZ + PRM (Amoeba)
├── argon-chemical-potential.py  ← Custom forces, alchemical free energy
├── input.pdb / input.prmtop / input.inpcrd / input.gro / input.top
└── ...
```

The `argon-chemical-potential.py` example is more advanced — it demonstrates building a system from scratch using the low-level API with `CustomNonbondedForce`, performing alchemical free energy calculations across multiple lambda windows, and analyzing results with the MBAR statistical method. This is an excellent next step once you are comfortable with the basic pipeline.

Sources: [examples directory](examples/python-examples)

## Project Structure at a Glance

Understanding where the key components live in the repository helps you navigate the codebase as you go deeper:

```
openmm/
├── wrappers/python/openmm/
│   ├── __init__.py            ← Core engine: System, Integrator, Context
│   └── app/
│       ├── __init__.py        ← Application layer public API
│       ├── simulation.py      ← Simulation class (high-level runner)
│       ├── forcefield.py      ← ForceField class & built-in force field XML
│       ├── modeller.py        ← Modeller (add solvent, hydrogens, membranes)
│       ├── topology.py        ← Topology, Chain, Residue, Atom
│       ├── pdbfile.py         ← PDB parser
│       ├── amberprmtopfile.py ← Amber file readers
│       ├── gromacstopfile.py  ← GROMACS file readers
│       ├── charmmpsffile.py   ← CHARMM file readers
│       ├── data/              ← Bundled force field XML files
│       └── ...reporters       ← Output: DCD, PDB, XTC, checkpoint, state
├── openmmapi/                ← C++ core API (System, Force, Integrator)
├── platforms/                ← CUDA, OpenCL, HIP, CPU, Reference backends
├── plugins/                  ← Amoeba, Drude, RPMD, CPU-PME plugins
├── examples/python-examples/ ← Ready-to-run example scripts
└── docs-source/              ← Documentation source (Sphinx RST)
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L37), [__init__.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/__init__.py#L1-L61), [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L1-L44)

# Installation and Platform Setup



This page covers everything you need to get OpenMM running on your machine — from a one-command install to a full source build with GPU acceleration. By the end, you will understand how OpenMM's platform architecture maps to your hardware, which installation path is right for you, and how to verify that everything works correctly.

---

## Understanding the OpenMM Platform Architecture

Before installing anything, it is worth understanding *what* you are installing. OpenMM is not a single monolithic binary — it is a **core library** plus a collection of **platform plugins**, each targeting a specific compute backend. The core (`libOpenMM`) provides the simulation API, while platforms translate that API into optimized hardware-specific code. This architecture, defined in the top-level [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L81-L83), means you only build the platforms relevant to your hardware.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "OpenMM Runtime Architecture"
        APP["Your Simulation Code<br/>(Python / C++)"]
        CTX["Context"]
        
        subgraph Platforms["Platform Layer"]
            REF["Reference Platform<br/>(Scalar, portable)"]
            CPU["CPU Platform<br/>(SIMD: SSE2/AVX)"]
            CUDA["CUDA Platform<br/>(NVIDIA GPUs)"]
            OCL["OpenCL Platform<br/>(Multi-vendor GPUs)"]
            HIP["HIP Platform<br/>(AMD GPUs)"]
        end
    end

    APP --> CTX
    CTX --> Platforms
    
    style REF fill:#e8e8e8,color:#333
    style CPU fill:#e8e8e8,color:#333
    style CUDA fill:#76b900,color:#fff
    style OCL fill:#cc6699,color:#fff
    style HIP fill:#ed1c24,color:#fff
```

The platform layer is what makes OpenMM unique among molecular dynamics toolkits — the same simulation code can run on a laptop CPU, an NVIDIA data-center GPU, or an AMD workstation without modification. You simply select the platform at runtime. For a deeper look at how this abstraction works internally, see [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system).

---

## Quick Install with Conda or Pip (Recommended)

For the vast majority of users, the pre-built packages from conda-forge are the best option. They include the core library, all platforms that can reasonably be pre-built, Python wrappers, and the standard plugin set.

### Step 1: Install via Conda

Conda handles binary dependencies (CUDA runtime, Python, NumPy) automatically and is the officially recommended method.

```bash
# Install Miniconda if you don't have it: https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html

# Create a dedicated environment (recommended)
conda create -n openmm-env python=3.11 -c conda-forge
conda activate openmm-env

# Install OpenMM with all plugins
conda install -c conda-forge openmm
```

The conda-forge package bundles the core library (v8.5.0 as defined in [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L166-L169)), the Reference, CPU, and CUDA platforms, and all four standard plugins (Amoeba, RPMD, Drude, CPU PME). The conda-forge release process is documented in [CONDA_FORGE_RELEASES.md](devtools/CONDA_FORGE_RELEASES.md#L1-L10).

### Step 2: Install via Pip (Alternative)

If you prefer pip, OpenMM is also available on PyPI. Note that pip packages may not include GPU platform support on all systems — conda is generally more reliable for GPU-accelerated installs.

```bash
pip install openmm
```

### GPU Driver Prerequisites

If you plan to use a GPU platform, ensure you have modern drivers installed **before** installing OpenMM:

| GPU Vendor | Minimum Driver | Additional SDK |
|---|---|---|
| **NVIDIA** | CUDA 11.x+ driver | CUDA Toolkit (for source builds only) |
| **AMD** | ROCm 5.x+ driver | ROCm HIP SDK (for source builds only) |
| **Intel** | Latest OpenCL driver | None required |

For pre-built conda packages, the CUDA runtime is bundled automatically — you do **not** need to install the full CUDA Toolkit separately.

> [!TIP]
> **Conda vs. Pip for GPU workloads**: The conda-forge OpenMM package ships with the CUDA runtime libraries bundled, so you never need to match CUDA versions manually. With pip, the CUDA runtime must already be present on your system and version-compatible. For production GPU simulations, conda is strongly recommended.

---

## Platform Overview and Hardware Mapping

Each platform in OpenMM targets a specific compute device. The build system in [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L332-L370) auto-detects available SDKs and enables the corresponding platforms. Here is the complete mapping:

| Platform | Library Name | Target Hardware | Kernel Source | Auto-Detected by CMake |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Reference** | `libOpenMM` (core) | Any CPU (scalar) | C++ | Always built |
| **CPU** | `libOpenMMCPU` | x86_64 / ARM (SIMD) | C++ with asmjit JIT | Default ON |
| **CUDA** | `libOpenMMCUDA` | NVIDIA GPUs | `.cu` (compiled at runtime) | Requires CUDAToolkit |
| **OpenCL** | `libOpenMMOpenCL` | NVIDIA / AMD / Intel GPUs | `.cl` (compiled at runtime) | Requires OpenCL SDK |
| **HIP** | `libOpenMMHIP` | AMD GPUs | `.hip` (compiled at runtime) | Requires ROCm HIP |

Key architectural points from the source code:

- The **Reference platform** is always compiled into the core `libOpenMM` library and serves as the correctness baseline. It uses pure scalar C++ with no architecture-specific optimizations ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L81)).
- The **CPU platform** leverages the **asmjit** JIT compiler for runtime code generation and includes SIMD-optimized kernels via the `vecmath` library ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L249-L254)). It explicitly blocks Clang 3.6 due to known AVX bugs ([platforms/cpu/CMakeLists.txt](platforms/cpu/CMakeLists.txt#L27-L32)).
- The **CUDA platform** requires `CUDAToolkit` to be found by CMake's `FIND_PACKAGE` ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L333-L336)).
- The **HIP platform** searches `ROCM_PATH` and `/opt/rocm` for the HIP SDK ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L347-L352)).
- GPU platforms share common compute code from the [`platforms/common/`](platforms/common/) directory, which is only built when at least one GPU platform is enabled ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L359-L362)).

### Supported CPU Architectures

The build system detects and configures for multiple CPU architectures using the [`cmake_modules/TargetArch.cmake`](cmake_modules/TargetArch.cmake) module ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L33-L47)):

| Architecture | CMake Flag | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| x86_64 / i386 | `X86=ON` | SSE2 required; asmjit JIT enabled |
| ARM (AArch64) | `ARM=ON` | 64-bit only; `__ARM64__` defined |
| PowerPC | `PPC=ON` | `__PPC__` defined |
| LoongArch64 | `LOONGARCH64=ON` | LSX extensions enabled (`-mlsx`) |

---

## Building from Source

Building from source is necessary when you need custom platform configurations, are working on a platform without pre-built packages, or are contributing to OpenMM development. The process is managed entirely by CMake (minimum version 3.17, per [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L30)).

> [!TIP]
> **When to build from source**: You only need a source build if (1) you are modifying OpenMM itself, (2) you need a platform configuration not available in conda-forge, or (3) you are on an unsupported OS. For all other cases, `conda install -c conda-forge openmm` is faster, safer, and easier to maintain.

### Prerequisites

Install all build dependencies via conda (the officially supported method):

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge cmake make cython swig doxygen numpy setuptools
```

For GPU platform support, add the appropriate SDK:

```bash
# CUDA platform (NVIDIA)
# Install CUDA Toolkit from https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads

# HIP platform (AMD)
conda install -c conda-forge hip-devel hipcc rocm-cmake rocm-device-libs
```

### Build Flow (Linux and macOS)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Clone or download source"] --> B["mkdir build && cd build"]
    B --> C["ccmake .. (configure)"]
    C --> D["Adjust CMake variables"]
    D --> E["Press 'g' to generate"]
    E --> F["make (build)"]
    F --> G["make test (verify)"]
    G --> H["make install"]
    H --> I["make PythonInstall"]
    I --> J["python -m openmm.testInstallation"]
    
    style J fill:#76b900,color:#fff
```

**Step 1 — Configure with CMake:**

```bash
mkdir build && cd build
ccmake ..
```

Critical CMake variables to set:

| Variable | Recommended Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` | Your conda env path (e.g., `$CONDA_PREFIX`) | Installation destination |
| `PYTHON_EXECUTABLE` | Auto-detected, or set manually | Python for wrappers |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB` | `ON` if CUDAToolkit found | Build CUDA platform |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB` | `ON` if OpenCL found | Build OpenCL platform |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_HIP_LIB` | `ON` if HIP found | Build HIP platform |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CPU_LIB` | `ON` (default) | Build optimized CPU platform |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_PYTHON_WRAPPERS` | `ON` (default) | Build Python API |

The Python wrappers have a hard dependency on three plugins — Amoeba, RPMD, and Drude — and will produce a build error if any is disabled ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L416-L423)).

**Step 2 — Build and Install:**

```bash
make              # Compile everything
make test         # Run ~317 unit tests
make install      # Install libraries and headers
make PythonInstall  # Install Python wrappers
```

**Step 3 — Verify:**

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

### Build Flow (Windows)

On Windows, the process uses Visual Studio 2017+ and the CMake GUI:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Install Visual Studio 2017+"] --> B["Open Anaconda Prompt"]
    B --> C["conda install cython swig doxygen numpy"]
    C --> D["mkdir build && cd build"]
    D --> E["cmake-gui .."]
    E --> F["Select VS generator & Configure"]
    F --> G["Adjust variables & Generate"]
    G --> H["Open OpenMM.sln in VS"]
    H --> I["Build Solution (Release)"]
    I --> J["Build INSTALL target"]
    J --> K["Build PythonInstall target"]
    K --> L["Build RUN_TESTS target"]
    
    style L fill:#76b900,color:#fff
```

**Critical**: Launch `cmake-gui.exe` from the Anaconda Prompt, **not** from the Windows Start Menu. This ensures CMake can locate conda-installed tools like SWIG and Cython ([docs-source/usersguide/library/02_compiling.rst](docs-source/usersguide/library/02_compiling.rst#L288-L298)).

The default install prefix on Windows is `%ProgramFiles%/OpenMM` ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L54-L56)), but for conda environments you should set `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` to your environment's root directory.

---

## Plugins

OpenMM ships with four official plugins that extend the core simulation capabilities. All are enabled by default in both conda packages and source builds:

| Plugin | Directory | Provides |
|---|---|---|
| **Amoeba** | [`plugins/amoeba/`](plugins/amoeba/) | Polarizable force field with multipole electrostatics |
| **RPMD** | [`plugins/rpmd/`](plugins/rpmd/) | Ring Polymer Molecular Dynamics |
| **Drude** | [`plugins/drude/`](plugins/drude/) | Drude polarizable force field |
| **CPU PME** | [`plugins/cpupme/`](plugins/cpupme/) | CPU-optimized Particle Mesh Ewald |

Each plugin is a separate CMake subdirectory with its own libraries, headers, and tests ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L373-L400)). The CMake cache variables `OPENMM_BUILD_AMOEBA_PLUGIN`, `OPENMM_BUILD_RPMD_PLUGIN`, `OPENMM_BUILD_DRUDE_PLUGIN`, and `OPENMM_BUILD_PME_PLUGIN` control whether each is built. If you are building Python wrappers, all three of Amoeba, RPMD, and Drude **must** remain enabled — disabling any one will cause a hard build error ([CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L416-L423)).

---

## Verifying Your Installation

OpenMM includes a comprehensive installation test script at [`wrappers/python/openmm/testInstallation.py`](wrappers/python/openmm/testInstallation.py) that validates every component of your setup:

```bash
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

This script performs the following checks ([wrappers/python/openmm/testInstallation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/testInstallation.py#L31-L95)):

1. **Import validation** — Confirms all OpenMM Python modules (`openmm.app`, `openmm`, `openmm.unit`) are importable
2. **Version reporting** — Prints the OpenMM library version and git revision
3. **Platform enumeration** — Lists every available platform (Reference, CPU, CUDA, OpenCL, HIP)
4. **Force computation test** — Creates a test system (alanine dipeptide with AMBER99SB + TIP3P) and computes forces on every detected platform
5. **Cross-platform accuracy** — Compares force vectors between all platforms, reporting median relative differences; flags any pair exceeding 10⁻⁴ tolerance

A successful run ends with: `All differences are within tolerance.` If a platform fails to compute forces, the script reports the specific error — this usually indicates a driver or SDK problem.

Typical output looks like:

```
OpenMM Version: 8.5
Git Revision: <hash>

There are 4 Platforms available:

1 Reference - Successfully computed forces
2 CPU - Successfully computed forces
3 CUDA - Successfully computed forces
4 OpenCL - Successfully computed forces

Median difference in forces between platforms:

Reference vs. CPU: 2.5e-06
Reference vs. CUDA: 3.1e-06
Reference vs. OpenCL: 2.8e-06
...

All differences are within tolerance.
```

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Problem | Likely Cause | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| `ImportError: libOpenMM.so not found` | Library path not set | Add install `lib/` to `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (Linux) or `DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH` (macOS) |
| CUDA platform not listed | CUDAToolkit not found at build time | Install CUDA Toolkit; re-run CMake; verify `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB=ON` |
| HIP platform not listed | ROCm not in search path | Set `ROCM_PATH` environment variable; re-run CMake |
| `openmm.testInstallation` import failure | Python wrappers not installed | Run `make PythonInstall` or `conda install -c conda-forge openmm` |
| Clang 3.6 build failure (CPU) | Known AVX bug in Clang 3.6 | Upgrade to Clang 3.7+ or switch to GCC ([platforms/cpu/CMakeLists.txt](platforms/cpu/CMakeLists.txt#L27-L32)) |
| Large force differences between platforms | GPU driver mismatch | Update GPU drivers to latest vendor-recommended version |

For additional help, consult the GitHub [discussion forum](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions) or the [issue tracker](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues) ([SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md#L1-L15)).

---

## Installation Decision Guide

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["I need OpenMM"] --> Q1{"Building from source?"}
    
    Q1 -- "No" --> CONDA["conda install -c conda-forge openmm"]
    Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"Need GPU support?"}
    
    Q2 -- "No" --> BUILD_CPU["cmake + make<br/>(CPU + Reference only)"]
    Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3{"Which GPU?"}
    
    Q3 -- "NVIDIA" --> BUILD_CUDA["Install CUDA Toolkit<br/>+ cmake + make"]
    Q3 -- "AMD" --> BUILD_HIP["Install ROCm HIP SDK<br/>+ cmake + make"]
    Q3 -- "Other/Intel" --> BUILD_OCL["Install OpenCL SDK<br/>+ cmake + make"]
    
    CONDA --> VERIFY["python -m openmm.testInstallation"]
    BUILD_CPU --> VERIFY
    BUILD_CUDA --> VERIFY
    BUILD_HIP --> VERIFY
    BUILD_OCL --> VERIFY
    
    style VERIFY fill:#76b900,color:#fff
```

---

## Summary

OpenMM's installation is designed to be as simple as `conda install -c conda-forge openmm` for most users, with the platform architecture ensuring that the same Python code runs optimally on whatever hardware you have. The source build path exists for developers and specialized deployments, with CMake providing fine-grained control over which platforms and plugins are compiled. After installation, always run `python -m openmm.testInstallation` to confirm everything is working correctly before starting production simulations.

---

**Next Steps**: Now that OpenMM is installed and verified, continue to the [Quick Start](2-quick-start) page to run your first simulation, or explore the [Architecture Overview](7-architecture-overview) to understand how the platform system you just installed actually works under the hood.

# Latest Updates



OpenMM has had a busy spring. Between the official 8.5.0 release in March, a quick 8.5.1 patch in April, and a rapidly evolving set of post-release commits pushing toward the next feature frontier -- multistate sampling -- there is a lot to digest. This page summarizes what has shipped, what is actively being built, and what the community has been discussing.

---

## Release Timeline

```mermaid
timeline
    title OpenMM Release & Milestone Timeline (2026)
    2026-01-28 : Planning for 8.5
    2026-02-13 : 8.5 Beta
    2026-03-11 : RC candidate
    2026-03-20 : 8.5.0 Official Release
    2026-03-25 : OpenMM-ML 1.6 (PythonForce migration)
    2026-04-10 : 8.5.1 Patch Release
    2026-04-17 : ReplicaExchangeReporter (post-8.5.1 dev)
```

---

## OpenMM 8.5.0 -- What Shipped

The [8.5.0 release](https://zenodo.org/records/19136598), published on March 20, 2026, is the most feature-rich drop in recent memory. The release was preceded by a structured beta/RC cycle documented in [Discussion #5194](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5194), where maintainer Peter Eastman solicited last-minute testing -- particularly of the new GPU minimizer.

### Headline Features

| Feature | PR / Reference | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| **GPU L-BFGS Minimizer** | [PR #1237](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/1237) | Energy minimization now runs entirely on the GPU, eliminating host-device round trips. For large systems this can be dramatically faster. |
| **PythonForce** | [PR #5122](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5122) | A new Force subclass that calls back into Python to compute forces and energy. The primary motivation is **machine learning potentials** -- it unifies support for a far wider range of ML models than TorchForce alone ever could. |
| **LCPO Surface Area** | [PR #5130](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5130) | For GBSA implicit solvent, LCPO is a more accurate (but slower) approximation for the nonpolar solvation term compared to the default ACE method. |
| **Device Querying API** | [PR #5192](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5192), closes [#52](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/52) | After 13 years as an open request, you can now query available platforms and devices programmatically before creating a Context. This is a quality-of-life win for anyone running multi-GPU or HPC workflows. |
| **Next-Gen OpenFF Support** | [PR #5181](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5181) | Internal changes to support upcoming Open Force Field releases, including templates that can match whole molecules. |
| **Additional Gromacs VSite** | [PR #5155](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5155) | GromacsTopFile now supports vsite type 3fad, improving compatibility with GROMACS topology files. |

### PythonForce: The ML Gateway

PythonForce deserves special attention. Unlike TorchForce, which leverages PyTorch's autograd to back-propagate forces from energy, PythonForce requires users to return both energy and forces explicitly. As Eastman noted in the [beta discussion](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5194), it "always needs to output both forces and energy" because the returned value is a plain number, not a tensor with a computation graph.

The payoff came almost immediately: [OpenMM-ML 1.6](https://github.com/openmm/openmm-ml/releases), released March 25, migrated nearly every model backend -- MACE, AIMNet2, NequIP, TorchMD-Net, ANI, FeNNol, Orb -- to PythonForce, and added support for arbitrary [ASE Calculator](https://wiki.fysik.dtu.dk/ase/)-based models. That is a significant expansion of the ML potential ecosystem accessible from OpenMM with minimal boilerplate.

An independent [arXiv preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.18271) by Wang and Yan also describes a plugin approach to PythonForce callbacks for accelerated Python modules, underscoring that the community sees this interface as a general-purpose extensibility point.

---

## OpenMM 8.5.1 -- Patch Fixes

The [8.5.1 patch](https://zenodo.org/records/19501238), released April 10, 2026, addresses four targeted bugs discovered during beta testing and early production use:

1. **[#5236](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5236)**: A leaked variable in the template system could cause spurious constraint assignments. This was caught and fixed by contributor Jeff Wagner with an accompanying test.
2. **[#5242](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5242)**: The new GPU minimizer could lose precision during line search energy comparisons. Evan Pretti's fix ensures the energy difference is computed on the CPU before precision reduction.
3. **[#5243](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5243)**: Multiple forces could end up running concurrently on the worker thread, a subtle race condition now resolved.
4. **[#5251](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5251)**: The pressure calculation in `MonteCarloFlexibleBarostat` was incorrect and has been fixed.

---

## Post-8.5.1 Development: Multistate Sampling Takes Shape

The most significant ongoing work is the construction of a **native multistate sampling framework** directly inside OpenMM. This has been a long-standing gap -- users have relied on [openmmtools' MultistateSampler](https://openmmtools.readthedocs.io/en/stable/multistate.html) for replica exchange and SAMS, but that lives outside the core library.

### Infrastructure Layer

The first commit landed on April 2: [PR #5231](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5231) ("Infrastructure for multistate sampling") introduces a `computeRelativeEnergies()` method, allowing a single Context to evaluate the energy of a configuration across multiple thermodynamic states. This is the low-level primitive that all multistate methods will build on.

### ReplicaExchangeSampler

On April 10, [PR #5257](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5257) added `ReplicaExchangeSampler`, and on April 17, [PR #5261](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5261) followed with `ReplicaExchangeReporter`. The design discussion in [Issue #5235](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5235) lays out the key open questions:

- **What methods to include**: At minimum one parallel (replica exchange) and one serial (simulated tempering / SAMS) algorithm.
- **Customizability**: The sampler's internal methods (`simulateReplica()`, `exchangeReplicas()`) are designed to be overridable in subclasses.
- **Output and analysis**: How to partition trajectory output -- by replica or by state -- and what built-in analysis to provide.
- **Multi-context GPU scaling**: Whether to support multiple Contexts on multiple GPUs simultaneously. Eastman is currently treating this as out of scope for the initial implementation.

This is a foundational change. If OpenMM ships native replica exchange, it eliminates the dependency on openmmtools for a large class of free energy workflows and positions the toolkit as a more complete platform for enhanced sampling.

### PythonForce Subset Restriction

[PR #5246](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5246) extends PythonForce with a `setParticles()` method, allowing the force to be applied to only a subset of particles. When you are computing an ML potential for just the ligand in a large solvated system, this avoids passing irrelevant atom positions through the callback and can **greatly improve performance**. The [API documentation](https://docs.openmm.org/development/api-python/generated/openmm.openmm.PythonForce.html) now reflects this capability.

---

## Performance and Internal Improvements

Several recent commits target performance without changing the public API:

| Commit | Description | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| [e4728a2](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/e4728a2160d2f25ca108d7fddeb1dd20654e644e) (by ramdoys) | Switched `atomFlags` from `std::map` to `unordered_map` | Hash-based lookup for atom flags is faster than the red-black tree, particularly for large systems. |
| [6717a85](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/6717a85cc4255c7e3985d5cfdb022fbc9106830f) | Reduced memory used by `SerializationNode` | Serialization for checkpointing and state transfer is lighter on RAM. |
| [26df7a8](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/26df7a872512ce427bb3d7be817ebf37fe99fff7) | Cache coefficients for long-range correction | Avoids recomputing dispersion correction coefficients every step; cache is cleared on `updateParametersInContext()`. |
| [2c287f1](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/2c287f10fadd01b2a9422ab87c3d33fd92ff767d) | Fix inefficient sorting for single-atom blocks | A sorting bug affecting neighbor list construction when a block contained only one atom; fix applied to CUDA, OpenCL, and HIP backends. |
| [068495f](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/068495f3700d627319618efe9ef4ce9ed0e822d2) | Fix compilation error on some AMD GPUs | Resolved a build issue specific to certain AMD GPU architectures under the HIP platform. |

These are the kind of commits that do not make headlines but cumulatively matter. The `unordered_map` switch, for instance, is a textbook example of choosing the right data structure for the access pattern -- and it came from an external contributor.

---

## Notable Issues and Community Discussions

### Open Issues Worth Watching

**[GPU access lost in Docker containers (#5267)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5267)**: A user running long simulations with CUDA 12.2 inside Docker on an RTX 4090 reports that NVML suddenly returns "Unknown Error" after hours of operation. The process silently falls back to CPU. This is not an OpenMM bug per se -- it is a known [NVIDIA Container Toolkit issue](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-docker/issues/1730) where containers using `runc` with systemd cgroup management can abruptly lose GPU access. The workaround is to either switch Docker's cgroup driver to `cgroupfs` or run `nvidia-ctk system create-dev-char-symlinks --create-all` at boot. If you are deploying OpenMM in containers on Ubuntu 22.04 (where systemd cgroups are the default), you should proactively apply one of these mitigations.

**[DrudeSCFIntegrator regression (#5245)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5245)**: A user reports that Drude particles "fly away" -- drifting from 2.46 nm to 4.50 nm in a single step -- when using `DrudeSCFIntegrator` in OpenMM 8.2.0 and later, compared to correct behavior in 8.1.0. The test case is minimal and reproducible. The Drude integrator has had [historical energy drift issues](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/3233), but this specific regression appears to be a new bug introduced in the 8.2 timeframe.

**[GBN2 Born radii question (#5260)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5260)**: A user from Adrian Roitberg's group questions whether OpenMM uses the correct Born radii for GBN2 (mbondi3) versus OBC2 (mbondi2). Maintainer Evan Pretti points out that the XML force field files (e.g., `gbn2.xml`) should call the appropriate `_mbondi3_radii()` function, but the issue highlights that the mapping between AMBER `igb` values and OpenMM's internal handling is not always obvious to users. This connects to a [broader discussion about GB energy discrepancies](https://github.com/openmm/openmmforcefields/issues/380) between OpenMM and AMBER.

**[Missing Python 3.13 Linux wheel (#5266)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5266)**: The 8.5.1 release on PyPI is missing a `cp313` wheel for Linux (and a `cp310` wheel for mac-x64). This appears to be a build/publishing oversight rather than an intentional exclusion.

**[Replica-averaged restraint force (#5262)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5262)**: Researchers working on NMR chemical shift restraints have a [custom force](https://github.com/mercadde/openmm-napshift) based on openmm-torch that computes ensemble-average restraints across parallel replicas. The current implementation is described as "hacky" -- it requires pausing multiple simulations, accumulating shifts in Python, and passing averages back. The user is asking whether the new multistate sampling infrastructure (specifically [Issue #4018](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/4018)) will enable more efficient kernel-level communication between replicas. Eastman has acknowledged this is worth considering but has not committed to a timeline.

### Long-Standing Open Requests

Several older issues remain open and continue to attract discussion:

- **[Batch computations (#2535)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/2535)**: The ability to evaluate energies of many conformations simultaneously on a single GPU. This would be a game-changer for high-throughput screening of small molecules but raises significant architectural questions. Still open since 2020.
- **[Improved random number generator (#3716)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/3716)**: A proposal to replace Mersenne Twister (CPU) and KISS (GPU) with PCG64 DXSM for better statistical properties and speed. The [reference implementation](https://github.com/imneme/pcg-cpp) exists, but the change has not been prioritized.
- **[Memory optimization for large simulations (#4051)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/4051)**: A 1.2 million-atom simulation showed an 8 GB RAM spike during setup (unpacking state/system/integrator files) before settling to ~5 GB during runtime. For Folding@home work units, this spike limits which donor machines can accept the work.

### Recently Closed Issues of Note

- **[Midtown splines for faster PME (#5104)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5104)**: After careful analysis, Eastman [closed this as not planned](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5104#issuecomment-2773017439). The proposed 6th-order midtown splines are only C0 continuous (discontinuous forces), and their Gaussian width constraint is incompatible with OpenMM's automatic parameter selection scheme. "The C0 continuity is a dealbreaker," he concluded. A good example of the project evaluating academic proposals rigorously before committing to implementation.
- **[Device querying (#52, #5157)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5157)**: Both the original 2013 request and the 2025 follow-up are now resolved by the API shipped in 8.5.0.
- **[Constant-pH simulation (#172)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/172)**: Closed after 13 years. The discussion about implementing Mongan/Stern NCMC-based constant-pH methods has been resolved, though the details of what was merged are not documented in the closing comment.

---

## Ecosystem Context

Two external developments are worth tracking in relation to these OpenMM updates:

**NVIDIA MPS for OpenMM throughput**: A March 2026 [NVIDIA Developer Blog post](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/maximizing-openmm-molecular-dynamics-throughput-with-nvidia-multi-process-service/) demonstrates how NVIDIA Multi-Process Service can dramatically increase OpenMM throughput by running multiple simulations concurrently on a single GPU. For small systems (23K atoms like DHFR), total throughput more than doubles on an H100. This is directly relevant to the [batch computation request (#2535)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/2535) -- while OpenMM does not yet support native batching, MPS provides an external workaround that requires no code changes.

**Academic multistate methods**: The [MT-REXEE paper](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jctc.4c01268) (Friedman, Hsu, and Shirts, JCTC 2025) describes multiple topology replica exchange of expanded ensembles, implemented in GROMACS. The authors note that the method "does not necessitate modifications to the MD code." As OpenMM builds its own native multistate sampling infrastructure, supporting these kinds of advanced exchange protocols -- including multi-topology swaps -- is likely to become a point of comparison.

---

## Summary

The 8.5.x cycle represents a meaningful step forward for OpenMM. The GPU minimizer and PythonForce together modernize two of the most performance-critical and extensibility-critical parts of the stack. The multistate sampling work currently in development, if it lands well, could be the headline feature of 8.6.

The project continues to show the pattern that has kept it relevant for over a decade: a small core team (primarily Eastman, with contributions from Pretti, Wagner, and others) making conservative, well-tested API additions while rigorously evaluating academic proposals (as with midtown splines). The tension between "we need batch computation" and "that requires fundamental architectural changes" remains unresolved, but MPS and the evolving multistate infrastructure both offer partial answers from different directions.

If you are running production simulations, upgrade to 8.5.1 -- the barostat and minimizer fixes are substantive. If you are using ML potentials, install OpenMM-ML 1.6 and take advantage of the PythonForce migration. And if you are running in Docker, check your cgroup driver configuration before your next long simulation.

# Community and Support



OpenMM is, at its core, an academic project. It does not have a corporate support desk, a paid SLA, or a dedicated community manager. What it does have is a surprisingly functional support ecosystem built around GitHub, a handful of companion packages, and the collective patience of computational chemists, biophysicists, and ML researchers who depend on it. Understanding how that ecosystem works -- and where its gaps are -- will save you significant time when something goes wrong.

## Where to Get Help

The support landscape for OpenMM is more fragmented than you might expect for a project with nearly 1,900 GitHub stars. There is no single canonical help channel. Instead, help is distributed across several venues, each with different strengths and response patterns.

### GitHub Discussions (Primary Forum)

The [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions) board is the closest thing OpenMM has to an official forum. It is organized into five categories:

| Category | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **General** | Release announcements, project-level updates |
| **Q&A** | Usage questions, debugging help |
| **Ideas** | Feature proposals and design discussions |
| **Polls** | Community consensus-gathering |
| **Show and Tell** | Community projects and demos |

Discussions are further annotated with labels like `faq`, `bug`, `cookbook`, `benchmarks`, `documentation`, `enhancement`, and `machine-learning`. The Q&A category is the most active for day-to-day support. Recent threads there range from practical questions like [How to exactly reproduce a simulation?](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5263) to migration concerns like [OpenMM alternative equivalent files for Amber prmtop files?](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5264).

Peter Eastman, the project's primary maintainer, is a consistent presence in these threads. He posts release announcements (e.g., [OpenMM 8.5.1](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5260) in April 2026) and frequently answers technical questions directly. However, many Q&A threads remain unanswered, particularly those involving edge cases in ML potential integration or niche platform issues. The signal-to-noise ratio is decent, but do not expect Stack Overflow levels of turnaround.

### GitHub Issues (Bug Reports and Feature Requests)

If you have a reproducible bug, the [issue tracker](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues) is the right place. The repository currently tracks 395 open issues and 19 open pull requests. A significant portion of open issues are long-lived feature requests that serve as design discussions rather than actionable tickets. A few notable examples:

- [Batch computations (#2535)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/2535) -- opened in January 2020, still open. This is a feature request for evaluating energies of many conformations in parallel on a single GPU, which would dramatically improve throughput for small systems.
- [Improved random number generator (#3716)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/3716) -- opened in July 2022, proposing a move from Mersenne Twister and KISS to PCG64 DXSM.
- [Ways to optimize memory usage for large simulations? (#4051)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/4051) -- a community discussion started after a user ran a 1.2 million atom simulation.

The issue tracker also houses active bug reports. For example, a user reported that `DrudeSCFIntegrator` produces flying Drude particles in OpenMM 8.2.0 and later ([#5245](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5245)), with a clear minimal reproduction script. These targeted, well-documented reports tend to get attention faster than vague feature requests.

### Bi-Monthly Community Meetings

The OpenMM team holds periodic community meetings that influence the project roadmap. Evidence of these shows up in issue discussions where maintainers reference decisions made in meetings. For instance, in the [Classes for multistate sampling (#5235)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5235) design discussion, Peter Eastman writes: "This came up in a meeting, that you should be able to extend the sampling classes and override methods to customize them." Similarly, the [device querying (#5157)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5157) discussion references a meeting where the team acknowledged that device-querying utilities already exist in OpenMM's internals and could be wrapped into public APIs.

These meetings are not heavily advertised outside GitHub, which is a missed opportunity. If you are doing serious work with OpenMM -- particularly if you are building tools on top of it -- tracking the General discussions and release-planning threads (e.g., [Planning for 8.5 release](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5248)) is the best way to stay informed.

### External Communities

OpenMM questions also surface on external platforms, though these are not officially maintained by the project:

- **Matter Modeling Stack Exchange** -- The `openmm` tag on [Matter Modeling SE](https://mattermodeling.stackexchange.com/questions/tagged/openmm) hosts conceptual questions about the toolkit, such as [What exactly is an integrator?](https://mattermodeling.stackexchange.com/questions/13963/what-exactly-is-an-integrator). These tend to be educational rather than debugging-focused.
- **PLUMED Users (Google Groups)** -- The [PLUMED community](https://groups.google.com/g/plumed-users) occasionally discusses OpenMM in the context of enhanced sampling plugins and interoperability.
- **Biophysical research labs** -- Many labs maintain their own internal documentation. The [Chodera Lab](https://www.choderalab.org/publications/tag/OpenMM) at MSKCC, for example, is a major contributor to both OpenMM and its ecosystem packages.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[You have a question] --> B{What kind?}
    B -->|How do I use X?| C[GitHub Discussions Q&A]
    B -->|I found a bug| D[GitHub Issues]
    B -->|I want feature X| E[GitHub Discussions Ideas]
    B -->|Conceptual / educational| F[Matter Modeling SE]
    B -->|Plugin-specific| G[Plugin repo issues]
    C --> H{Answered?}
    D --> I{Reproducible?}
    H -->|No| J[Stack Overflow]
    H -->|Yes| K[Done]
    I -->|Yes| L[Attach script + env info]
    I -->|No| M[Debug first, then file]
    L --> N[Maintainer triages]
```

## Documentation and Learning Resources

Before asking for help, you should consult the official documentation. OpenMM's docs are thorough but have a reputation for being dense.

| Resource | URL | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| User Guide | [docs.openmm.org/latest/userguide](https://docs.openmm.org/latest/userguide/introduction.html) | Three parts: application layer, library API, mathematical theory |
| Python API | [docs.openmm.org/latest/api-python](https://docs.openmm.org/latest/api-python/) | Complete class reference |
| C++ API | [docs.openmm.org/latest/api-c++](https://docs.openmm.org/latest/api-c++) | For plugin and platform developers |
| FAQ | [openmm.org/faq](https://openmm.org) | Linked from the User Guide introduction |
| GitHub Examples | [github.com/openmm/openmm/tree/master/examples](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/tree/master/examples) | Runnable Python scripts |
| Cookbook | [openmm.github.io/openmm-cookbook](https://openmm.github.io/openmm-cookbook/) | Community-contributed Jupyter notebooks |

### The OpenMM Cookbook

The [OpenMM Cookbook](https://github.com/openmm/openmm-cookbook) is a separate repository that hosts Jupyter notebook tutorials and recipes. It is rendered at `openmm.github.io/openmm-cookbook` and provides practical, copy-pasteable examples. Each notebook can be opened directly in Google Colab with dependencies auto-installed. The cookbook has its own CI pipeline that tests notebooks against both the latest release and nightly development builds of OpenMM.

If you are transitioning from another MD engine, the cookbook is often more immediately useful than the API reference. Discussions labeled `cookbook` on GitHub track candidate recipes that could be added.

## The Plugin Ecosystem

OpenMM's architecture is designed for extensibility through a [plugin system](https://github.com/openmm/openmmexampleplugin). This has spawned a rich ecosystem of companion packages, many of which have their own support channels.

### OpenMMTools

[OpenMMTools](https://github.com/choderalab/openmmtools) (319 stars, 86 forks) is the most important companion package. Developed primarily by the Chodera Lab, it provides:

- High-quality Langevin integrators (g-BAOAB, VVVR, and other splittings)
- Nonequilibrium integrators for free energy calculations (NCMC)
- An MCMC framework for mixing Monte Carlo and MD-based methods
- Enhanced sampling methods including replica exchange and SAMS
- Alchemical factories for absolute and relative free energy calculations
- A suite of test systems for benchmarking

Its documentation is at [openmmtools.readthedocs.io](https://openmmtools.readthedocs.io). The package is under active development (most recent release 0.26.0 in January 2026) and has its own [232 open issues](https://github.com/choderalab/openmmtools/issues). If you are working with replica exchange or free energy methods, you will almost certainly end up here.

### OpenMM-ML

[OpenMM-ML](https://github.com/openmm/openmm-ml) provides the `MLPotential` class for running machine learning potentials (NequIP, MACE, etc.) within OpenMM's simulation framework. Peter Eastman announces OpenMM-ML releases on GitHub Discussions (e.g., [OpenMM-ML 1.6](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5255) in March 2026). Compatibility issues between OpenMM-ML and specific ML architectures are a recurring source of community questions, such as [Current OpenMM seems to be incompatible with latest NequIP](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/discussions/5249).

### Other Notable Ecosystem Packages

| Package | Purpose | Link |
|---|---|---|
| **openmmforcefields** | Small molecule parameterization (GAFF, SMIRNOFF/OpenFF, espaloma) | [conda-forge](https://conda-forge.org/) |
| **OpenSMOG** | Coarse-grained structure-based models via SMOG 2 | [smog-server.org](https://smog-server.org/smog2/OpenSMOG) |
| **openmm-torch** | PyTorch-based custom forces for NMR restraints and similar | [github.com/openmm/openmm-torch](https://github.com/openmm/openmm-torch) |
| **OpenMMDL** | Streamlined setup/analysis of protein-ligand MD simulations | [github.com/wolberlab/OpenMMDL](https://github.com/wolberlab/OpenMMDL) |
| **Folding@home** | Distributed computing integration (uses OpenMM as its simulation engine) | [foldingathome.org](https://foldingathome.org/) |

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Core
        O[OpenMM Core]
    end
    
    subgraph Official Plugins
        A[Amoeba Plugin]
        D[Drude Plugin]
        R[RPMD Plugin]
    end
    
    subgraph Community Packages
        T[OpenMMTools]
        ML[OpenMM-ML]
        FF[openmmforcefields]

    end

    O --> R
```
