```mermaid
    O --> FF
    O --> SM
    O --> FAH
    
    T -.->|Enhanced Sampling| O
    ML -.->|ML Potentials| O
    FF -.->|Parameterization| O
```

## How to Report a Bug Effectively

If you are going to file an issue, do it right. The maintainers are academics with limited time, and a well-structured report dramatically increases your chances of getting a fix. Based on patterns in the issue tracker, here is what separates reports that get addressed from those that languish:

**Do:**

1. Specify your OpenMM version, Python version, and platform (CUDA/OpenCL/CPU, driver version, OS).
2. Provide a minimal, self-contained reproduction script. The [DrudeSCFIntegrator bug report (#5245)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5245) is a textbook example: a 50-line script that anyone can run.
3. Include the full stack trace and any error messages.
4. Check if the issue has been reported before. Search both open and closed issues.

**Do not:**

1. File a bug that is really a usage question. Use Discussions Q&A instead.
2. Report a bug against an old version without first testing on the latest release.
3. Bundle multiple unrelated issues into a single report.
4. Omit your environment details and expect maintainers to guess.

For reference, look at how the [GPU access lost in Docker containers (#5267)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5267) issue was filed: it specifies the OpenMM version (8.2), CUDA version (12.2), NVIDIA Container Runtime version (1.17.4), GPU model (RTX 4090), and provides a clear description of the failure mode. This is the standard.

## Contributing to OpenMM

If you want to give back rather than just take, the project has a clear contribution pathway documented in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md). The repository also maintains a [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) (added in September 2020 via [PR #2833](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/2833)).

Contribution opportunities range from documentation fixes (the recent [Update patch documentation (#5208)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/pull/5208) by Yulian Manchev is a good example) to core feature implementation. The [device querying (#5157)](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5157) discussion explicitly noted that utility functions already exist in OpenMM internals and just need to be wrapped into public APIs -- a relatively low-effort contribution.

For plugin development, the [openmmexampleplugin](https://github.com/openmm/openmmexampleplugin) repository provides a comprehensive template with implementations for Reference, OpenCL, and CUDA platforms, serialization support, test cases, and a Python API via SWIG.

## Citing OpenMM

OpenMM depends on academic research grants for funding. If you use it in your work, cite the [OpenMM 8 paper](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcb.3c07692):

> P. Eastman, R. Galvelis, R. P. Pelaez, C. R. A. Abreu, S. E. Farr, E. Gallicchio, A. Gorenko, M. M. Henry, F. Hu, J. Huang, A. Kramer, J. Michel, J. A. Mitchell, V. S. Pande, J. PGLM Rodrigues, J. Rodriguez-Guerra, A. C. Simmonett, S. Singh, J. Swails, P. Turner, Y. Wang, I. Zhang, J. D. Chodera, G. De Fabritiis, and T. E. Markland. "OpenMM 8: Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Machine Learning Potentials." J. Phys. Chem. B 128(1), pp. 109-116 (2023).

Citations are not just an academic courtesy -- they are the mechanism by which the project justifies continued funding. This is worth remembering.

## The Honest Assessment

OpenMM's community support works, but it works because of a small number of highly active individuals rather than a broad base of contributors. Peter Eastman carries a disproportionate share of the maintenance burden. The GitHub Discussions board has improved the situation compared to the old SimTK forums, but response times are inconsistent, and many questions go unanswered. The plugin ecosystem is strong -- OpenMMTools, OpenMM-ML, and openmmforcefields fill real gaps -- but fragmentation means that users often do not know which package to file issues against.

The project would benefit from more visible contribution guidelines for non-core developers, better indexing of answered questions (a curated FAQ pulled from the best Discussions threads would be invaluable), and more proactive communication about the bi-monthly community meetings. If you are a heavy user, the single best thing you can do is answer one question in Discussions for every question you ask.

# About Contributors



OpenMM is not just a toolkit -- it is one of the most foundational pieces of infrastructure in computational molecular biology. With over 7,300 commits, 1.9k stars on GitHub, and a deployment scale that peaked at an estimated 280,000 GPUs during the COVID-19 pandemic via Folding@home, the project owes its longevity and reach to a relatively small but extraordinarily dedicated group of contributors. Some have been with the project since its Stanford origins; others bring expertise from industry, national labs, and competing simulation packages.

What follows is a look at the people behind the code.

---

## Peter Eastman -- The Architect

If OpenMM has a single identifiable author, it is [Peter Eastman](https://github.com/peastman). He is the original creator of the library, having built it at the Vijay S. Pande lab at Stanford University, and he remains the most prolific contributor by a wide margin. A glance at the commit log tells the story: across the last several months alone, Peter authored or merged the majority of commits touching core simulation features -- from [ReplicaExchangeSampler](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/efd891695c7e242a92bc793cc429f82ac8f14bcd) and [ReplicaExchangeReporter](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/46376ea3e4d0ff37cdaa5e55e034dbf5c3296b81) to low-level fixes for [memory usage in SerializationNode](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/6717a85cc4255c7e3985d5cfdb022fbc9106830f), [inefficient sorting in single-atom blocks](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/2c287f10fadd01b2a9422ab87c3d33fd92ff767d), and [worker thread scheduling](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/5d8d5874b9692f02a3547fbf96efd18126f949bb).

Peter's background is unusual for a molecular dynamics developer. He spent seven years writing commercial bioinformatics software at Agilent Technologies and Silicon Genetics before returning to academia, earning his Ph.D. at Stanford with a focus on algorithms for protein MD simulations. As his [Simbios profile](http://simbios.stanford.edu/Bios/eastman.htm) notes, his passion lies in "designing elegant APIs and creating tools that help people to solve problems." This design-first philosophy is visible throughout OpenMM: the clean separation of the platform abstraction layer, the modularity of the force and integrator hierarchies, and the thoughtful Python wrappers all bear his fingerprints.

Beyond OpenMM itself, Peter is also the primary author of [Lepton](https://github.com/openmm/lepton), the mathematical expression parser that powers OpenMM's CustomIntegrator and CustomForce, and he has contributed to the broader SimTK ecosystem including [Simbody](https://github.com/simbody/simbody) and [PDBFixer](https://github.com/openmm/pdbfixer). He has co-authored landmark publications including [OpenMM 7](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005659) and [OpenMM 8](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcb.3c08559), and he curates the [SPICE dataset](https://github.com/openmm/spice-dataset) for training machine learning potentials.

Peter is affiliated with Stanford University and is a member of 26 projects on the SimTK platform, with over 2,600 forum posts spanning nearly two decades.

---

## John D. Chodera -- The Scientific Catalyst

[John Chodera](https://github.com/jchodera) is a computational chemist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and one of the most influential voices in the OpenMM ecosystem. He is a co-author on every major OpenMM publication -- from [OpenMM 4 (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1021/ct3008574) through [OpenMM 8 (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcb.3c08559) -- and his lab at MSKCC has been instrumental in pushing OpenMM into new scientific domains.

Chodera's contributions extend well beyond code commits. He is the driving force behind the [Open Force Field Initiative](https://openforcefield.org/), which uses OpenMM as its primary simulation engine, and the [openmmforcefields](https://github.com/openmm/openmmforcefields) repository. His group maintains [OpenMMTools](https://github.com/choderalab/openmmtools), a widely used library of utilities for replica exchange, free energy calculations, and enhanced sampling that fills gaps in the core API.

He is also a regular presence in OpenMM's issue tracker, frequently CC'd on [design discussions](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/issues/5235) about multistate sampling, replica exchange infrastructure, and machine learning potential integration. His 2021 Nature Chemistry paper on SARS-CoV-2 simulations -- which relied on OpenMM via Folding@home -- remains one of the most high-profile validations of the toolkit's scalability.

---

## Anton Gorenko -- The Platform Builder

The introduction of AMD GPU support in OpenMM 8.2.0 was one of the most significant architectural changes in years, and it was largely the work of [Anton Gorenko](https://github.com/agorenko), a developer at [StreamHPC](https://streamcomputing.eu/). The [8.2.0 release notes](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/releases/tag/8.2.0) explicitly acknowledge this: "Many thanks to Anton Gorenko for his amazing work on this!"

The HIP platform that Anton built delivers roughly double the performance of the OpenCL platform on recent AMD GPUs, bringing OpenMM to a hardware ecosystem that had previously been a pain point for researchers without NVIDIA hardware. This was not a trivial port -- it required deep familiarity with AMD's HIP framework, careful kernel optimization, and extensive testing across different GPU architectures. The [fix for compilation errors on certain AMD GPUs](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/068495f3700d627319618efe9ef4ce9ed0e822d2) that Peter merged shortly afterward underscores the ongoing complexity of supporting a second vendor.

---

## Evan Pretti -- The Precision-Minded Contributor

[Evan Pretti](https://github.com/epretti) is a researcher affiliated with the Shell research group in the Department of Chemical Engineering at UC Santa Barbara. His most recent contribution to the core repository is a [precision fix in the energy minimizer](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/1c528ca8429ce38d7e6d16989162085ff669de88) that takes line search energy differences on the CPU before reducing precision -- the sort of subtle numerical fix that prevents silent accuracy degradation.

Evan has a broader interest in replica exchange and parallel simulation methodologies. He independently developed [MultiOpenMM](https://github.com/epretti/multiopenmm), a package for running parallel molecular dynamics simulations (including replica exchange) within a single OpenMM context, which can dramatically improve GPU utilization when simulating many small replicas. He has also built tools for crystal free energy calculations ([PyPhase](https://evan.pretti.net/software.html)) and colloidal crystal structure analysis (_paccs_), with support from the Molecular Sciences Software Institute (MolSSI).

[Jeff Wagner](https://github.com/jwagner) is associated with the [Open Force Field Consortium](https://openforcefield.org/) and has contributed both to the core OpenMM repository and to the openmmforcefields package. His most recent core contribution is a [fix for a leaked variable causing spurious template constraint assignment](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/13c568d08d5a9829a6de621e94cdaebd014f4f7d) (#5236), which was significant enough to be included in the [8.5.1 patch release](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/releases).

Jeff's work on openmmforcefields -- including converting Amber ion parameters and supporting SMIRNOFF-based force fields -- directly benefits the community of researchers using OpenMM for drug design and biomolecular simulation.

## Yulian Manchev -- The Documentation Contributor

[Yulian Manchev](https://github.com/ymanchev) made a focused but important contribution by [updating the patch documentation](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/bc6fe72928817f33edfbec3150e40bcfc636c2c7) (#5208), clarifying the definition and purpose of patches in the force field XML format. Documentation improvements like this might seem minor, but they directly reduce the barrier for users trying to understand how OpenMM's force field system works -- a common pain point for newcomers.

Yulian's research background is in molecular simulation using machine learning potentials. He has published work on [FFLUX molecular simulations driven by atomic Gaussian process regression models](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.27323), connecting him to the broader wave of ML/MM hybrid approaches that OpenMM 8 was designed to support.

## ramdoys -- The Performance Optimizer

The contributor known as [ramdoys](https://github.com/ramdoys) made a targeted performance improvement by [switching atomFlags to an unordered_map](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/e4728a2160d2f25ca108d7fddeb1dd20654e644e) (#5247), reducing the allocation overhead and improving lookup performance. This is the kind of data-structure-level optimization that requires familiarity with the hot paths in the codebase and a willingness to profile before proposing changes.

## How OpenMM's Contribution Model Works

The project's contribution model, described in its [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md), is intentionally lightweight:

1. **Open an issue first.** For bug fixes, the core developers confirm the behavior. For new features, the community discusses design before code is written.
2. **Submit a pull request.** For larger features, work-in-progress PRs prefixed with "WIP" are encouraged for early feedback.
3. **Automated testing.** The full test suite runs on every PR and reruns on every push to the branch.
4. **Review and merge.** Core developers review code quality, test coverage, serialization support, and API consistency before merging.

The [New Feature Checklist](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) mandates documentation, tests, serialization support, and compatibility across all API layers (C++, Python wrappers) for any significant addition. This is a demanding bar, but it is part of the reason OpenMM has maintained backwards compatibility across major version transitions.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["Contributor opens<br>issue/discussion"] --> B["Core team reviews<br>and provides feedback"]
    B --> C["Contributor submits<br>pull request"]
    C --> D["Automated test suite<br>runs on CI"]
    D --> E{"Tests pass?"}
    E -->|No| C
    E -->|Yes| F["Core developers<br>review code"]
    F --> G{"Approved?"}
    G -->|Requested changes| C
    G -->|Yes| H["Merged to master"]
```

---

## What This Means for You as a Developer

If you are considering contributing to OpenMM, a few things are worth knowing:

**The codebase is deep.** OpenMM spans C++ core libraries, CUDA and OpenCL kernel implementations, a HIP platform, Python wrappers via SWIG, serialization infrastructure, plugin architectures, and documentation. The surface area is enormous, but the modularity means you can contribute meaningfully to a single layer without understanding the whole system.

**The maintainer is responsive but stretched thin.** Peter Eastman reviews essentially every PR and issue. The recent commit cadence -- multiple substantive merges per week -- reflects a high level of engagement, but it also means that PRs requiring deep architectural review may take time.

**Performance contributions are especially valued.** Recent merges like the [unordered_map optimization](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/e4728a2160d2f25ca108d7fddeb1dd20654e644e), [long-range correction caching](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/26df7a872512ce427bb3d7be817ebf37fe99fff7), and [serialization memory reduction](https://github.com/openmm/openmm/commit/6717a85cc4255c7e3985d5cfdb022fbc9106830f) show that even incremental optimizations are welcomed and merged promptly.

**The project has outsized impact.** During the COVID-19 pandemic, a [Nature Chemistry paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-021-00707-0) described how an estimated 280,000 GPUs were running OpenMM via Folding@home to simulate SARS-CoV-2 proteins. Your contribution, however small, ships to that scale.

# Architecture Overview



OpenMM is a high-performance molecular dynamics simulation toolkit whose architecture separates the **declaration of what to simulate** from the **decision of how to simulate it**. This decoupling is the single most important design principle in the codebase: users define physical systems through a platform-agnostic public API, while the execution engine transparently dispatches computations to whatever hardware backend is available — CUDA GPUs, OpenCL devices, HIP accelerators, SIMD-optimized CPUs, or a portable reference implementation. The entire system is structured around a factory-driven kernel abstraction that makes this possible.

## Top-Level Layer Model

The repository organizes code into six principal layers, each with a distinct responsibility in the simulation pipeline. Understanding these layers is the prerequisite for navigating any part of the codebase effectively.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph PythonLayer["Python Application Layer"]
        SW["wrappers/python/"]
        APP["openmm.app (Simulation, Modeller, ForceField)"]
    end

    subgraph CoreAPI["Core C++ API"]
        SYS["openmmapi/include/openmm/<br/>System, Context, Force, Integrator"]
        IMPL["openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/<br/>ContextImpl, ForceImpl"]
    end

    subgraph KernelAbstraction["Kernel Abstraction Layer (olla)"]
        PLAT["Platform.h"]
        KERN["Kernel / KernelImpl"]
        KFACT["KernelFactory.h"]
        KNAMES["kernels.h (40+ kernel interfaces)"]
    end

    subgraph Platforms["Platform Implementations"]
        REF["Reference"]
        CPU["CPU (SSE/AVX/AVX2)"]
        CUDA["CUDA"]
        HIP["HIP/ROCm"]
        OCL["OpenCL"]
    end

    subgraph SharedCode["Shared Platform Code"]
        COM["platforms/common/<br/>ComputeContext, BondedUtilities<br/>CommonKernels, ExpressionUtilities"]
    end

    subgraph Plugins["Plugin Ecosystem"]
        AMOEBA["Amoeba (polarizable FF)"]
        DRUDE["Drude (Drude particles)"]
        RPMD["RPMD (path integrals)"]
    end

    APP --> SYS
    SW --> SYS
    SYS --> IMPL
    IMPL --> PLAT
    PLAT --> KFACT
    PLAT --> KERN
    KNAMES -.->|kernel interfaces| KERN
    REF --> KNAMES
    CPU --> COM
    CUDA --> COM
    HIP --> COM
    OCL --> COM
    AMOEBA --> PLAT
    DRUDE --> PLAT
    RPMD --> PLAT

    style PythonLayer fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2980b9
    style CoreAPI fill:#fef9e7,stroke:#f39c12
    style KernelAbstraction fill:#fdedec,stroke:#e74c3c
    style Platforms fill:#eafaf1,stroke:#27ae60
    style SharedCode fill:#f4ecf7,stroke:#8e44ad
    style Plugins fill:#fdf2e9,stroke:#e67e22
```

Each layer maps to a top-level directory in the repository. The `openmmapi/` directory contains the user-facing C++ API classes. The `olla/` directory (the name is a nod to the molecular dynamics library OLLA) defines the platform and kernel abstraction machinery. The `platforms/` directory holds every hardware-specific backend. The `wrappers/` directory provides Python bindings generated via SWIG. Plugins reside in `plugins/`, and `serialization/` handles XML-based state persistence.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt), [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h), [Kernel.h](olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h)

## The Platform and Kernel Abstraction

The central architectural innovation of OpenMM is the **Platform-Kernel-Factory** pattern, defined entirely within the `olla/` layer. This pattern ensures that simulation logic never contains hardware-specific code — instead, every computable operation is declared as an abstract "kernel," and each platform provides its own concrete implementation via factories.

### Core Abstraction Classes

The abstraction is built on four classes defined in `olla/include/openmm/`:

| Class | Header | Role |
|-------|--------|------|
| **Platform** | [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L64-L297) | Static registry of all available platforms; factory for creating `Kernel` objects; provides platform-specific properties (device selection, precision mode, etc.) |
| **Kernel** | [Kernel.h](olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h#L44-L107) | Opaque handle wrapping a `KernelImpl*`; provides type-safe access via `getAs<T>()` template method |
| **KernelImpl** | [KernelImpl.h](olla/include/openmm/KernelImpl.h#L43-L76) | Abstract base for platform-specific computation; subclasses define concrete `execute()` or equivalent APIs |
| **KernelFactory** | [KernelFactory.h](olla/include/openmm/KernelFactory.h#L42-L59) | Abstract factory with a single `createKernelImpl()` method; each Platform registers factories keyed by kernel name |

The lifecycle flows as follows: when a `Context` is constructed, it queries `Platform::findPlatform()` with the set of kernel names required by the user's `System` and `Integrator`. The platform with the highest `getSpeed()` rating that supports all required kernels is selected. That platform then creates `Kernel` objects on demand, each wrapping a platform-specific `KernelImpl` produced by a registered `KernelFactory`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Context as Context / ContextImpl
    participant Platform
    participant Factory as KernelFactory
    participant Kernel
    participant Impl as "KernelImpl (Platform-Specific)"

    User->>Context: new Context(system, integrator)
    Context->>Platform: findPlatform(kernelNames)
    Platform-->>Context: fastest matching Platform
    Note over Context: For each Force & Integrator
    Context->>Platform: createKernel("CalcNonbondedForce", context)
    Platform->>Factory: createKernelImpl("CalcNonbondedForce", platform, context)
    Factory-->>Platform: new CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel(...)
    Platform-->>Context: Kernel(wrapping impl)
    User->>Integrator: step(1000)
    Integrator->>Kernel: "getAs<CalcNonbondedForceKernel>().execute(...)"
    Kernel->>Impl: execute(context, includeForces, includeEnergy)
    Impl-->>Kernel: energy value
```

### The Kernel Catalog

The file [kernels.h](olla/include/openmm/kernels.h) defines over **40 distinct kernel interfaces**, each as an abstract class inheriting from `KernelImpl`. Every kernel has a static `Name()` method returning its string identifier. These kernels fall into several categories:

| Category | Example Kernels | Purpose |
|----------|----------------|---------|
| **Orchestration** | `CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel`, `UpdateStateDataKernel` | Begin/finish force computation; get/set positions, velocities, time |
| **Constraints** | `ApplyConstraintsKernel`, `VirtualSitesKernel` | Enforce distance constraints (SETTLE, SHAKE, CCMA) |
| **Bonded Forces** | `CalcHarmonicBondForceKernel`, `CalcHarmonicAngleForceKernel`, `CalcPeriodicTorsionForceKernel` | Standard bonded interactions |
| **Nonbonded Forces** | `CalcNonbondedForceKernel`, `CalcCustomNonbondedForceKernel`, `CalcGBSAOBCForceKernel` | Electrostatics, van der Waals, implicit solvent |
| **Special Forces** | `CalcGayBerneForceKernel`, `CalcCustomManyParticleForceKernel`, `CalcATMForceKernel` | Anisotropic potentials, N-body custom forces, alchemical free energy |
| **Integrators** | `IntegrateVerletStepKernel`, `IntegrateLangevinMiddleStepKernel`, `IntegrateCustomStepKernel` | Time-stepping algorithms |
| **Thermostats/Barostats** | `ApplyAndersenThermostatKernel`, `ApplyMonteCarloBarostatKernel`, `RemoveCMMotionKernel` | Temperature/pressure control |
| **Energy Minimization** | `MinimizeKernel` | L-BFGS minimization |

Each platform registers factories for the subset of kernels it supports. The Reference platform registers all of them; the CPU platform registers a performance-critical subset; GPU platforms register the most expensive kernels (nonbonded, PME) while sometimes delegating simpler operations to shared code.

Sources: [kernels.h](olla/include/openmm/kernels.h#L57-L120), [kernels.h](olla/include/openmm/kernels.h#L200-L400)

## The Core API Layer

The `openmmapi/` directory defines the public API that all users interact with, regardless of programming language. This layer is responsible for two things: **declaring the physical system** and **mediating between the user's description and the kernel abstraction**.

### The Four Pillars: System, Force, Integrator, Context

**System** ([System.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/System.h#L46-L200)) is a pure data container. It holds the number of particles and their masses, a list of `Force` objects, a list of distance constraints, periodic box dimensions, and optional virtual site definitions. It contains absolutely no computation logic — it is a declarative description of the molecular system.

**Force** ([Force.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Force.h#L41-L126)) is the abstract base class for all interactions. Each subclass (e.g., `NonbondedForce`, `HarmonicBondForce`, `CustomGBForce`) defines methods for adding interaction parameters. Crucially, `Force` also defines a protected `createImpl()` method that returns a `ForceImpl` — this is the bridge to the kernel layer. Forces support **force groups** (32 bit-flags from 0–31) enabling multiple-time-step integration strategies, and they declare whether they use periodic boundary conditions.

**Integrator** ([Integrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Integrator.h#L44-L201)) is the abstract base for time-stepping algorithms. Its public API is minimal: `step(int steps)`, `getStepSize()`, `setStepSize()`. Internally, it defines `getKernelNames()` (returning the integrator kernels it needs), `initialize(ContextImpl&)`, and `computeKineticEnergy()`. Each concrete integrator (`VerletIntegrator`, `LangevinMiddleIntegrator`, `CustomIntegrator`, etc.) binds to its platform-specific kernel at Context creation time.

**Context** ([Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L51-L200)) is the central object that brings everything together. It stores the complete simulation state (time, positions, velocities, parameters), owns a reference to the Platform, and delegates all computation to `ContextImpl`. Users interact with the simulation exclusively through Context: calling `getState()` to retrieve snapshots, `setPositions()` to modify coordinates, or `setParameter()` to adjust global variables.

### The Internal Implementation Bridge

The `openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/` directory contains the **implementation classes** that translate public API calls into kernel invocations. The two most important are:

- **ContextImpl** ([ContextImpl.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h#L43-L200)): The non-public counterpart to `Context`. It holds references to the Platform, all `ForceImpl` objects, and the bound `Integrator`. It orchestrates the per-timestep loop: call `updateContextState()` on each ForceImpl, call `beginComputation()` on the orchestration kernel, call `calcForcesAndEnergy()` on each ForceImpl, call `finishComputation()`, then invoke the integrator kernel's step function.

- **ForceImpl** ([ForceImpl.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ForceImpl.h#L44-L131)): The internal counterpart to each `Force` subclass. Created by `Force::createImpl()` when a Context is constructed, each ForceImpl caches force parameters in a format efficient for the target platform, creates its required kernels, and provides `calcForcesAndEnergy()` for per-force computation. It also provides `updateContextState()` for forces that modify simulation state (like barostats).

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class System {
        +addParticle(mass) int
        +addForce(Force*) int
        +addConstraint(p1, p2, distance) int
        +getNumParticles() int
        +getForce(index) Force
    }

    class Force {
        <<abstract>>
        #createImpl() ForceImpl*
        +setForceGroup(group)
        +usesPeriodicBoundaryConditions() bool
    }

    class Integrator {
        <<abstract>>
        +step(steps)
        +getStepSize() double
        #getKernelNames() vector~string~
        #initialize(ContextImpl&)
        #computeKineticEnergy() double
    }

    class Context {
        +getState(types) State
        +setPositions(positions)
        +setParameter(name, value)
        +getPlatform() Platform
    }

    class ContextImpl {
        -forceImpls: vector~ForceImpl*~
        -platform: Platform*
        +calcForcesAndEnergy()
        +updateContextState()
    }

    class ForceImpl {
        <<abstract>>
        +initialize(ContextImpl&)
        +calcForcesAndEnergy() double
        +updateContextState()
        +getKernelNames() vector~string~
    }

    class Platform {
        +createKernel(name, context) Kernel
        +findPlatform(kernelNames) Platform&
        +registerKernelFactory(name, factory)
        +getSpeed() double
    }

    class Kernel {
        +getAs~T~() T&
        +getName() string
    }

    System "1" *-- "*" Force
    Context "1" o-- "1" System
    Context "1" o-- "1" Integrator
    Context "1" *-- "1" ContextImpl
    Force ..> ForceImpl : creates via createImpl()
    ContextImpl "1" o-- "*" ForceImpl
    ContextImpl "1" o-- "1" Platform
    Platform "1" o-- "*" Kernel
```

Sources: [System.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/System.h#L46-L200), [Force.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Force.h#L41-L126), [Integrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Integrator.h#L44-L201), [Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L51-L200), [ContextImpl.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h#L43-L200), [ForceImpl.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ForceImpl.h#L44-L131)

## Platform Implementations

Each directory under `platforms/` provides a complete backend that registers itself as a `Platform` subclass and implements the kernel interfaces for its target hardware. The structure is highly regular: every platform contains a `*Platform.cpp` (registration and property management), a `*KernelFactory.cpp` (kernel instantiation), and a `*Kernels.cpp` (concrete kernel implementations).

### Platform Comparison

| Platform | Directory | Hardware | Speed Rating | Key Properties | Kernel Coverage |
|----------|-----------|----------|-------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Reference** | `platforms/reference/` | Any CPU (portable C++) | 1.0 | `Threads` | Full (all 40+ kernels) |
| **CPU** | `platforms/cpu/` | x86 with SSE4.1/AVX/AVX2 | ~10–100 | `CpuThreads`, `CpuDeterministicForces` | Subset: nonbonded, GBSA, Langevin, custom forces |
| **CUDA** | `platforms/cuda/` | NVIDIA GPUs | ~100–1000 | `DeviceIndex`, `DeviceName`, `Precision`, `UseBlockingSync`, `TempDirectory`, `DisablePmeStream`, `DeterministicForces`, `UseCpuPme` | Full (most comprehensive GPU platform) |
| **OpenCL** | `platforms/opencl/` | GPUs, CPUs via OpenCL | ~50–500 | `OpenCLDeviceIndex`, `OpenCLPlatformIndex`, `Precision` | Full |
| **HIP** | `platforms/hip/` | AMD GPUs via ROCm | ~100–1000 | `HipDeviceIndex`, `HipPrecision`, `HipUseBlockingSync` | Full |

The **Reference platform** ([ReferencePlatform.cpp](platforms/reference/src/ReferencePlatform.cpp#L43-L100)) is pedagogically important: it registers every single kernel against a single `ReferenceKernelFactory`, which dispatches all kernel creation to `ReferenceKernels.cpp`. This makes it the most readable entry point for understanding how any kernel works.

The **CPU platform** ([CpuPlatform.cpp](platforms/cpu/src/CpuPlatform.cpp#L43-L80)) exploits SIMD vectorization. It conditionally compiles different kernel variants for SSE, AVX, and AVX2 instruction sets (visible in files like `CpuNonbondedForceAvx.cpp`, `CpuNonbondedForceAvx2.cpp`). It deliberately omits some kernels it cannot accelerate, relying on the Reference platform as a fallback for those operations.

The **CUDA platform** ([CudaPlatform.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp#L43-L80)) provides the highest performance for NVIDIA hardware. It supports configurable precision modes (single, mixed, double), device selection by index or name, and options for PME stream control and temporary directory placement.

### The Common Platform Layer

The `platforms/common/` directory contains code shared across GPU platforms (CUDA, OpenCL, HIP). This is a significant architectural choice: rather than duplicating algorithm logic across three GPU backends, the common layer implements the **algorithms** in a hardware-agnostic way while each GPU platform provides the **primitive operations** (memory allocation, kernel launches, FFT).

Key shared components include:

- **ComputeContext** — abstract base for GPU resource management; each GPU platform subclasses it
- **BondedUtilities** — bonded force calculation helpers
- **CommonCalcNonbondedForce** — shared nonbonded force logic with cutoff and PME support
- **ExpressionUtilities** — Lepton expression compilation for custom forces
- **IntegrationUtilities** — shared integration helpers
- **kernels/** — GPU kernel source templates (`.cu` and `.cl` variants)

Sources: [ReferencePlatform.cpp](platforms/reference/src/ReferencePlatform.cpp#L43-L100), [CpuPlatform.cpp](platforms/cpu/src/CpuPlatform.cpp#L43-L80), [CudaPlatform.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp#L43-L80), [platforms/common/src](platforms/common/src)

## The Plugin System

OpenMM's plugin architecture enables third-party force fields and simulation methods to be distributed as separate shared libraries, loaded at runtime without recompiling the core. The `Platform::loadPluginLibrary()` method ([Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L255-L275)) dynamically loads a shared object and invokes its `registerPlatforms()` entry point, which registers any new Platform subclasses and their kernel factories.

The `plugins/` directory contains four built-in plugins that demonstrate the pattern:

| Plugin | Directory | Extension Provided |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|
| **Amoeba** | `plugins/amoeba/` | `AmoebaMultipoleForce`, `AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce`, `AmoebaVdwForce`, `HippoNonbondedForce`, `AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce` — polarizable force field with induced dipoles |
| **Drude** | `plugins/drude/` | `DrudeForce`, `DrudeLangevinIntegrator`, `DrudeSCFIntegrator` — Drude polarizable particle model |
| **RPMD** | `plugins/rpmd/` | `RPMDIntegrator` — ring-polymer molecular dynamics for nuclear quantum effects |
| **CpuPME** | `plugins/cpupme/` | CPU-optimized PME plugin for platforms that benefit from a separate PME implementation |

Each plugin mirrors the core structure: it defines new `Force` subclasses in its own `openmmapi/` subdirectory, provides platform-specific kernel implementations (reference, CUDA, OpenCL, HIP) in its `platforms/` subdirectory, and includes serialization and Python wrappers.

> [!TIP]
> Plugin force classes follow the exact same `Force` → `ForceImpl` → `KernelImpl` chain as core forces. When writing a plugin, your new `Force` subclass must implement `createImpl()`, your `ForceImpl` must list required kernel names in `getKernelNames()`, and each target platform must register a factory for those kernel names. The system will not discover your kernels otherwise.

Sources: [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L255-L275), [PluginInitializer.h](olla/include/openmm/PluginInitializer.h), [plugins/](plugins/)

## Supporting Infrastructure

### Third-Party Libraries

The `libraries/` directory bundles vetted dependencies that OpenMM relies on for core computation. These are not external in the traditional sense — they are compiled directly into the OpenMM libraries, ensuring consistent builds across platforms.

| Library | Purpose | Used By |
|---------|---------|---------|
| **lepton** | Expression parsing and compilation for custom forces | `CustomBondForce`, `CustomNonbondedForce`, `CustomIntegrator`, `ExpressionUtilities` |
| **sfmt** | SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister random number generator | Langevin and Monte Carlo integrators |
| **jama** | Jama matrix library (eigenvalue decomposition) | Normal mode analysis, constraint algorithms |
| **quern** | Minimum-norm least-squares solver | Constraint enforcement (SETTLE, CCMA) |
| **lbfgs** | Limited-memory BFGS optimization | `LocalEnergyMinimizer` |
| **pocketfft** | PocketFFT for Fast Fourier Transforms | PME electrostatics on CPU |
| **vkfft** | VKFFT for GPU FFT | PME electrostatics on GPU platforms |
| **vecmath** | SIMD vector math (OpenMM's own Vec3, SimdFloat, etc.) | All platforms |
| **asmjit** | JIT assembler for dynamic code generation | `CustomIntegrator` expression compilation on CPU |
| **csha1** | SHA-1 hash computation | Build system kernel source encoding |
| **hilbert** | Hilbert space-filling curves | Neighbor list spatial sorting |
| **irrxml** | XML parser | Serialization/XML state files |

### Serialization and Checkpointing

The `serialization/` directory provides XML-based serialization for the entire simulation state, enabling system definitions, force parameters, integrator configurations, and particle states to be saved and restored across sessions. This is critical for reproducibility and workflow continuity. The serialization layer maps directly to the core API classes — every `Force`, `Integrator`, and `System` subclass has a corresponding serialization adapter.

Sources: [libraries/](libraries/), [serialization/](serialization/)

## Directory Structure Reference

```

│   └── cpupme/                    # CPU PME plugin
│

│   ├── lepton/                    # Expression compiler
│   ├── sfmt/                      # SIMD random number generator

│   ├── vkfft/                     # GPU FFT
│   └── vecmath/                   # SIMD math primitives
│

├── tests/                         # Comprehensive test suite
└── examples/                      # C++ and Python example programs
```

## How a Simulation Request Flows Through the Architecture

To consolidate the architectural picture, consider what happens when a user calls `integrator.step(1000)`:

1. **Integrator.step()** invokes the platform-specific integration kernel (e.g., `IntegrateLangevinMiddleStepKernel`).
2. The integration kernel calls **ContextImpl.calcForcesAndEnergy()**, which orchestrates the force loop.
3. **ContextImpl** iterates over all `ForceImpl` objects, first calling `updateContextState()` on each (allowing barostats and thermostats to modify state).
4. The orchestration kernel's **beginComputation()** initializes force buffers.
5. Each `ForceImpl.calcForcesAndEnergy()` invokes its platform-specific kernel (e.g., `CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel::execute()`), which runs GPU kernels or CPU loops.
6. The orchestration kernel's **finishComputation()** performs final reductions and validation.
7. The integration kernel reads forces and velocities, applies the integration algorithm, updates positions and velocities through the `UpdateStateDataKernel`, then calls `ApplyConstraintsKernel` if constraints exist.

This entire pipeline is hardware-agnostic at the orchestration level — only steps 5 and 7 involve platform-specific code.

> [!TIP]
> When debugging performance, the key insight is that the force computation loop in `ContextImpl` is the hottest path. Platform selection via `Platform::findPlatform()` happens once at Context creation, so the overhead is zero during simulation. If a particular Force is slow, check whether the selected platform actually provides an optimized kernel for it (some platforms fall back to Reference for less common forces).

Sources: [ContextImpl.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h#L43-L200), [ForceImpl.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ForceImpl.h#L44-L131), [kernels.h](olla/include/openmm/kernels.h#L57-L120)

## Where to Go Next

This page has mapped the architectural landscape at the structural level. The following pages in this guide descend into the specific mechanisms:

- **[Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system)** — detailed examination of how Platform registration, kernel factory chains, and the `findPlatform()` selection algorithm work
- **[System and Context](11-system-and-context)** — deep dive into the System definition model and Context lifecycle management
- **[CUDA Platform Implementation](9-cuda-platform-implementation)** — walkthrough of the most performant backend, including memory management, kernel compilation, and PME stream pipelining
- **[Plugin Architecture](20-plugin-architecture)** — how to write and load custom plugins with new Force types and platform implementations
- **[Serialization and Checkpointing](23-serialization-and-checkpointing)** — the XML serialization format and binary checkpoint system

# Platform and Kernel System



OpenMM's defining architectural achievement is its ability to execute identical molecular dynamics simulations across radically different hardware — CPU cores, NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and OpenCL devices — without the user writing a single platform-specific line of code. This is made possible by the **Platform and Kernel system**, a layered abstraction that decouples the *what* of a computation (the physics) from the *where* and *how* (the hardware). Understanding this system is the prerequisite for everything that follows: reading platform-specific implementations, extending OpenMM with custom forces, or writing plugins.

## The Architectural Problem

A molecular dynamics simulation requires dozens of distinct computational operations: bonded force evaluation, nonbonded pair interactions, constraint enforcement, integration, thermostat application, barostat scaling, virtual site computation, and checkpoint serialization. Each of these must execute efficiently on very different hardware architectures. Rather than scattering `#ifdef` preprocessor guards throughout the codebase, OpenMM introduces a **double dispatch** architecture: a *Platform* acts as a hardware-aware factory registry, and *Kernels* are type-erased computation objects whose concrete implementations live entirely within platform-specific libraries.

Sources: [Platform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L60-L80), [Kernel.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h#L46-L60)

## Core Abstraction Layers

The system is built on four foundational classes arranged in a strict hierarchy. The `Platform` class serves as the top-level registry — it holds a map of named `KernelFactory` objects and provides a global static registry of all loaded platforms. When a kernel is requested by name, the platform delegates to the appropriate factory, which instantiates a concrete `KernelImpl` subclass. The `Kernel` wrapper then provides type-erased access to that implementation via `dynamic_cast`.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Platform {
        <<abstract>>
        +getName() string
        +getSpeed() double
        +registerKernelFactory(name, factory)
        +createKernel(name, context) Kernel
        +supportsKernels(kernelNames) bool
        +getDevices(filters) DeviceList
        +contextCreated(context, properties)
        -kernelFactories: map~string, KernelFactory*~
        -defaultProperties: map~string, string~
        +registerPlatform(platform)$
        +findPlatform(kernelNames)$ Platform
        +loadPluginLibrary(file)$
    }

    class KernelFactory {
        <<abstract>>
        +createKernelImpl(name, platform, context) KernelImpl*
    }

    class Kernel {
        +getName() string
        +getImpl() KernelImpl&
        +getAs~T~() T&
        -impl: KernelImpl*
    }

    class KernelImpl {
        <<abstract>>
        +getName() string
        +getPlatform() Platform
        -name: string
        -platform: Platform*
        -referenceCount: int
    }

    Platform "1" *-- "*" KernelFactory : owns
    Platform ..> Kernel : creates
    Kernel "1" *-- "1" KernelImpl : wraps
    KernelFactory ..> KernelImpl : instantiates
```

Sources: [Platform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L98-L175), [KernelFactory.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/KernelFactory.h#L38-L45), [KernelImpl.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/KernelImpl.h#L42-L62), [Kernel.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h#L71-L82)

## The Kernel Catalog: Named Operations in `kernels.h`

The central design decision is that every computational operation in OpenMM is identified by a **string name**. The file [kernels.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/kernels.h) defines approximately 50 abstract kernel classes — one for each type of operation the system must perform. Each kernel class inherits from `KernelImpl` and declares a `static Name()` method returning its canonical string identifier, along with a pure virtual API specific to that operation.

These kernel classes fall into distinct functional categories, shown in the table below.

| Category | Representative Kernels | String Names |
|----------|----------------------|--------------|
| **Computation Orchestration** | `CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel`, `UpdateStateDataKernel` | `"CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel"`, `"UpdateTime"` |
| **Constraint Handling** | `ApplyConstraintsKernel`, `VirtualSitesKernel` | `"ApplyConstraints"`, `"VirtualSites"` |
| **Bonded Forces** | `CalcHarmonicBondForceKernel`, `CalcHarmonicAngleForceKernel`, `CalcPeriodicTorsionForceKernel`, `CalcRBTorsionForceKernel` | `"CalcHarmonicBondForce"`, `"CalcHarmonicAngleForce"`, `"CalcPeriodicTorsionForce"`, `"CalcRBTorsionForce"` |
| **Nonbonded Forces** | `CalcNonbondedForceKernel`, `CalcCustomNonbondedForceKernel`, `CalcGBSAOBCForceKernel` | `"CalcNonbondedForce"`, `"CalcCustomNonbondedForce"`, `"CalcGBSAOBCForce"` |
| **Integration** | `IntegrateVerletStepKernel`, `IntegrateLangevinStepKernel`, `IntegrateBrownianStepKernel`, `IntegrateCustomStepKernel` | `"IntegrateVerletStep"`, `"IntegrateLangevinStep"`, `"IntegrateBrownianStep"`, `"IntegrateCustomStep"` |
| **Thermostats & Barostats** | `ApplyAndersenThermostatKernel`, `ApplyMonteCarloBarostatKernel` | `"ApplyAndersenThermostat"`, `"ApplyMonteCarloBarostat"` |
| **Energy Minimization** | `MinimizeEnergyKernel`, `CalcHarmonicAngleForceKernel` | `"MinimizeEnergy"`, ... |
| **Special Forces** | `CalcGayBerneForceKernel`, `CalcCustomCVForceKernel`, `CalcATMForceKernel`, `CalcRMSDForceKernel` | `"CalcGayBerneForce"`, `"CalcCustomCVForce"`, `"CalcATMForce"`, `"CalcRMSDForce"` |

The `CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel` deserves special attention: it brackets all force evaluation with `beginComputation()` and `finishComputation()`, giving the platform a chance to clear GPU buffers, initiate async transfers, or aggregate partial energy results from multiple devices. This is where the CUDA platform, for example, can split work across multiple GPUs and merge results.

Sources: [kernels.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/kernels.h#L73-L97), [kernels.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/kernels.h#L102-L175)

## Platform Registration and Discovery

Platforms are discovered through a two-phase process: **static registration** at library load time, and **dynamic discovery** via plugin loading.

### Static Registration

Each built-in platform registers itself into the global platform registry when the shared library is loaded. The `Platform::registerPlatform()` static method adds a platform to an internal static vector. The `ContextImpl` constructor, created when the user constructs a `Context`, triggers this chain: it either accepts an explicitly named platform or calls `Platform::findPlatform()`, which iterates over all registered platforms, checks `supportsKernels()` for the required kernel set, and returns the one with the highest `getSpeed()` value.

### Plugin Loading

Platforms that are distributed separately (such as the CUDA platform on systems without CUDA hardware) are loaded as dynamic libraries at runtime. The `Platform::loadPluginsFromDirectory()` method scans directories for shared library files, calling `loadPluginLibrary()` on each. Each plugin library exposes an initialization function (via `PluginInitializer`) that registers its platform and kernel factories. The `OPENMM_PLUGIN_DIR` environment variable controls the default search path, with a sensible platform-specific fallback.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Application Starts] --> B[Static Platform Registration]
    B --> C["Reference, CPU, OpenCL, HIP\nregistered automatically"]
    C --> D[User calls loadPluginsFromDirectory]
    D --> E{"CUDA/HIP .so/.dll found?"}
    E -->|Yes| F[Plugin Initializer runs]
    F --> G[Platform + KernelFactories registered]
    E -->|No| H[Continue without GPU platform]
    G --> I[User creates Context]
    H --> I
    I --> J{"findPlatform(kernelNames)"}
    J --> K{"Check each platform:\nsupportsKernels()?"}
    K -->|All kernels supported| L[Select highest getSpeed]
    L --> M[Context bound to Platform]
```

Sources: [Platform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L240-L270), [PluginInitializer.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/PluginInitializer.h)

## How Context Binds to a Platform

The `ContextImpl` constructor is where the abstract becomes concrete. It receives a `System`, an `Integrator`, and either a `Platform` pointer or platform name. It calls `contextCreated()` on the platform, which initializes platform-specific data structures, and then iterates over every `ForceImpl` created for the system's forces, calling `getKernelNames()` on each and requesting those kernels from the platform. Each `ForceImpl` holds its kernel as a member and invokes it during force computation.

The key insight is that the `ForceImpl` layer (defined in the public API) is *platform-agnostic* — it knows what kernel names it needs but not how they are implemented. The `KernelImpl` layer (defined in `kernels.h`) provides the platform-specific API. The concrete platform implementation (e.g., `CudaKernels.h`) provides the actual GPU-accelerated code.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Context as ContextImpl
    participant Platform as Platform
    participant Factory as KernelFactory
    participant Kernel as Kernel
    participant Impl as KernelImpl (e.g. CudaNonbondedForce)

    User->>Context: Context(system, integrator, platform)
    Context->>Platform: contextCreated(context, properties)
    Platform-->>Context: PlatformData initialized
    
    loop For each Force in System
        Context->>Platform: createKernel("CalcNonbondedForce", context)
        Platform->>Factory: createKernelImpl("CalcNonbondedForce", ...)
        Factory-->>Platform: new CudaNonbondedForceImpl(...)
        Platform-->>Context: Kernel wrapping CudaNonbondedForceImpl
    end
    
    Note over Context: Simulation loop begins
    Context->>Kernel: getAs<CalcNonbondedForceKernel>().execute(...)
    Kernel->>Impl: execute(context, includeForces, includeEnergy)
```

Sources: [ContextImpl.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h#L55-L70), [ForceImpl.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ForceImpl.h#L82-L101), [Platform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L155-L170)

## Concrete Platform Implementations

OpenMM ships with five built-in platforms, each living in its own directory under `platforms/`. Every platform follows the same structural pattern: a `XxxPlatform` class (subclassing `Platform`), a `XxxKernelFactory` (subclassing `KernelFactory`), a `XxxKernels.h` header containing concrete kernel implementations, and a `XxxPlatform.cpp` that registers all kernel factories in the constructor.

| Platform | Directory | Hardware Target | Speed Rating | Key Characteristics |
|----------|-----------|----------------|--------------|-------------------|
| **Reference** | `platforms/reference/` | Any CPU (scalar) | ~1.0 | Baseline correctness reference, no optimization, supports double precision |
| **CPU** | `platforms/cpu/` | Any CPU (SIMD) | ~10–50 | Vectorized with SSE/AVX/NEON, includes PME via CPU plugin |
| **CUDA** | `platforms/cuda/` | NVIDIA GPUs | ~100–1000 | Multi-GPU support, configurable precision (single/mixed/double), PME stream |
| **OpenCL** | `platforms/opencl/` | Any GPU via OpenCL | ~50–500 | Cross-vendor GPU support, deprecated in favor of HIP |
| **HIP** | `platforms/hip/` | AMD GPUs | ~100–500 | AMD ROCm backend, newer replacement for OpenCL on AMD |

The **CUDA platform** demonstrates the full power of the system. Its `CudaPlatform` class defines 8 platform-specific properties — `DeviceIndex`, `DeviceName`, `Precision`, `UseCpuPme`, `UseBlockingSync`, `TempDirectory`, `DisablePmeStream`, and `DeterministicForces` — that users can set via `context.setPropertyValue()` or pass as a dictionary in Python. Its `PlatformData` manages multiple `CudaContext` objects for multi-GPU execution, a thread pool for CPU fallback work, and synchronization primitives.

The **Reference platform** is intentionally minimal. Its `PlatformData` stores raw `std::vector<Vec3>` pointers for positions, velocities, and forces, along with `ReferenceConstraints` and `ReferenceVirtualSites` objects. Its speed rating of ~1.0 serves as the baseline for the `findPlatform()` selection algorithm.

Sources: [CudaPlatform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/platforms/cuda/include/CudaPlatform.h#L50-L155), [ReferencePlatform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/platforms/reference/include/ReferencePlatform.h#L57-L82), [CudaKernelFactory.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernelFactory.h#L37-L42), [ReferenceKernelFactory.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/platforms/reference/include/ReferenceKernelFactory.h#L37-L42)

## The Kernel Lifecycle

Every kernel follows a predictable lifecycle governed by the `ContextImpl` and the `ForceImpl` that owns it:

1. **Creation**: `Platform::createKernel()` calls the registered `KernelFactory`, which instantiates a `KernelImpl` subclass. The `Kernel` wrapper takes ownership via an internal reference count.
2. **Initialization**: The `ForceImpl::initialize()` method retrieves the kernel via `getAs<T>()` and calls its type-specific `initialize(system, force)` method, which typically allocates GPU buffers, compiles compute kernels, or precomputes lookup tables.
3. **Execution**: During each timestep, `ForceImpl::calcForcesAndEnergy()` calls the kernel's `execute()` method. The kernel reads particle state from the platform's internal buffers (which may reside in GPU memory) and writes forces and energy contributions.
4. **Parameter Updates**: When the user modifies force parameters, `copyParametersToContext()` propagates the changes to the kernel, which may reinitialize GPU data structures.
5. **Destruction**: When the `Context` is destroyed, `Platform::contextDestroyed()` cleans up platform-wide resources, and the `Kernel` wrapper decrements the reference count, eventually deleting the `KernelImpl`.

> [!TIP]
> The `Kernel::getAs<T>()` template method is the primary mechanism for type-safe access to platform-specific kernel APIs. The call uses `dynamic_cast` internally, which means that requesting the wrong type will throw `std::bad_cast` — a useful diagnostic if kernel name mismatches occur during development.

Sources: [Kernel.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h#L71-L88), [KernelImpl.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/KernelImpl.h#L57-L59), [ForceImpl.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ForceImpl.h#L52-L55)

## Platform Properties and Device Selection

Each platform can define an arbitrary set of **properties** — named string values that control hardware selection and runtime behavior. The `Platform` base class provides `getPropertyNames()`, `getPropertyDefaultValue()`, and `setPropertyDefaultValue()` for managing these. Properties can be set at two levels: as **defaults** on the platform (affecting all future contexts) or as **per-context overrides** via the context constructor.

The `getDevices()` method is particularly important for GPU platforms. It returns a list of available hardware devices as a vector of property maps. Each map contains the properties needed to select that specific device (e.g., `{"DeviceIndex": "0", "DeviceName": "GeForce RTX 4090"}`). Users can pass these maps directly to the `Context` constructor. The optional `filters` parameter allows narrowing the list — for example, requesting only devices that support double precision.

```python
# Python example: querying and selecting CUDA devices
import openmm as mm

platform = mm.Platform.getPlatformByName('CUDA')
devices = platform.getDevices()
for d in devices:
    print(f"Device {d['DeviceIndex']}: {d['DeviceName']}")

# Select a specific device for a Context
context = mm.Context(system, integrator, platform, 
                     {'DeviceIndex': '1', 'Precision': 'mixed'})
```

Sources: [Platform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L100-L145)

## Directory Layout of the Platform System

Understanding the physical code organization clarifies the architectural boundaries. The platform system spans three distinct areas of the repository:

```
olla/                          ← Core abstraction layer (no physics)
├── include/openmm/
│   ├── Platform.h             ← Abstract platform interface + global registry
│   ├── Kernel.h               ← Type-erased kernel wrapper
│   ├── KernelImpl.h           ← Abstract kernel base class
│   ├── KernelFactory.h        ← Abstract factory interface
│   ├── kernels.h              ← 50+ abstract kernel API definitions
│   └── PluginInitializer.h    ← Plugin loading entry point
└── src/                       ← Platform/Kernel/KernelFactory implementations

openmmapi/include/openmm/
├── internal/
│   ├── ContextImpl.h          ← Platform binding orchestration
│   └── ForceImpl.h            ← Platform-agnostic force implementation
└── (Force classes)            ← Public API, no platform knowledge

platforms/
├── reference/                 ← Reference platform (correctness baseline)
│   ├── include/
│   │   ├── ReferencePlatform.h
│   │   ├── ReferenceKernelFactory.h
│   │   └── ReferenceKernels.h
│   └── src/
├── cuda/                      ← NVIDIA GPU platform
│   ├── include/
│   │   ├── CudaPlatform.h
│   │   ├── CudaKernelFactory.h
│   │   ├── CudaKernels.h
│   │   └── CudaContext.h / CudaArray.h / CudaProgram.h
│   └── src/
├── cpu/                       ← SIMD-optimized CPU platform
├── opencl/                    ← OpenCL GPU platform
└── hip/                       ← AMD ROCm platform

plugins/                       ← External platforms (loaded dynamically)
├── amoeba/                    ← Amoeba polarizable force field
├── drude/                     ← Drude polarizable model
├── cpupme/                    ← CPU PME plugin
└── rpmd/                      ← Ring polymer MD
```

The `olla/` directory (named after the internal project codename) contains the pure abstraction machinery with zero physics knowledge. The `openmmapi/` directory contains the public-facing API that users interact with. The `platforms/` directory contains the concrete implementations, each with its own CMake target and test suite.

Sources: [olla/include/openmm/](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Platform.h), [platforms/](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/platforms/reference/include/ReferencePlatform.h), [openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h)

## Platform Selection Algorithm

When no platform is explicitly specified, `Platform::findPlatform()` performs the selection. The algorithm is straightforward but has important nuances:

1. For each registered platform, call `supportsKernels(kernelNames)` — this checks whether the platform has a `KernelFactory` registered for *every* requested kernel name.
2. Filter to only platforms that support all kernels.
3. Among the candidates, select the one with the highest `getSpeed()` value.
4. If no platform supports all kernels, throw an `OpenMMException`.

This means that if you use a force class that is only implemented by certain platforms (e.g., a plugin force), the system will automatically select a compatible platform. The speed heuristic ensures that GPU platforms are preferred over CPU platforms when both are available and both support the required kernels.

> [!TIP]
> When developing custom forces or integrators, you must ensure the kernel names returned by `ForceImpl::getKernelNames()` or `Integrator::getKernelNames()` are actually registered by the target platform. A missing kernel registration is the most common cause of "no Platform supports all kernels" exceptions.

Sources: [Platform.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L265-L270), [ForceImpl.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ForceImpl.h#L103-L106)

## Summary of the Contract Between Layers

The entire system rests on a set of explicit contracts between its layers:

| Contract | Between | Mechanism |
|----------|---------|-----------|
| Kernel name registry | `Platform` ↔ `KernelFactory` | String-keyed map in `Platform::kernelFactories` |
| Kernel API | `kernels.h` ↔ Platform implementations | Abstract virtual methods in kernel classes |
| Force-to-kernel binding | `ForceImpl` ↔ `Platform` | `getKernelNames()` returns required strings |
| State data access | `UpdateStateDataKernel` ↔ `ContextImpl` | Positions/velocities/forces via platform buffers |
| Property configuration | `Platform` ↔ `Context` | String-keyed property map at construction |
| Platform discovery | Global registry ↔ Plugins | `loadPluginsFromDirectory()` + static init |

Understanding these contracts is essential before diving into any specific platform's implementation details. The [CUDA Platform Implementation](9-cuda-platform-implementation) page explores how the CUDA platform fulfills these contracts with multi-GPU orchestration and mixed-precision arithmetic. The [CPU and OpenCL Platforms](10-cpu-and-opencl-platforms) page covers the SIMD vectorization strategies and OpenCL compute kernel compilation. For the broader picture of how platforms fit into the overall simulation setup, see [Architecture Overview](7-architecture-overview).

# CUDA Platform Implementation



The CUDA Platform is OpenMM's highest-performance execution backend, translating the abstract simulation API into native CUDA kernel launches on NVIDIA GPUs. It occupies the most privileged position in the platform hierarchy — returning a speed score of 100 and supporting double precision — and serves as the reference for what a fully-featured GPU platform looks like in OpenMM's architecture. This page dissects its internal design, from device management through kernel dispatch to the multi-GPU parallelism model, grounding every claim in source evidence.

## Platform Registration and Property System

The CUDA Platform enters the runtime through the `registerPlatforms()` entry point, which constructs a `CudaPlatform` instance and registers it via `Platform::registerPlatform()` [CudaPlatform.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp#L52-L60). The constructor performs three critical initialization tasks: it registers deprecated property name mappings for backward compatibility with older scripts that prefixed properties with `"Cuda"`, it creates a single `CudaKernelFactory` and registers it for every kernel name the platform supports, and it defines the full set of platform properties with their defaults [CudaPlatform.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp#L62-L142).

The platform exposes 10 configurable properties, each accessible through static accessor methods on `CudaPlatform` [CudaPlatform.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaPlatform.h#L60-L130):

| Property | Default | Purpose |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `DeviceIndex` | `""` (auto) | Selects which CUDA device(s) to use (comma-separated for multi-GPU) |
| `DeviceName` | `""` | Reports the CUDA device name; can filter by name |
| `UseBlockingSync` | `"false"` | Controls whether CUDA syncs or spin-loops while waiting for results |
| `Precision` | `"single"` | Numerical precision: `"single"`, `"mixed"`, or `"double"` |
| `UseCpuPme` | `"false"` | Offloads PME reciprocal-space computation to the CPU |
| `TempDirectory` | System temp | Directory for temporary files (e.g., kernel compilation artifacts) |
| `DisablePmeStream` | `"false"` | Disables the separate CUDA stream used for PME |
| `DeterministicForces` | `"false"` | Forces fully deterministic force computation (potential performance cost) |
| `CudaCompiler` | `""` | **Deprecated** — ignored, retained for backward compatibility |
| `CudaHostCompiler` | `""` | **Deprecated** — ignored, retained for backward compatibility |

The deprecated property replacement map (`deprecatedPropertyReplacements`) ensures that legacy code referencing `"CudaDeviceIndex"`, `"CudaPrecision"`, etc. is silently redirected to the unprefixed property names [CudaPlatform.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp#L63-L70). The `getSpeed()` method unconditionally returns 100, giving CUDA the highest priority among all platforms during automatic selection [CudaPlatform.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp#L144-L146).

Device enumeration via `getDevices()` queries CUDA runtime with `cuDeviceGetCount`, iterates over available devices, and returns a vector of property maps containing each device's name, compute capability, and supported precision modes [CudaPlatform.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp#L167-L200).

## CudaContext: The Device Abstraction Layer

`CudaContext` is the architectural heart of the CUDA platform. It extends `ComputeContext` — the common abstract base shared with OpenCL and HIP platforms — and encapsulates everything required to execute computations on a single CUDA device [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L66-L67). When a simulation is parallelized across multiple GPUs, one `CudaContext` is created per device, and the collection is stored in `CudaPlatform::PlatformData::contexts` [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L56-L63).

### Construction and Device Binding

The constructor accepts the `System`, a `deviceIndex`, synchronization and precision flags, a temporary directory path, a reference to the parent `PlatformData`, and an optional `originalContext` for linked contexts [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L75-L76). It binds to the specified CUDA device, creates a `CUcontext`, and stores device properties including the compute capability (`computeCapability`), GPU architecture (`gpuArchitecture`), and the blocking-sync flag [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L593-L610). A worker thread is created for each context when running in multi-device mode, ensuring that blocking calls to one device do not stall others.

### Precision Model

The platform supports three precision modes, controlled by the `Precision` property:

- **Single precision** (`"single"`): All computations in `float` (32-bit). Fastest but may accumulate numerical error.
- **Mixed precision** (`"mixed"`): Forces accumulated in 64-bit fixed-point (`long long`), positions stored in `float` with a separate correction array. This is the recommended balance of speed and accuracy.
- **Double precision** (`"double"`): All computations in `double` (64-bit). Slowest but most accurate.

The precision state is tracked by the `useDoublePrecision` and `useMixedPrecision` boolean members [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L600). The `getSupportsDoublePrecision()` method unconditionally returns `true` since all CUDA devices with compute capability ≥ 1.3 support double-precision arithmetic [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L396-L399).

### Core Data Arrays

`CudaContext` owns the primary simulation state arrays, each wrapped as a `CudaArray` object:

| Array | Contents | Precision Notes |
|-------|----------|-----------------|
| `posq` | Position (xyz) + charge (w) per atom | `float4` or `double4` |
| `posqCorrection` | Position correction for mixed precision | Exists only when `useMixedPrecision` is true |
| `velm` | Velocity (xyz) + inverse mass (w) per atom | `float4` or `double4` |
| `force` | Force per atom as 64-bit fixed-point (`long long`) | Always 64-bit — CUDA's atomic add on `unsigned long long` |
| `energyBuffer` | Per-block energy accumulation buffer | Reduced to scalar by `reduceEnergy()` |
| `energyParamDerivBuffer` | Energy derivatives with respect to parameters | For parameter sensitivity analysis |
| `atomIndexDevice` | Atom index mapping array | Used for reordering operations |

The force array is notable: it uses 64-bit fixed-point representation regardless of the precision mode, because CUDA hardware guarantees atomic 64-bit integer operations on global memory (`getSupports64BitGlobalAtomics()` returns `true`), enabling race-free parallel force accumulation [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L389-L393). Attempting to access a floating-point force buffer throws an exception [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L234-L250).

### Periodic Box Management

Periodic boundary conditions are maintained in both `double4` and `float4` formats to match the current precision mode, avoiding runtime casts in kernels [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L425-L491). The `setPeriodicBoxVectors()` method simultaneously updates both representations along with the box size and its inverse, while getter methods like `getPeriodicBoxSizePointer()` return a `void*` pointing to whichever representation matches the active precision [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L461-L491).

### Utility Subsystems

`CudaContext` aggregates four utility objects that provide higher-level abstractions over raw kernel launches:

- **`CudaIntegrationUtilities`** — constraint solver (SETTLE, SHAKE), velocity Verlet integration helpers [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L494-L497).
- **`CudaExpressionUtilities`** — compiles and evaluates Lepton mathematical expressions as CUDA kernels [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L499-L503).
- **`CudaBondedUtilities`** — manages bonded force kernel arguments and dispatch [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L505-L509).
- **`CudaNonbondedUtilities`** — manages neighbor list construction, interaction block sorting, and nonbonded force kernel dispatch [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L511-L524).

### Kernel Compilation and Execution

`CudaContext` provides two compilation paths: `createModule()` for direct CUDA module compilation using the CUDA driver API, and `compileProgram()` which returns a `ComputeProgram` wrapper compatible with the common abstraction layer [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L201-L302). The `executeKernel()` method encapsulates kernel launch configuration — it accepts a `CUfunction`, argument array, work unit count, optional block size, and optional shared memory size, handling the grid/block dimension calculation internally [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L319-L320). The `computeThreadBlockSize()` helper determines the largest feasible block size given a per-thread shared memory requirement [CudaContext.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h#L326-L327).

## Kernel Factory and Dispatch Architecture

The `CudaKernelFactory` implements the `KernelFactory` interface and serves as the central dispatch point for all kernel creation requests [CudaKernelFactory.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernelFactory.h#L36-L39). Its `createKernelImpl()` method follows a two-phase dispatch strategy based on whether the simulation is using a single GPU or multiple GPUs in parallel.

### Single-GPU Path

When only one device is active (`data.contexts.size() == 1`), the factory delegates almost entirely to the common kernel layer (`CommonKernels` namespace), wrapping the `CudaContext` reference:

Sources: [CudaKernelFactory.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaKernelFactory.cpp#L79-L166)

```
CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel     → CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel
UpdateStateDataKernel         → CommonUpdateStateDataKernel
ApplyConstraintsKernel        → CommonApplyConstraintsKernel
VirtualSitesKernel            → CommonVirtualSitesKernel
MinimizeKernel                → CommonMinimizeKernel
CalcNonbondedForceKernel      → CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel (CUDA-specific)
CalcConstantPotentialForceKernel → CudaCalcConstantPotentialForceKernel (CUDA-specific)
All bonded/torsion/custom forces → CommonCalc*Kernel wrappers
All integrators               → CommonIntegrate*Kernel wrappers
Thermostats/Barostats         → CommonApply*Kernel wrappers
```

### Multi-GPU Parallel Path

When multiple devices are active (`data.contexts.size() > 1`), the factory intercepts force kernels and creates parallel variants that distribute work across all `CudaContext` instances [CudaKernelFactory.cpp](platforms/cuda/src/CudaKernelFactory.cpp#L47-L78):

| Kernel | Parallel Variant |
|--------|-----------------|
| `CalcForcesAndEnergy` | `CudaParallelCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel` |
| `CalcNonbondedForce` | `CudaParallelCalcNonbondedForceKernel` |
| `CalcHarmonicBondForce` | `CommonParallelCalcHarmonicBondForceKernel` |
| `CalcCustomNonbondedForce` | `CommonParallelCalcCustomNonbondedForceKernel` |
| `CalcCustomExternalForce` | `CommonParallelCalcCustomExternalForceKernel` |
| `CalcCustomHbondForce` | `CommonParallelCalcCustomHbondForceKernel` |
| `CalcCustomCompoundBondForce` | `CommonParallelCalcCustomCompoundBondForceKernel` |
| All angle/torsion/bond forces | `CommonParallelCalc*ForceKernel` |

Kernels not listed in the parallel block fall through to the single-device path and execute on the primary device's context only.

## CUDA-Specific Kernel Implementations

While the vast majority of computation logic lives in the common layer, the CUDA platform defines four kernel classes with CUDA-specific behavior in [CudaKernels.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernels.h#L46-L143):

**`CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel`** — Wraps the begin/end of each force computation cycle. Its `beginComputation()` and `finishComputation()` methods handle autoclear buffer zeroing, energy reduction, and multi-device synchronization [CudaKernels.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernels.h#L46-L83).

**`CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel`** — Extends `CommonCalcNonbondedForceKernel` with a CUDA-specific `initialize()` that sets up the PME grid and nonbonded interaction parameters using CUDA's native kernel launch mechanisms [CudaKernels.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernels.h#L88-L102).

**`CudaCalcConstantPotentialForceKernel`** — Extends `CommonCalcConstantPotentialForceKernel` similarly, providing CUDA-optimized initialization for the constant potential electrostatics method [CudaKernels.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernels.h#L107-L121).

**`CudaCalcCustomCVForceKernel`** and **`CudaCalcATMForceKernel`** — Both override `getInnerComputeContext()` to extract the `CudaContext` from a linked `ContextImpl`'s platform data, enabling nested context evaluation for collective-variable and alchemical free-energy calculations [CudaKernels.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernels.h#L126-L142).

## Native CUDA Kernel Sources

The `platforms/cuda/src/kernels/` directory contains raw `.cu` files that provide the lowest-level GPU computation primitives. These are compiled into PTX/Cubin modules at runtime (for shared builds) or at build time (for static builds):

| Kernel File | Purpose |
|-------------|---------|
| `common.cu` | Utility kernels: buffer clearing, energy reduction, charge setting |
| `utilities.cu` | Mathematical utility functions used across force kernels |
| `vectorOps.cu` | SIMD vector operations (vec3, vec4 arithmetic) |
| `nonbonded.cu` | Pairwise nonbonded force evaluation (Lennard-Jones + Coulomb) |
| `findInteractingBlocks.cu` | Neighbor list construction and interaction block identification |
| `sort.cu` | Radix sort for atom reordering and spatial decomposition |
| `fft.cu` | Complex-to-complex 3D FFT for PME reciprocal space |
| `fftR2C.cu` | Real-to-complex 3D FFT for PME |
| `parallel.cu` | Multi-GPU communication and force aggregation kernels |

## Multi-GPU Parallel Execution Model

The `CudaPlatform::PlatformData` class orchestrates parallel execution across multiple CUDA devices [CudaPlatform.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaPlatform.h#L133-L150). Its key members include a vector of `CudaContext*` pointers (one per device), a vector of per-context energy accumulators, a `ThreadPool` for CPU-side parallelism, and flags controlling center-of-mass motion removal, peer-to-peer GPU access, PME stream behavior, and deterministic force computation.

The `initializeContexts()` method performs the second phase of initialization — after all force kernels have been created but before simulation begins — ensuring each `CudaContext` is fully ready. The `syncContexts()` method barriers all devices, ensuring that multi-device force computations have completed before energy aggregation [CudaPlatform.h](platforms/cuda/include/CudaPlatform.h#L139-L140).

> [!TIP]
> When using multiple GPUs with the CUDA platform, the `DeviceIndex` property accepts a comma-separated list (e.g., `"0,1,2"`) to distribute the simulation across that many devices. The platform automatically partitions atoms among devices and uses the `CudaParallel*Kernel` variants to coordinate work. Peer-to-peer access (`peerAccessSupported`) is probed at initialization to determine whether direct GPU-to-GPU memory transfer is available, which significantly affects inter-device communication overhead.

## CUDA vs. Common Layer: The Delegation Pattern

The CUDA platform achieves maximum code reuse through a systematic delegation pattern. The architectural relationship can be understood as three concentric layers:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "OpenMM Public API"
        A[Context / System / Force classes]
    end
    
    subgraph "CUDA Platform Layer"
        B[CudaPlatform<br/>Property management & registration]
        C[CudaKernelFactory<br/>Kernel creation dispatch]
        D[CudaContext<br/>Device state & kernel execution]
        E[CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/>CUDA-specific force/energy wrapper]
        F[CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel<br/>CUDA-specific nonbonded init]
    end
    
    subgraph "Common Abstraction Layer"
        G[ComputeContext<br/>Abstract base for CudaContext]
        H[CommonKernels<br/>Platform-agnostic kernel implementations]
        I[CommonCalcNonbondedForceKernel<br/>Shared nonbonded logic]
        J[CommonIntegrate*Kernel<br/>Shared integrator logic]
        K[CommonCalc*ForceKernel<br/>Shared force logic]
    end
    
    subgraph "CUDA Native Layer"
        L["*.cu kernel files<br/>Raw CUDA device code"]
        M[CudaArray / CudaQueue / CudaSort<br/>CUDA runtime wrappers]
    end
    
    A --> B
    A --> C
    B --> D
    C --> E
    C --> F
    C --> H
    C --> I
    C --> J
    C --> K
    D --> G
    D --> M
    E --> D
    F --> I
    H --> G
    I --> D
    J --> D
    K --> D
    M --> L
```

The `CudaContext` serves as the bridge: it implements `ComputeContext` (the common abstraction) while simultaneously exposing CUDA-specific APIs (`createModule()`, `executeKernel()`, `CUcontext` access) that the common layer calls polymorphically through virtual dispatch.
