This pattern is visible across every bonded force (e.g., [HarmonicBondForce.h#L88-L97](openmmapi/include/openmm/HarmonicBondForce.h#L88-L97)), nonbonded forces ([NonbondedForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/NonbondedForce.h#L339-L339)), and custom forces. The constraint is that you cannot change the *topology*—the set of particles involved in each interaction is immutable after Context creation. Only numeric parameter values (force constants, charges, distances) can be updated in place.

> [!TIP]
> When using `updateParametersInContext()` with `NonbondedForce`, exception parameters are also updatable. However, the number of exceptions and the particles they involve cannot change. For alchemical transformations where you need to modify which pairs interact, use parameter offsets (`addParticleParameterOffset`) instead of modifying exceptions directly.

## Complete Force Class Reference

The following table provides a comprehensive index of every standard Force class in the `openmmapi/include/openmm/` directory:

| Force Class | Category | PBC Required | Particle Scope | Energy Expression |
|------------|----------|-------------|----------------|-------------------|
| `HarmonicBondForce` | Bonded | Optional (off) | Pairs | k(r−r₀)² |
| `HarmonicAngleForce` | Bonded | Optional (off) | Triplets | k(θ−θ₀)² |
| `PeriodicTorsionForce` | Bonded | Optional (off) | Quartets | k(1+cos(nφ−φ₀)) |
| `RBTorsionForce` | Bonded | Optional (off) | Quartets | Σ Cᵢ(cos φ)ⁱ |
| `CMAPTorsionForce` | Bonded | Optional (off) | 5/8 particles | Spline-interpolated grid |
| `NonbondedForce` | Nonbonded | Method-dependent | All pairs | Coulomb + LJ 12-6 |
| `GBSAOBCForce` | Implicit solvent | Optional | All pairs | GB-OBC + surface area |
| `CustomNonbondedForce` | Custom | Optional | All pairs / groups | User expression |
| `CustomBondForce` | Custom | No | Pairs | User expression |
| `CustomAngleForce` | Custom | No | Triplets | User expression |
| `CustomTorsionForce` | Custom | No | Quartets | User expression |
| `CustomExternalForce` | Custom | No | Single particles | User expression |
| `CustomGBForce` | Custom | Optional | All pairs | User expression |
| `CustomHbondForce` | Custom | Optional | Donor-acceptor | User expression |
| `CustomCVForce` | Custom CV | Per sub-force | Collective variables | User expression |
| `CustomCentroidBondForce` | Custom | Optional | Group centroids | User expression |
| `CustomCompoundBondForce` | Custom | No | Arbitrary sets | User expression |
| `CustomManyParticleForce` | Custom | No | N-body | User expression |
| `CustomVolumeForce` | Custom | N/A | System volume | User expression |
| `RMSDForce` | Utility | No | All / subset | RMSD value |
| `ATMForce` | Enhanced sampling | N/A | N/A | Accelerated MD |
| `GayBerneForce` | Anisotropic | Optional | All pairs | Gay-Berne |
| `ConstantPotentialForce` | Electrostatics | Yes | All pairs | Constant potential |
| `RGForce` | Utility | No | All / subset | Radius of gyration |
| `LCPOForce` | Surface area | No | All particles | LCPO surface area |
| `OrientationRestraintForce` | Restraint | No | Particle frames | Orientational restraint |

## Relationship to Other Architecture Layers

Force classes occupy a central position in OpenMM's architecture. They are consumed by the `System`, instantiated into platform-specific `ForceImpl` objects by the `Context`, and their execution is orchestrated by the `Integrator`. The force group mechanism at the `Force` base class level directly feeds into the multiple time step logic described in [Integrator Hierarchy](12-integrator-hierarchy).

For plugin developers, the Force/ForceImpl duality is the extension point: a new force type requires a new `Force` subclass in the public API and corresponding `ForceImpl` subclasses for each target platform, as detailed in [Plugin Architecture](20-plugin-architecture). The Amoeba polarizable force field plugin demonstrates this pattern extensively with force types like `AmoebaMultipoleForce` and `AmoebaVdwForce` that live outside the core API.

For users who prefer a higher-level interface, the [ForceField and System Generation](15-forcefield-and-system-generation) page describes how XML force field definitions are automatically translated into these Force objects, and [Custom Forces and Integrators](17-custom-forces-and-integrators) provides deeper treatment of the expression language and advanced custom force composition patterns.

# Simulation Class



The `Simulation` class is your primary entry point for running molecular dynamics simulations with OpenMM in Python. It wraps the lower-level OpenMM objects — **Topology**, **System**, **Integrator**, and **Context** — into a single, convenient interface that handles the most common simulation workflows: minimizing energy, advancing time steps, collecting trajectory data, and checkpointing progress. If you are just getting started with OpenMM, this is the class you will use most often.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L43-L56), [__init__.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/__init__.py#L20)

## How Simulation Fits Into OpenMM

Before diving into the API, it helps to see where `Simulation` lives in the broader OpenMM architecture. The class sits in the **Python application layer** (`openmm.app`), bridging the gap between the core C++ simulation engine (exposed through `openmm` as `mm`) and the high-level tools for loading molecular structures and force fields.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Python Application Layer (openmm.app)"
        FF["ForceField<br/>forcefield.py"]
        PDB["PDBFile / AmberPrmtopFile<br/>file parsers"]
        MOD["Modeller<br/>modeller.py"]
        SIM["<b>Simulation</b><br/>simulation.py"]
        R1["Reporters<br/>(StateDataReporter, DCDReporter, ...)"]
    end

    subgraph "Core API (openmm)"
        SYS["System"]
        INT["Integrator"]
        CTX["Context"]
        ST["State"]
    end

    subgraph "Platform Layer"
        PLAT["Platform<br/>(CUDA, OpenCL, CPU, Reference)"]
    end

    FF -->|"createSystem()"| SYS
    PDB -->|"topology, positions"| SIM
    MOD -->|"topology, positions"| SIM
    SYS --> SIM
    INT --> SIM
    SIM -->|"creates internally"| CTX
    SIM -->|"platform, properties"| PLAT
    R1 --> SIM
    CTX --> ST
    SIM -->|"getState()"| ST
```

The key insight is that `Simulation` **creates the `Context` for you**. At the core API level (described in [System and Context](11-system-and-context)), you would manually call `mm.Context(system, integrator, platform)`. The `Simulation` class automates this step while also managing reporters and providing convenience methods for common operations.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L97-L105)

## The Reporter Architecture

One of the most important design patterns in `Simulation` is the **reporter system**. Instead of manually extracting positions and energies every N steps, you attach reporter objects to the simulation's `reporters` list. Each reporter declares when it needs data and what data it needs, and the simulation loop coordinates all reporters efficiently.

Every reporter implements two methods:

| Method | Purpose | Return Value |
|---|---|---|
| `describeNextReport(simulation)` | Declares how many steps until the next report is needed, and which state data (positions, velocities, forces, energy) is required | A `dict` with keys: `steps`, `periodic`, `include` |
| `report(simulation, state)` | Processes the current state to write output files, print data, or save checkpoints | None |

The simulation's internal loop ([`_simulate()`](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L197-L262)) queries every reporter before each batch of steps to find the earliest requested report, takes only as many steps as needed, then collects the shared state data once and passes it to all reporters that are due. This avoids redundant `getState()` calls when multiple reporters trigger at the same step.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L197-L282)

## Creating a Simulation

The constructor requires three core objects and accepts optional arguments for platform selection and state restoration:

```python
simulation = Simulation(topology, system, integrator, platform=None, platformProperties=None, state=None)
```

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `topology` | `Topology` | Yes | Describes the molecular structure (atoms, bonds, residues) |
| `system` | `System` or XML filename | Yes | The OpenMM `System` defining forces and constraints |
| `integrator` | `Integrator` or XML filename | Yes | The integration algorithm and its parameters |
| `platform` | `Platform` | No | If specified, runs on this platform (e.g., CUDA, OpenCL, CPU) |
| `platformProperties` | `dict` | No | Platform-specific properties (e.g., `{'DeviceIndex': '0'}`) |
| `state` | XML filename | No | A serialized `State` to restore positions, velocities, and parameters |

All three core arguments (`topology`, `system`, `integrator`) can also be provided as **XML filenames** — OpenMM will deserialize them automatically. This is useful for restarting simulations from saved files.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L58-L114)

## A Minimal Working Example

Here is the most common pattern for creating and running a simulation, taken directly from OpenMM's official examples. This pattern is identical across all supported file formats (PDB, Amber, CHARMM, GROMACS, Tinker):

```python
from openmm.app import *
from openmm import *
from openmm.unit import *

# 1. Load structure and create the system
pdb = PDBFile('input.pdb')
forcefield = ForceField('amber19-all.xml', 'amber19/tip3pfb.xml')
system = forcefield.createSystem(pdb.topology,
    nonbondedMethod=PME,
    nonbondedCutoff=1*nanometer,
    constraints=HBonds)

# 2. Choose an integrator
integrator = LangevinMiddleIntegrator(
    300*kelvin,       # temperature
    1/picosecond,     # friction coefficient
    0.004*picoseconds # time step
)

# 3. Create the Simulation
simulation = Simulation(pdb.topology, system, integrator)

# 4. Set initial positions
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)

# 5. Minimize energy
simulation.minimizeEnergy()

# 6. Attach reporters
simulation.reporters.append(DCDReporter('output.dcd', 1000))
simulation.reporters.append(StateDataReporter(stdout, 1000,
    step=True, potentialEnergy=True, temperature=True))

# 7. Run
simulation.step(10000)
```

Sources: [simulateAmber.py](examples/python-examples/simulateAmber.py#L1-L16), [simulatePdb.py](examples/python-examples/simulatePdb.py#L1-L16)

## Core Methods

### `step(steps)` — Advance the Simulation

This is the simplest way to advance the simulation. It integrates the system forward by exactly `steps` time steps. During execution, it delegates to the internal [`_simulate()`](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L197) method, which also triggers any reporters whose `reportInterval` has been reached.

```python
simulation.step(10000)  # Advance 10,000 time steps
```

Internally, the integrator is called in batches of 10 steps at a time. This design ensures that Python can respond to `Ctrl+C` interrupts promptly, rather than being blocked inside a single long C++ call for thousands of steps.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L144-L149), [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L227-L232)

### `minimizeEnergy()` — Local Energy Minimization

Before running dynamics, it is standard practice to minimize the system's energy to remove bad contacts in the initial structure. This method delegates to `mm.LocalEnergyMinimizer.minimize()`.

```python
simulation.minimizeEnergy()
```

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `tolerance` | 10 kJ/mol/nm | RMS force convergence criterion |
| `maxIterations` | 0 (unlimited) | Maximum minimization iterations |
| `reporter` | None | Optional `MinimizationReporter` callback |

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L125-L142)

### `runForClockTime(time)` — Time-Bounded Simulation

This method is designed for cluster or cloud environments where you have a fixed wall-clock budget. It runs the simulation until the specified time elapses, then optionally writes checkpoint and state files.

```python
# Run for 4 hours, saving checkpoints every 30 minutes
simulation.runForClockTime(4*hours,
    checkpointFile='checkpoint.chk',
    stateFile='state.xml',
    checkpointInterval=0.5*hours)
```

If no units are attached to the time arguments, they default to **hours**. This is the only method in `Simulation` with implicit unit behavior.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L151-L195)

### `currentStep` — Tracking Progress

A property that reads and writes the current step counter through the underlying `Context`:

```python
print(simulation.currentStep)   # Read current step
simulation.currentStep = 1000   # Set step counter (useful when restarting)
```

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L116-L123)

## Built-In Reporters

OpenMM ships with six reporter classes that cover the most common output needs. Each is added to the simulation via `simulation.reporters.append()`.

### Trajectory Reporters

| Reporter | File Format | Key Parameters | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PDBReporter` | PDB | `file`, `reportInterval`, `enforcePeriodicBox`, `atomSubset` | Visual inspection, small systems |
| `PDBxReporter` | mmCIF/PDBx | Same as PDBReporter | Macromolecular Crystallographic Info standard |
| `DCDReporter` | DCD | `file`, `reportInterval`, `append`, `enforcePeriodicBox`, `atomSubset` | Long trajectories, efficient binary format |
| `XTCReporter` | XTC | `file`, `reportInterval`, `append`, `enforcePeriodicBox`, `atomSubset` | GROMACS-compatible trajectories, compressed |

Both `DCDReporter` and `XTCReporter` support the `append` parameter to continue writing to an existing file, and the `atomSubset` parameter to write only selected atoms (e.g., protein-only output from a solvated system).

Sources: [pdbreporter.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/pdbreporter.py#L36-L44), [dcdreporter.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/dcdreporter.py#L35-L42), [xtcreporter.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/xtcreporter.py#L32-L56)

### Data Reporter

`StateDataReporter` writes simulation observables to a file (or `stdout`) in CSV format. You control exactly which columns appear via boolean flags:

```python
simulation.reporters.append(StateDataReporter(
    'data.csv', 1000,                # file, interval
    step=True,                       # step number
    time=True,                       # simulation time
    potentialEnergy=True,            # potential energy
    kineticEnergy=True,              # kinetic energy
    totalEnergy=True,                # total energy
    temperature=True,                # instantaneous temperature
    volume=True,                     # periodic box volume
    density=True,                    # system density
    progress=True,                   # progress bar
    remainingTime=True,              # estimated time remaining
    speed=True,                      # steps/second
    separator=','                    # column delimiter
))
```

The reporter automatically detects the total system mass on first invocation and calculates derived quantities (temperature, density) from kinetic energy and box volume.

Sources: [statedatareporter.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/statedatareporter.py#L49-L58), [statedatareporter.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/statedatareporter.py#L214-L289)

### Checkpoint Reporter

`CheckpointReporter` periodically saves either a full **checkpoint** (binary, platform-specific) or a serialized **State** (XML, portable). Checkpoints include internal data like random number generator states for exact reproducibility; states contain only public data (positions, velocities, parameters).

```python
# Binary checkpoint (exact restart, same platform required)
simulation.reporters.append(CheckpointReporter('checkpoint.chk', 5000))

# XML state (portable across platforms)
simulation.reporters.append(CheckpointReporter('state.xml', 5000, writeState=True))
```

Each checkpoint **overwrites** the previous one — only the latest state is retained in the file.

Sources: [checkpointreporter.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/checkpointreporter.py#L36-L77)

## Saving and Restoring Simulation State

Beyond the reporter-based approach, `Simulation` provides four methods for manual state persistence. Understanding the distinction between **checkpoints** and **states** is critical.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Checkpoint (Binary)"
        CP["saveCheckpoint()"]
        CPL["loadCheckpoint()"]
    end

    subgraph "State (XML)"
        SV["saveState()"]
        STL["loadState()"]
    end

    CP -->|"Exact reproducibility<br/>Platform-specific<br/>RNG state included"| CPL
    SV -->|"Portable<br/>Cross-platform<br/>RNG state NOT included"| STL
```

| Feature | `saveCheckpoint()` / `loadCheckpoint()` | `saveState()` / `loadState()` |
|---|---|---|
| **Format** | Binary | XML |
| **Portability** | Same platform, hardware, and OpenMM version only | Cross-platform, cross-version |
| **RNG State** | Included (exact trajectory reproducibility) | Not included (trajectory will differ) |
| **Restored Data** | Positions, velocities, internal states | Positions, velocities, parameters |
| **Use Case** | Interrupted job recovery on same machine | Transferring state to different hardware |

Both methods use **safe saving** internally — they write to a temporary file first and then atomically rename it. This prevents data corruption if the process is killed mid-write.

> [!TIP]
> When restarting a simulation after loading a checkpoint or state, you do **not** need to call `setPositions()` again. The loaded data fully restores the context state. However, you should still re-attach your reporters since the `reporters` list is not serialized.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L283-L360), [checkpointreporter.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/checkpointreporter.py#L54-L76)

## Selecting a Platform and Device

You can control which hardware platform the simulation runs on by passing a `Platform` object. This is useful for GPU acceleration or reproducible benchmarking:

```python
from openmm import Platform

# Run on CUDA (NVIDIA GPU)
platform = Platform.getPlatformByName('CUDA')
simulation = Simulation(topology, system, integrator, platform,
    platformProperties={'DeviceIndex': '0', 'Precision': 'mixed'})

# Run on the Reference platform (CPU, slow, for debugging)
platform = Platform.getPlatformByName('Reference')
simulation = Simulation(topology, system, integrator, platform)
```

Platform properties are passed as a dictionary. Available properties vary by platform — see [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system) for details. Each platform also exposes a `getDevices()` method that returns available hardware devices with their properties, which can be passed directly as `platformProperties`.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L97-L105), [TestSimulation.py](wrappers/python/tests/TestSimulation.py#L299-L321)

## Internal Simulation Loop

For deeper understanding (or if you plan to write custom reporters), it is worth knowing how the simulation loop works. The [`_simulate()`](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L197-L262) method orchestrates everything:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start _simulate()"] --> B{"currentStep < endStep<br/>and time remaining?"}
    B -->|No| Z["Return"]
    B -->|Yes| C["Query all reporters:<br/>describeNextReport()"]
    C --> D["Find minimum steps<br/>until next report"]
    D --> E["Integrate in batches<br/>of 10 steps"]
    E --> F{"Any reporter<br/>due now?"}
    F -->|No| B
    F -->|Yes| G["Classify reporters by<br/>wrapped/unwrapped PBC preference"]
    G --> H["Optimize: choose the<br/>larger group + 'either' reporters"]
    H --> I["getState() once<br/>with combined requirements"]
    I --> J["Call report() on<br/>each due reporter"]
    J --> B
```

Two important optimization details in this loop: (1) the integrator steps in batches of 10 to keep Python responsive to interrupts, and (2) when multiple reporters need state data at the same step, the simulation computes a **union** of their requested data fields and calls `getState()` only once, then passes the shared state to each reporter individually.

Sources: [simulation.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/simulation.py#L197-L282)

## Typical Simulation Workflow

Putting it all together, here is the canonical flowchart for a complete simulation pipeline using the `Simulation` class:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load structure<br/>(PDB, Amber, GROMACS, ...)"] --> B["Create System<br/>forcefield.createSystem()"]
    B --> C["Choose Integrator<br/>(Langevin, Verlet, ...)"]
    C --> D["Create Simulation<br/>Simulation(topology, system, integrator)"]
    D --> E["Set initial positions<br/>simulation.context.setPositions()"]
    E --> F["Minimize energy<br/>simulation.minimizeEnergy()"]
    F --> G["Attach reporters<br/>(trajectory + data + checkpoint)"]
    G --> H["Run simulation<br/>simulation.step() or runForClockTime()"]
    H --> I{"Need to pause?"}
    I -->|Yes| J["Save checkpoint/state<br/>simulation.saveCheckpoint()"]
    J --> K["Later: reload and continue<br/>simulation.loadCheckpoint()"]
    K --> H
    I -->|No| L["Simulation complete"]
```

## Next Steps

Now that you understand the `Simulation` class, here are the natural next topics to explore:

- **[ForceField and System Generation](15-forcefield-and-system-generation)** — Learn how `ForceField.createSystem()` builds the `System` object with specific force field parameters, cutoffs, and constraints.
- **[Integrator Hierarchy](12-integrator-hierarchy)** — Understand the different integration algorithms (Langevin, Verlet, Brownian, Nosé-Hoover) and when to use each.
- **[Modeller and Topology](16-modeller-and-topology)** — Explore how to modify systems (add solvent, add ions, delete atoms) before creating your simulation.
- **[System and Context](11-system-and-context)** — For advanced use cases, learn how to bypass `Simulation` and work directly with the core API for maximum control.

# ForceField and System Generation



The `ForceField` class is the central bridge between chemical topology and executable simulation systems in OpenMM. It accepts a molecular `Topology` — a purely structural description of atoms, bonds, residues, and chains — and transforms it into a fully parameterized `System` object containing all the physics: forces, constraints, masses, virtual sites, and periodic boundary conditions. This page dissects the architecture of that transformation, from XML definition through template matching to force generation, providing intermediate developers with the knowledge needed to extend, debug, and customize the system-building pipeline.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L195-L220)

## Architectural Overview

The ForceField system follows a three-stage pipeline that converts declarative XML force field definitions into a concrete `System` object. At a high level, the flow is: **load** XML definitions into in-memory registries, **match** residues in a `Topology` to registered templates, and **generate** forces by invoking registered generator objects. Each stage is independently extensible, and the pipeline is orchestrated by a single `ForceField` instance.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Stage1["Stage 1: Loading & Registration"]
        XML["XML Force Field Files<br/>(amber14-all.xml, charmm36.xml, ...)"]
        XML --> |"etree.parse()"| PARSE["XML Parser"]
        PARSE --> ATOMTYPES["Atom Type Registry<br/>_atomTypes{}"]
        PARSE --> TEMPLATES["Residue Template Registry<br/>_templates{}"]
        PARSE --> PATCHES["Patch Registry<br/>_patches{}"]
        PARSE --> GENERATORS["Force Generator List<br/>_forces[]"]
        PARSE --> SCRIPTS["Post-build Scripts<br/>_scripts[]"]
        PARSE --> INCL["<Include> Directives<br/>(recursive)"]
        INCL --> PARSE
    end

    subgraph Stage2["Stage 2: Template Matching"]
        TOPO["Topology Object<br/>(atoms, bonds, residues, chains)"]
        TOPO --> SIG["_createResidueSignature()<br/>element-based hashing"]
        SIG --> LOOKUP["Signature Lookup in<br/>_templateSignatures{}"]
        LOOKUP --> MATCH["compiled.matchResidueToTemplate()<br/>(Cython accelerated)"]
        MATCH -->|unmatched| PATCHTRY["_applyPatchesToMatchResidues()"]
        MATCH -->|unmatched| GEN["_templateGenerators[]<br/>(e.g. SMIRNOFF, OpenFF)"]
        PATCHTRY --> MATCH
        GEN --> MATCH
        MATCH -->|matched| TFOR["templateForResidue{}<br/>mapping + atom types"]
    end

    subgraph Stage3["Stage 3: System Generation"]
        TFOR --> SYS["createSystem()"]
        SYS --> PARTICLES["Add Particles<br/>(mass, virtual sites)"]
        SYS --> CONSTRAINTS["Apply Constraints<br/>(HBonds, AllBonds, HAngles)"]
        SYS --> TOPOLOGY["_findBonds/Angles/Torsions"]
        TOPOLOGY --> FGEN["generator.createForce()<br/>for each registered generator"]
        FGEN --> NB["NonbondedGenerator"]
        FGEN --> BOND["HarmonicBondGenerator"]
        FGEN --> ANGLE["HarmonicAngleGenerator"]
        FGEN --> TORSION["PeriodicTorsionGenerator"]
        FGEN --> CUSTOM["Custom*Generators"]
        FGEN --> POST["postprocessSystem()<br/>(exclusions, etc.)"]
        POST --> RESULT["OpenMM System Object"]
    end

    Stage1 --> Stage2 --> Stage3
```

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L222-L429), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1231-L1508)

## ForceField Initialization and XML Loading

### Constructor and File Resolution

A `ForceField` is instantiated with one or more XML file paths. The constructor accepts absolute paths, relative paths (resolved against the current working directory), names of built-in force fields (resolved against the `openmm/app/data/` directory), or open file-like objects. Internally, it delegates to `loadFile()` which handles the full parsing pipeline.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L198-L220)

The file resolution mechanism consults a list of data directories via `_getDataDirectories()`, which returns paths to the bundled `openmm/app/data/` directory as well as any user-configured directories from the `OPENMM_DATA_PATH` environment variable. This is how a simple call like `ForceField('amber14-all.xml')` locates the bundled definition without requiring absolute paths.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L53-L78)

### XML Structure and Include Directives

Force field XML files follow a hierarchical `<ForceField>` root element structure. They support `<Include>` directives for modular composition — the file `amber14-all.xml` is a minimal aggregator that includes four sub-files for proteins, DNA, RNA, and lipids:

```xml
<ForceField>
 <Include file="amber14/protein.ff14SB.xml"/>
 <Include file="amber14/DNA.OL15.xml"/>
 <Include file="amber14/RNA.OL3.xml"/>
 <Include file="amber14/lipid17.xml"/>
</ForceField>
```

The parser resolves `<Include>` paths relative to the parent file's directory and processes them recursively. Circular includes are prevented by tracking already-loaded files. Each sub-file contributes atom types, residue templates, patches, force generators, and scripts to the shared registries.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L270-L282), [amber14-all.xml](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data/amber14-all.xml#L1-L6)

### Registry Loading Sequence

`loadFile()` processes XML trees in a strict, ordered sequence to ensure dependencies are satisfied before use:

1. **Atom types** — parsed from `<AtomTypes>/<Type>` elements into `_atomTypes{}`, keyed by type name. Each atom type records a `class`, `mass`, and optional `element`.
2. **Residue templates** — parsed from `<Residues>/<Residue>` elements into `_templates{}`, keyed by residue name. Templates store atom definitions (name, type, charge), internal bonds, external bonds, virtual sites, and constraints. An `override` attribute governs precedence when multiple files define the same residue name.
3. **Patches** — parsed from `<Patches>/<Patch>` elements into `_patches{}`. Patches can add, remove, or change atoms and bonds in matched templates.
4. **Force generators** — each XML child element whose tag is in the `parsers` dictionary triggers a `parseElement()` static method that creates and registers a generator. The `parsers` dictionary maps tag names like `"HarmonicBondForce"`, `"NonbondedForce"`, etc. to their respective generator class methods.
5. **Scripts** — `<Script>` elements register Python code strings that execute after system building completes. `<InitializationScript>` elements execute immediately during loading.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L284-L428)

### The Atom Type Registry

Atom types are the fundamental vocabulary of the force field. Each type maps a name to a class, mass, and element. The `registerAtomType()` method enforces consistency — if a type is registered twice, the definitions must be identical, or a `ValueError` is raised. Atom classes group related types into sets within `_atomClasses{}`; the empty string key `'': set()` always contains all registered types. This class grouping is essential for parameter lookup by class rather than exact type name.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L438-L462)

### The Residue Template Registry

Residue templates define the atomic composition, connectivity, and default parameters for each residue type. The `registerResidueTemplate()` method implements a **priority-based override system**: each template carries an `overrideLevel` (default 0). When a duplicate name is registered, the higher-override-level template replaces the lower one; equal levels raise an error. Templates are also indexed by **element signature** — a tuple of sorted element symbols in the residue — via `_createResidueSignature()`, enabling fast candidate filtering during template matching.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L464-L488), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1715-L1730)

## Built-in Force Field Bundles

OpenMM ships with a substantial library of pre-defined force fields in `wrappers/python/openmm/app/data/`. These cover the major biomolecular and small-molecule force field families:

| Category | Files | Description |
|----------|-------|-------------|
| **AMBER Protein** | `amber14-all.xml`, `amber19-all.xml` | Bundled protein + nucleic acid + lipid definitions |
| **AMBER Legacy** | `amber96.xml`, `amber99sb.xml`, `amber99sbildn.xml`, `amber99sbnmr.xml`, `amberfb15.xml` | Individual historical protein force fields |
| **AMBER Implicit** | `amber03_obc.xml`, `amber10_obc.xml`, `amber96_obc.xml`, `amber99_obc.xml` | GBSA-OBC implicit solvent variants |
| **CHARMM** | `charmm36.xml`, `charmm36_2024.xml` | Protein + nucleic acid + lipid parameters |
| **CHARMM Polarizable** | `charmm_polar_2013.xml`, `charmm_polar_2019.xml`, `charmm_polar_2023.xml` | Drude polarizable force fields |
| **Amoeba** | `amoeba2009.xml`, `amoeba2013.xml`, `amoeba2018.xml` | Multipole-based polarizable force fields |
| **Water Models** | `tip3p.xml`, `tip3pfb.xml`, `tip4pew.xml`, `tip4pfb.xml`, `tip5p.xml`, `spce.xml`, `opc.xml`, `opc3.xml`, `swm4ndp.xml` | Standard and optimized water models |
| **Implicit Solvent** | `implicit/*.xml` | GB-Neck and related implicit solvent models |
| **Carbohydrates** | `glycam-hydrogens.xml` | GLYCAM force field |

Sources: [data/](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data)

## Nonbonded Methods and Constraint Enums

The `ForceField` module defines a set of **singleton enum classes** that serve as symbolic constants for nonbonded treatment and constraint strategies. Each is instantiated once at module level and used by name throughout the API.

### Nonbonded Treatment Methods

| Singleton | `NonbondedForce` Method Constant | Description |
|-----------|----------------------------------|-------------|
| `NoCutoff` | `NoCutoff` | No cutoff; all pairs interact directly. Suitable for gas phase or very small systems. |
| `CutoffNonPeriodic` | `CutoffNonPeriodic` | Truncate interactions at a cutoff distance; no periodic boundary conditions. Gas phase clusters. |
| `CutoffPeriodic` | `CutoffPeriodic` | Truncate interactions at a cutoff distance; use periodic boundary conditions for minimum image convention. |
| `Ewald` | `Ewald` | Standard Ewald summation for electrostatics with a cutoff. Accurate but slower than PME. |
| `PME` | `PME` | Particle Mesh Ewald for electrostatics; Lennard-Jones uses reaction field. The default for biomolecular simulations. |
| `LJPME` | `LJPME` | PME for both electrostatics and Lennard-Jones. More accurate dispersion treatment at additional cost. |

### Constraint Strategies

| Singleton | Constraints Applied | Typical Use |
|-----------|--------------------|-------------|
| `None` | None (besides template-specified) | Gas phase, maximum flexibility |
| `HBonds` | Bonds involving hydrogen | SHAKE-like; allows 2 fs timestep |
| `AllBonds` | All bonds | SETTLE-like; bonds fully constrained |
| `HAngles` | All bonds + angles with two H atoms (or H-X-H where X=O) | Maximum constraint; allows 4+ fs timestep with LINCS/SETTLE |

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L144-L190)

## The `createSystem()` Method

`createSystem()` is the primary public interface that transforms a `Topology` into an `System`. It accepts the topology and a rich set of configuration parameters that control nonbonded treatment, constraints, mass repartitioning, and force field-specific options.

### Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `topology` | `Topology` | *(required)* | The molecular topology to parameterize |
| `nonbondedMethod` | Singleton | `NoCutoff` | Nonbonded interaction treatment (see table above) |
| `nonbondedCutoff` | `Quantity` | `1.0*nm` | Cutoff distance for nonbonded interactions |
| `constraints` | Singleton | `None` | Constraint strategy (`None`, `HBonds`, `AllBonds`, `HAngles`) |
| `rigidWater` | `bool` or `None` | `None` | Force rigid water regardless of constraints; `None` uses force field default |
| `removeCMMotion` | `bool` | `True` | Add a `CMMotionRemover` to prevent global drift |
| `hydrogenMass` | `Quantity` | `None` | Repartition mass to hydrogens; mass subtracted from parent heavy atom |
| `residueTemplates` | `dict` | `{}` | Manual override of template selection per residue |
| `ignoreExternalBonds` | `bool` | `False` | Skip external bond checking during template matching |
| `switchDistance` | `Quantity` | `None` | Enable Lennard-Jones switching function at this distance |
| `flexibleConstraints` | `bool` | `False` | Add force parameters even for constrained degrees of freedom |
| `drudeMass` | `Quantity` | `0.4*amu` | Mass assigned to Drude particles |
| `**args` | `dict` | — | Force-field-specific keyword arguments (e.g., `ewaldErrorTolerance`) |

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1231-L1288)

### System Generation Pipeline

The `createSystem()` method executes a carefully ordered sequence of operations to produce the final `System`:

**Step 1 — Template Matching.** The method calls `_matchAllResiduesToTemplates()`, which iterates over every residue in the topology and attempts to find a matching template. For user-specified templates (via `residueTemplates`), a direct match is attempted first. For all other residues, the element-signature-based lookup runs, followed by patch application, template generators, and whole-molecule merging as fallback strategies.

**Step 2 — Atom Class Assignment.** After templates are matched, `data.setAtomClasses(self)` computes atom classes once for reuse by all generators — this is critical for Amoeba multipole forces where class-based lookups are frequent.

**Step 3 — Particle Creation.** An empty `mm.System()` is created and particles are added with masses from the matched atom types. If `hydrogenMass` is specified, mass is transferred from each heavy atom to its bonded hydrogens (excluding rigid water residues) to enable longer timesteps.

**Step 4 — Periodic Box Setup.** If the topology provides box vectors (e.g., from a PDB with CRYST1 records), they are set as default periodic box vectors. If a periodic nonbonded method is requested but no box vectors exist, a `ValueError` is raised.

**Step 5 — Topology Enumeration.** Bonds, angles, proper torsions, and improper torsions are enumerated from the bond graph. Angles are derived from all pairs of bonds sharing an atom; proper torsions from all pairs of angles sharing two atoms; impropers from all atoms with more than two bonds (all 3-atom subsets).

**Step 6 — Constraint Identification.** Bonds and angles are flagged for constraints based on the `constraints` parameter, `rigidWater` setting, and template-specified constraints. Template-specified constraints always take precedence.

**Step 7 — Virtual Site Setup.** Virtual sites defined in templates (types: `average2`, `average3`, `outOfPlane`, `localCoords`) are added to the System, and exclusion pairs are registered.

**Step 8 — Force Generation.** Each registered generator's `createForce()` method is called in registration order, receiving the System, the system data, nonbonded method, cutoff, and extra arguments. This is the core extensibility point — every `<HarmonicBondForce>`, `<NonbondedForce>`, etc. in the XML has been parsed into a generator that now materializes the actual `Force` object.

**Step 9 — Post-processing.** Generators that define a `postprocessSystem()` method are called to perform work that requires the complete set of forces. The most important example is `NonbondedGenerator.postprocessSystem()`, which creates 1-2-3 and 1-4 exclusion exceptions from the bond topology after all forces are present.

**Step 10 — Template Constraints.** Constraints explicitly defined in residue templates are applied last, overriding any previously-set constraint distances for the same atom pairs.

**Step 11 — Script Execution.** Any Python code registered via `<Script>` XML elements is executed in the local namespace, allowing force fields to perform arbitrary post-processing (e.g., adding custom forces or modifying parameters programmatically).

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1290-L1508)

## Template Matching Mechanism

Template matching is the most architecturally interesting component of the ForceField system. It must reliably map each residue in an arbitrary topology to exactly one parameterized template, handling ambiguity, missing templates, terminal modifications, and novel molecules.

### Element Signature Filtering

When matching a residue, the system first computes its **element signature** — a tuple of sorted element symbols for all atoms in the residue. For example, alanine (C₃H₇NO₂) produces the signature `('C', 'C', 'C', 'H', 'H', 'H', 'H', 'H', 'H', 'H', 'N', 'O', 'O')`. This signature is used as a key into `_templateSignatures{}`, which maps each signature to a list of candidate templates. This pre-filtering dramatically reduces the search space from all templates to only those with the same elemental composition.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1069-L1078), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1715-L1730)

### The Matching Cascade

`_matchAllResiduesToTemplates()` implements a multi-level fallback strategy for each residue:

1. **User override** — If the residue is in the `residueTemplates` dictionary, use that template directly.
2. **Custom matchers** — Iterate over `_templateMatchers[]` (registered via `registerTemplateMatcher()`), giving each a chance to override default matching logic.
3. **Signature-based lookup** — Find all templates with the same element signature, then call `compiled.matchResidueToTemplate()` (Cython-accelerated) to verify full structural compatibility (atom names, bond connectivity, external bond count, etc.).
4. **Patch application** — For unmatched residues, try applying registered patches via `_applyPatchesToMatchResidues()`. Patches modify templates by adding, removing, or changing atoms and bonds (e.g., N-terminal and C-terminal capping in AMBER force fields).
5. **Whole-molecule merging** — If a single residue still has no match, `_mergeMolecule()` performs a DFS from that residue through all bonded residues to create a `MergedResidue` spanning the entire molecule. This handles small molecule cases where a multi-atom molecule is stored as separate residues in the topology.
6. **Template generators** — Iterate over `_templateGenerators[]` (registered via `registerTemplateGenerator()`). Each generator is called with the ForceField and the unmatched residue; it may register new atom types, residue templates, and parameters. If a generator succeeds, matching is retried.
7. **Final error** — If all strategies fail, a `ValueError` is raised with a diagnostic message from `_findMatchErrors()` that suggests possible causes.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1511-L1583), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1586-L1608)

### Ambiguity Resolution

When multiple templates match a single residue, the system checks whether they assign **identical types and parameters** to all atoms via `areParametersIdentical()`. If they do, any one of them is used silently (this commonly occurs with ion templates like Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ that differ only in charge). If they differ, an exception is raised directing the user to specify the desired template via the `residueTemplates` argument.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1081-L1088)

## The Generator Architecture

Force generators are the mechanism by which XML force field definitions are translated into concrete `Force` objects. Each generator is a class that implements two required methods: a `parseElement()` static method that constructs the generator from an XML element, and a `createForce()` instance method that adds a Force to the System.

### Generator Registration and the `parsers` Dictionary

During XML loading, each child element of `<ForceField>` whose tag appears in the `parsers` dictionary triggers the corresponding `parseElement()` method. The parser typically creates a new generator instance and registers it with the ForceField via `registerGenerator()`. Multiple XML files can contribute to the same generator — for example, `NonbondedGenerator.parseElement()` checks if a NonbondedForce generator already exists and, if so, adds atom definitions to it rather than creating a duplicate.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L411-L416), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2765-L2793)

### Standard Generator Catalog

The `forcefield.py` module defines generators for the full range of standard OpenMM force types:

| Generator Class | XML Tag | OpenMM Force Produced |
|----------------|---------|----------------------|
| `HarmonicBondGenerator` | `<HarmonicBondForce>` | `HarmonicBondForce` |
| `HarmonicAngleGenerator` | `<HarmonicAngleForce>` | `HarmonicAngleForce` |
| `PeriodicTorsionGenerator` | `<PeriodicTorsionForce>` | `PeriodicTorsionForce` |
| `RBTorsionGenerator` | `<RBTorsionForce>` | `RBTorsionForce` |
| `CMAPTorsionGenerator` | `<CMAPTorsionForce>` | `CMAPTorsionForce` |
| `NonbondedGenerator` | `<NonbondedForce>` | `NonbondedForce` |
| `LennardJonesGenerator` | `<LennardJonesForce>` | `CustomNonbondedForce` (NBFix lookup table) |
| `GBSAOBCGenerator` | `<GBSAOBCForce>` | `GBSAOBCForce` |
| `CustomBondGenerator` | `<CustomBondForce>` | `CustomBondForce` |
| `CustomAngleGenerator` | `<CustomAngleForce>` | `CustomAngleForce` |
| `CustomTorsionGenerator` | `<CustomTorsionForce>` | `CustomTorsionForce` |
| `CustomNonbondedGenerator` | `<CustomNonbondedForce>` | `CustomNonbondedForce` |
| `CustomGBGenerator` | `<CustomGBForce>` | `CustomGBForce` |
| `CustomHbondGenerator` | `<CustomHbondForce>` | `CustomHbondForce` |
| `CustomManyParticleGenerator` | `<CustomManyParticleForce>` | `CustomManyParticleForce` |
| `DrudeGenerator` | `<DrudeForce>` | `DrudeForce` |

Additionally, for the Amoeba polarizable force field plugin, generators include: `AmoebaBondGenerator`, `AmoebaAngleGenerator`, `AmoebaOutOfPlaneBendGenerator`, `AmoebaTorsionGenerator`, `AmoebaPiTorsionGenerator`, `AmoebaStretchTorsionGenerator`, `AmoebaAngleTorsionGenerator`, `AmoebaTorsionTorsionGenerator`, `AmoebaStretchBendGenerator`, `AmoebaVdwGenerator`, `AmoebaMultipoleGenerator`, `AmoebaWcaDispersionGenerator`, `AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodGenerator`, `AmoebaUreyBradleyGenerator`, and `HippoNonbondedGenerator`.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2295-L2300), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2359), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2444), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2573), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2652), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2747), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2837), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L3036), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L3088)

### Generator Execution Pattern

Every generator follows a consistent execution pattern within `createForce()`:

1. Map the symbolic `nonbondedMethod` singleton (e.g., `PME`) to the corresponding `mm.NonbondedForce` integer constant.
2. Instantiate the appropriate OpenMM `Force` object.
3. Iterate over topology data (atoms, bonds, angles, torsions), looking up parameters by atom type or atom class.
4. Add parameters to the force object (e.g., `force.addParticle(charge, sigma, epsilon)`).
5. Configure force-level settings (cutoff, switching, error tolerance).
6. Add the force to the System via `sys.addForce(force)`.

The `postprocessSystem()` hook runs after all forces are added. The `NonbondedGenerator` uses this to call `nonbonded.createExceptionsFromBonds()`, which automatically creates 1-2-3 and 1-4 pair exceptions with the configured Coulomb and Lennard-Jones scaling factors.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L2795-L2836)

> [!TIP]
> The `NonbondedGenerator` uses a tolerance constant `SCALETOL = 1e-5` when validating that multiple `<NonbondedForce>` tags from different XML files specify consistent 1-4 scaling factors. If you encounter "different 1-4 scales" errors when combining force field files, check that the `coulomb14scale` and `lj14scale` attributes agree across all files to within this tolerance.

## Patches: Modifying Templates at Match Time

Patches provide a mechanism for conditionally modifying residue templates based on context — most commonly, terminal residue modifications in protein chains. Rather than defining separate templates for N-terminal, C-terminal, and internal forms of every amino acid, the force field defines a base template and applies patches to terminal residues.

A `<Patch>` element in the XML can perform five types of modifications: `AddAtom`, `ChangeAtom` (retype), `RemoveAtom`, `AddBond`/`RemoveBond`, and `AddExternalBond`/`RemoveExternalBond`. Patches are associated with residue names via `<ApplyToResidue>` in the patch definition or `<AllowPatch>` in the residue template.

When a residue fails to match any template directly, `_applyPatchesToMatchResidues()` generates all possible combinations of applicable single-residue patches for each unmatched residue and attempts matching with each patched template. For multi-residue patches (controlled by the `residues` attribute), `_matchToMultiResiduePatchedTemplates()` handles matching across clusters of residues.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L339-L409), [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1732-L1836)

## Extending the ForceField: Template Generators

For developers who need to parameterize molecules not covered by standard force fields — small drug molecules, non-standard residues, or cofactors — the `registerTemplateGenerator()` API provides a clean extension point. Template generators are callable objects invoked when all standard matching strategies fail.

```python
from openmm.app import ForceField

def my_small_molecule_generator(forcefield, residue):
    """Generate parameters for a custom ligand."""
    # Check if this residue is one we can handle
    if residue.name not in ('LIG', 'DRG'):
        return False
    # Register atom types needed by this molecule
    forcefield.registerAtomType({
        'name': 'lig-CA', 'class': 'CA', 'mass': '12.01', 'element': 'C'
    })
    # Load an ffxml file with the full template and parameters
    forcefield.loadFile('my_ligand.xml')
    return True

ff = ForceField('amber14-all.xml')
ff.registerTemplateGenerator(my_small_molecule_generator)
system = ff.createSystem(topology)
```

The generator function receives the `ForceField` object itself, allowing it to register new atom types (`registerAtomType()`), load additional XML files (`loadFile()`), or directly register residue templates (`registerResidueTemplate()`). If the generator cannot handle the residue, it must return `False` without modifying the ForceField. After a generator returns `True`, the system re-attempts template matching; if the new template still doesn't match, an exception is raised.

This pattern is the integration point used by packages like OpenFF and the SMIRNOFF format to bridge modern small-molecule force fields into the OpenMM ForceField pipeline.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L524-L568)

## Diagnostic and Debugging APIs

The ForceField class exposes several methods for diagnosing template matching failures and inspecting the parameter assignment process before committing to a full `createSystem()` call:

| Method | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `getUnmatchedResidues(topology)` | Returns a list of `Residue` objects for which no template exists, without raising exceptions. Useful for pre-flight checks. |
| `getMatchingTemplates(topology)` | Returns the template object matched to each residue. Useful for verifying that the intended template was selected. |
| `generateTemplatesForUnmatchedResidues(topology)` | Generates skeleton `_TemplateData` objects (with atom names and elements but no parameters) for unmatched residues, enabling automated template creation workflows. |

These methods build the `bondedToAtom` adjacency list internally via `_buildBondedToAtomList()` and run the matching cascade without the overhead of System creation. They are invaluable when debugging "No template found for residue" errors, as they allow targeted inspection of which residues fail and why.

Sources: [forcefield.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/forcefield.py#L1112-L1229)

## Typical Usage Patterns

### Basic System Creation

The most common usage pattern loads a bundled force field and calls `createSystem()` with a topology derived from a PDB or structure file:

```python
from openmm.app import *
from openmm import *

pdb = PDBFile('system.pdb')
forcefield = ForceField('amber14-all.xml')
system = forcefield.createSystem(
    pdb.topology,
    nonbondedMethod=PME,
    nonbondedCutoff=1.0*nanometer,
    constraints=HBonds
)
```

### Combining Multiple Force Fields

Multiple XML files can be composed by passing them all to the constructor, or by loading additional files after construction:

```python
# Approach 1: Constructor composition
ff = ForceField('amber14/protein.ff14SB.xml', 'amber14/lipid17.xml')

# Approach 2: Incremental loading
ff = ForceField('amber14-all.xml')
ff.loadFile('my_custom_lipid.xml')
```

When files define overlapping atom types or residue templates, the override level system resolves conflicts. If different files define the same force type (e.g., two `<NonbondedForce>` elements), the generators merge them — but 1-4 scaling factors must be consistent.

### Hydrogen Mass Repartitioning

Enabling longer simulation timesteps through hydrogen mass repartitioning is a single parameter:

```python
system = forcefield.createSystem(
    topology, nonbondedMethod=PME,
    hydrogenMass=3*amu  # Transfer mass to all non-water hydrogens
)
```

This transfers the difference between the requested mass and the current hydrogen mass from each bonded heavy atom, preserving the total mass of each X-H group while allowing a 4 fs timestep.

## Relationship to Other System Components

The ForceField is one part of the OpenMM system-building workflow. The `Modeller` class ([Modeller and Topology](16-modeller-and-topology)) builds and modifies `Topology` objects (adding hydrogens, adding solvents, aligning molecules) before they are passed to `ForceField.createSystem()`. The resulting `System` is then combined with an `Integrator` ([Integrator Hierarchy](12-integrator-hierarchy)) and a `Context` ([System and Context](11-system-and-context)) to begin simulation. The `Simulation` class ([Simulation Class](14-simulation-class)) orchestrates this entire pipeline end-to-end.

For developers looking to create entirely new force types or modify how standard forces are generated, the generator architecture described above provides the extension mechanism. For understanding how the generated `System` interacts with specific computing hardware, see the [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system) documentation.

# Modeller and Topology



The **Modeller** and **Topology** classes form the structural backbone of OpenMM's Python application layer — the bridge between raw molecular data (PDB files, force field XML) and simulation-ready `System` objects. While `Topology` is a pure data structure encoding the molecular graph, `Modeller` is an imperative editor that transforms topologies through a pipeline of preparation steps: adding hydrogens, solvating, inserting membranes, and converting water models. Together they answer the question: *how do I go from a static structure to a fully prepared simulation model?*

## Architectural Overview

The relationship between these two classes follows a clear separation of concerns. `Topology` owns the data; `Modeller` owns the mutations. Every mutation in `Modeller` produces a **new** `Topology` instance and a corresponding new position array — the original is never modified in place. This immutability-by-convention pattern makes it safe to branch preparation workflows or retry steps without corrupting prior state.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Data Layer"
        T["Topology<br/>Chain → Residue → Atom<br/>+ Bonds + Box Vectors"]
    end

    subgraph "Editing Layer"
        M["Modeller"]
        MH["addHydrogens()"]
        MS["addSolvent()"]
        MM["addMembrane()"]
        ME["addExtraParticles()"]
        MC["add() / delete()"]
    end

    subgraph "Upstream"
        PDB["PDBFile / PDBxFile"]
        FF["ForceField"]
        GD["GromacsTopFile"]
    end

    subgraph "Downstream"
        SYS["System (via ForceField.createSystem)"]
        SIM["Simulation"]
    end

    PDB -->|"loads into"| T
    GD -->|"loads into"| T
    FF -->|"provides templates<br/>& parameters"| M
    T -->|"initial state"| M
    M --> MH -->|"new Topology + positions"| M
    M --> MS -->|"new Topology + positions"| M
    M --> MM -->|"new Topology + positions"| M
    M --> ME -->|"new Topology + positions"| M
    M -->|"getTopology() /<br/>getPositions()"| FF
    FF -->|"createSystem()"| SYS
    T -->|"passed to"| SIM
    SYS -->|"consumed by"| SIM
```

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L52-L87), [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L68-L88)

## Topology: The Molecular Graph

`Topology` is a hierarchically-structured container whose organization mirrors a PDB file. A `Topology` contains `Chain` objects, each `Chain` contains `Residue` objects, and each `Residue` contains `Atom` objects. Separately, the topology stores a flat list of `Bond` objects connecting atom pairs, and optional periodic box vectors defining the simulation cell.

### Core Data Model

The four core entity classes — `Topology`, `Chain`, `Residue`, `Atom` — are constructed exclusively through factory methods on their parent. You never instantiate an `Atom` directly; you call `topology.addAtom()`, which assigns a contiguous global index and attaches the atom to the specified residue. This contiguity invariant is enforced at construction time and is critical for correctly mapping topology atoms to position arrays and `System` particles.

| Class | Factory Method | Key Attributes | Iterable |
|-------|---------------|----------------|----------|
| `Topology` | `Topology()` | `_chains`, `_bonds`, `_periodicBoxVectors` | `chains()`, `residues()`, `atoms()`, `bonds()` |
| `Chain` | `topology.addChain(id)` | `index`, `topology`, `id`, `_residues` | `residues()`, `atoms()` |
| `Residue` | `topology.addResidue(name, chain, ...)` | `name`, `index`, `chain`, `id`, `insertionCode`, `_atoms` | `atoms()`, `bonds()`, `internal_bonds()`, `external_bonds()` |
| `Atom` | `topology.addAtom(name, element, residue, ...)` | `name`, `element`, `index`, `residue`, `id`, `formalCharge` | — |
| `Bond` | `topology.addBond(atom1, atom2, ...)` | `atom1`, `atom2`, `type`, `order` | — (namedtuple) |

Sources: [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L82-L212), [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L395-L478)

### Bond Representations

`Bond` extends `namedtuple('Bond', ['atom1', 'atom2'])` with two optional fields: `type` and `order`. The bond type uses a set of singleton instances — `Single`, `Double`, `Triple`, `Aromatic`, and `Amide` — that are module-level constants in `topology.py`. This design allows bonds to be unpacked as plain 2-tuples (`atom1, atom2 = bond`) for backward compatibility while preserving rich metadata when available. Pickle support is carefully implemented via `__getnewargs__` and `__deepcopy__` to survive serialization round-trips.

Sources: [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L43-L67), [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L482-L517)

### Automatic Bond and Disulfide Creation

When structures are loaded from formats that lack explicit bond information (such as PDB files), `Topology` provides two methods for inferring connectivity:

`createStandardBonds()` loads an XML definition file ([residues.xml](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data/residues.xml)) containing bond patterns for standard amino acids and nucleotides, then walks each chain's residue sequence to instantiate bonds by atom name. The bond definitions use a prefix convention: `-C` refers to the preceding residue's C atom, and `+N` refers to the following residue's N atom — this elegantly handles peptide and phosphodiester backbone bonds across residue boundaries.

`createDisulfideBonds(positions)` identifies CYS residues with sulfur atoms lacking a hydrogen (the CYX state), then performs an O(n²) pairwise distance check with a 0.3 nm threshold to assign S-S bonds. It guards against multiple bonds to the same sulfur by scanning existing bonds before assignment.

Sources: [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L297-L394)

### Periodic Box Vectors

`Topology` stores optional periodic box vectors as a 3-tuple of `Vec3` objects, accessible through `getPeriodicBoxVectors()` and `setPeriodicBoxVectors()`. For the common case of rectangular boxes, `getUnitCellDimensions()` and `setUnitCellDimensions()` provide a simpler `Vec3` interface that internally converts to the full vector representation. These dimensions propagate through `Modeller` operations — when a new topology is created, the box vectors are copied from the source via `setPeriodicBoxVectors()`.

Sources: [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L237-L278)

### MergedResidue: A Parameterization Helper

`MergedResidue` is a pseudo-residue created by combining multiple `Residue` objects into one. It never resides in a `Topology`; instead, it is constructed transiently during force field parameterization to handle cases where multiple residues must be matched to a single template (e.g., terminal residue capping). Its `index` is set to -1, its `name` is `'Merged'`, and it aggregates atoms from all source residues without ownership — they remain the same objects found in the original residues.

Sources: [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L519-L547)

## Modeller: The Model Editor

`Modeller` wraps a `Topology` and a position array, then exposes a suite of editing methods that each produce a **new** `Topology` + positions pair. This is the central tool for preparing molecular systems for simulation. Its design philosophy is pipeline-oriented: you load a structure, apply a sequence of transformations (add hydrogens, solvate, add ions, add extra particles), then extract the final topology and positions for `ForceField.createSystem()`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load structure<br/>PDBFile / GromacsTopFile"] --> B["Create Modeller<br/>(topology, positions)"]
    B --> C{"Missing hydrogens?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["addHydrogens(forcefield, pH)"]
    C -->|No| E{"Need solvent?"}
    D --> E
    E -->|Yes| F{"Membrane simulation?"}
    E -->|No| G{"Extra particles needed?"}
    F -->|Yes| H["addMembrane(forcefield, lipidType, ...)"]
    F -->|No| I["addSolvent(forcefield, model, padding, ...)"]
    H --> G
    I --> G
    G -->|Yes| J["addExtraParticles(forcefield)"]
    G -->|No| K["Extract results<br/>getTopology() + getPositions()"]
    J --> K
    K --> L["ForceField.createSystem(topology)"]
```

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L52-L87)

### Structural Editing: add() and delete()

The `add()` method merges a second topology and its positions into the current model by copying both topologies into a fresh `Topology` instance. It preserves chain IDs, residue insertion codes, atom IDs, formal charges, and bond metadata through an atom-mapping dictionary. The `delete()` method is its inverse — it accepts a heterogeneous list of atoms, residues, chains, and bond tuples, then constructs a new topology excluding everything in the deletion set. Bond references that span deleted and retained atoms are automatically pruned. Both methods use `deepcopy` on positions to ensure complete independence from the source.

A convenience method `deleteWater()` simply delegates to `delete()` with a generator that filters residues named `"HOH"`.

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L89-L185)

### addHydrogens(): pH-Aware Protonation

`addHydrogens()` is the most chemically sophisticated method in `Modeller`. It adds missing hydrogen atoms to a model while intelligently selecting protonation states based on pH and local environment. The algorithm proceeds in several phases.

First, hydrogen definitions are loaded from [hydrogens.xml](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data/hydrogens.xml) via the private `_loadStandardHydrogenDefinitions()` method, which populates a class-level `_residueHydrogens` dictionary (loaded once, cached thereafter). Users can extend this with `loadHydrogenDefinitions()` for non-standard residues.

Second, for each residue, a **variant** is selected. The selection follows a priority chain: (1) explicit user override via the `variants` list, (2) disulfide detection for CYS → CYX, (3) pH-dependent selection for HIS (HID vs HIE vs HIP), with a hydrogen bond scoring heuristic that uses the internal `_CellList` spatial index to efficiently find potential hydrogen bond acceptors within 0.35 nm and a 50° angle tolerance. For other titratable residues (ASP/ASH, GLU/GLH, LYS/LYN), pH thresholds stored in the hydrogen definition XML determine the dominant form at the specified pH.

Third, hydrogen positions are computed. If a `ForceField` is provided, the method creates a temporary `System`, performs a local energy minimization on the new hydrogens only (existing atoms are held fixed) using the specified `Platform`. Without a force field, positions are estimated geometrically by projecting 0.1 nm along the anti-parallel direction of the sum of vectors to bonded neighbors.

The method returns a list recording which variant was actually selected for each residue, enabling inspection of the protonation decisions.

| Residue | Variants | Selection Rule |
|---------|----------|---------------|
| HIS | HID, HIE, HIP, HIN | pH > 6.5 → HID/HIE by H-bond scoring; pH ≤ 6.5 → HIP |
| CYS | CYS, CYX | CYX if sulfur has external bond (disulfide) |
| ASP | ASH, ASP | ASH at low pH, ASP at high pH |
| GLU | GLH, GLU | GLH at low pH, GLU at high pH |
| LYS | LYN, LYS | LYN at low pH, LYS at high pH |

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L696-L1108)

### addSolvent(): Solvation and Ion Placement

`addSolvent()` adds both water and ions to fill a periodic box, using a multi-step algorithm. It begins by loading a pre-equilibrated water box from the bundled [data/](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data) directory — separate PDB files exist for each supported water model (tip3p, spce, tip4pew, tip5p, swm4ndp). The box size can be specified in five mutually exclusive ways: explicit `boxVectors`, explicit `boxSize`, a `padding` distance around the solute's bounding sphere, a `numAdded` count, or by inheriting the existing topology's box vectors.

Water placement follows a clipping approach: water molecules within the sum of van der Waals radii (scaled by 0.561) of any solute atom are removed. Ion placement is handled by the private `_addIons()` method, which determines the system's total charge by creating a temporary `System` and summing partial charges from the `NonbondedForce` (or `AmoebaMultipoleForce`). Ions are placed by randomly selecting water molecules and replacing them — positive ions are placed at least 0.5 nm from each other and from other positive ions (and similarly for negatives) using the spatial index.

The `boxShape` parameter supports `'cube'`, `'dodecahedron'`, and `'octahedron'`, with non-rectangular shapes computed by the private `_computeBoxVectors()` method. A rhombic dodecahedron achieves the same minimum image distance as a cube at only 70.7% of the volume.

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L258-L668)

### addMembrane(): Lipid Bilayer Insertion

`addMembrane()` builds a complete membrane–water system around an already-oriented protein. It is based on the algorithm from Wolf et al., J. Comp. Chem. 31, pp. 2169–2174 (2010). The method includes both membrane and solvent creation in a single call because the two must be coordinated — waters must not intrude into the lipid bilayer, and lipid head groups need proper solvation.

Built-in support covers seven lipid types: POPC, POPE, DLPC, DLPE, DMPC, DOPC, and DPPC, each backed by a pre-equilibrated patch PDB file in the [data/](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data) directory. For other lipid types, users can pass any PDBFile or PDBxFile as the `lipidType` parameter.

The algorithm determines how many patch copies are needed in X and Y by computing `ceil((proteinExtent + 2*padding) / patchExtent)` for each axis, then tiles the membrane accordingly. Lipids are classified into upper and lower leaflets based on their mean Z position relative to the membrane center. The protein is temporarily scaled to 50% along X and Y; lipids within a cutoff of the scaled protein are removed in equal numbers from each leaflet. Finally, a short MD relaxation run scales the protein back to its original size while the membrane re-equilibrates around it.

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L1339-L1714)

### addExtraParticles(): Virtual Sites and Drude Particles

`addExtraParticles()` bridges the gap between a "physical" topology (containing only real atoms) and a force field's requirements. Some force fields define "extra particles" — virtual sites for water lone pairs, Drude oscillators for polarizable models — that have no corresponding element (`element is None`). This method matches every residue in the topology to a force field template, then adds or removes extra particles to achieve conformity.

The matching process uses `ForceField._matchAllResiduesToTemplates()` to find templates for each residue. For residues where the template contains more atoms than the topology, the extra atoms are identified as `element is None` entries in the template. Their positions are computed from the template's virtual site definitions or Drude particle type mappings. The method handles `MergedResidue` objects correctly, routing Drude particles and virtual sites to their parent residues within the merged group.

The deprecated `convertWater()` method performs a subset of this functionality — converting TIP3P water to TIP4P-Ew or TIP5P by adding virtual sites with hardcoded geometric parameters — but `addExtraParticles()` is the recommended replacement since it handles any force field generically.

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L1109-L1338), [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L187-L257)

### _CellList: Spatial Indexing

The private `_CellList` class provides O(1) expected-time neighbor queries by partitioning atom positions into a uniform grid of cells. It is used internally by `addHydrogens()` for hydrogen bond acceptor lookups and by `addSolvent()` for ion placement distance checks. The constructor computes cell dimensions from the position bounds and a `maxCutoff` parameter, then assigns each position to a cell. The `neighbors()` method returns atom indices from the 3×3×3 cell neighborhood surrounding the query position, handling periodic boundaries when box vectors are provided.

> [!TIP]
> The `_CellList` spatial index is created fresh for each `addHydrogens()` call with a cutoff of 0.35 nm, containing only acceptor atoms (oxygen and nitrogen). This keeps the index small and focused, avoiding the cost of indexing all atoms when only hydrogen bond scoring is needed.

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L1716-L1767)

## Typical Preparation Workflow

The most common sequence for preparing a protein simulation from a PDB structure follows this pattern. Each step transforms the model incrementally, and the final topology and positions are extracted for system creation:

```python
from openmm.app import *
from openmm import *

# 1. Load the structure
pdb = PDBFile('protein.pdb')
forcefield = ForceField('amber14-all.xml', 'opc.xml')

# 2. Create the modeller
modeller = Modeller(pdb.topology, pdb.positions)

# 3. Add missing hydrogens
modeller.addHydrogens(forcefield, pH=7.4)

# 4. Solvate with padding
modeller.addSolvent(forcefield, model='opc', padding=1.0*nanometer,
                    ionicStrength=0.15*molar)

# 5. Extract results
topology = modeller.getTopology()
positions = modeller.getPositions()

# 6. Create the simulation system
system = forcefield.createSystem(topology, nonbondedMethod=PME,
                                  nonbondedCutoff=1.0*nanometer)
```

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L64-L79)

## Key Design Patterns

**Immutability by reconstruction.** Every `Modeller` method that mutates the model does so by constructing a fresh `Topology` from scratch, copying over the retained entities, and replacing `self.topology` and `self.positions`. This means a method like `addHydrogens()` iterates over every chain, residue, atom, and bond in the source topology — the cost scales linearly with system size. For large systems, this is a deliberate tradeoff favoring correctness and simplicity over incremental mutation.

**Topology-contiguity invariant.** The `addAtom()` and `addResidue()` methods enforce that atoms within a residue must have contiguous global indices, and residues within a chain must be contiguous. This invariant allows position arrays to be sliced by residue or chain without indirection — `positions[residue.atoms()[0].index : residue.atoms()[-1].index + 1]` always yields the correct sub-array. This assumption is deeply embedded in both `Modeller` and `PDBFile`.

**Delegated charge computation.** Ion placement in `_addIons()` determines the system's total charge not from topology metadata but by creating a temporary `System` via `forcefield.createSystem()` and summing partial charges from the `NonbondedForce`. This ensures the charge calculation is always consistent with the force field's actual parameter assignment, even when residue templates or patch modifications alter expected charges.

> [!TIP]
> When using `addHydrogens()` with a `ForceField`, the method internally creates a temporary `System` and performs energy minimization on new hydrogens. If you specify a `platform` argument, this temporary system runs on that platform. For large systems, using `Platform.getPlatformByName('CPU')` can be faster for this brief minimization than waiting for GPU initialization overhead.

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L136-L181), [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L308-L326), [topology.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/topology.py#L167-L195)

## Data Files and Bundled Resources

The `Modeller` relies on a set of pre-equilibrated structural data files bundled in [wrappers/python/openmm/app/data/](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data). These include water box PDB files for each supported model (tip3p, spce, tip4pew, tip5p, swm4ndp), membrane patch PDB files for each lipid type, and XML definition files for standard bonds ([residues.xml](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data/residues.xml)) and hydrogen placements ([hydrogens.xml](wrappers/python/openmm/app/data/hydrogens.xml)). The water boxes are loaded directly by `addSolvent()` via `PDBFile`, and tiled to fill the requested periodic box. The membrane patches are loaded by `addMembrane()` and tiled in the XY plane to span the protein's extent plus padding.

Sources: [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L463-L478), [modeller.py](wrappers/python/openmm/app/modeller.py#L1402-L1407)

## Further Reading

Having understood how `Modeller` and `Topology` prepare structural models, the natural next step is to see how these prepared topologies are consumed by force fields and wrapped into simulation objects:

- **[ForceField and System Generation](15-forcefield-and-system-generation)** — how `ForceField.createSystem()` converts a `Topology` into a complete `System` with forces, constraints, and virtual sites
- **[Simulation Class](14-simulation-class)** — how the `Simulation` object orchestrates the `System`, `Integrator`, and `Topology` into a runnable simulation loop
- **[Custom Forces and Integrators](17-custom-forces-and-integrators)** — for advanced use cases where you need forces beyond what standard `ForceField` templates provide

# Custom Forces and Integrators



OpenMM's custom force and integrator framework is the system's most powerful extensibility mechanism. It allows developers to define arbitrary potential energy functions and integration algorithms purely through algebraic expressions — no C++ or CUDA code required. Every custom class inherits from the base `Force` or `Integrator` abstract class and feeds expression strings through the [Lepton expression engine](18-lepton-expression-engine), which compiles them into optimized, platform-native kernel code at runtime. This page provides a comprehensive architectural map of the entire custom subsystem, its shared parameter model, and practical implementation patterns for advanced developers.

## Architecture of the Custom Subsystem

The custom force and integrator classes form a unified framework built on three layers: the **API layer** (public headers in `openmmapi/include/openmm/`), the **expression compilation layer** (via the Lepton library in `libraries/lepton/`), and the **platform kernel layer** (implementations in `platforms/*/kernels/`). The architecture follows a clear separation between *what* to compute (the expression) and *how* to compute it (the platform-specific kernel).

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Developer Interface"
        CI["CustomIntegrator"]
        CBN["CustomBondForce"]
        CAN["CustomAngleForce"]
        CTO["CustomTorsionForce"]
        CEX["CustomExternalForce"]
        CNB["CustomNonbondedForce"]
        CGB["CustomGBForce"]
        CCB["CustomCompoundBondForce"]
        CCN["CustomCentroidBondForce"]
        CHB["CustomHbondForce"]
        CMP["CustomManyParticleForce"]
        CCV["CustomCVForce"]
        CVO["CustomVolumeForce"]
    end

    subgraph "Compilation Pipeline"
        LEPTON["Lepton Expression Engine"]
        AST["Parsed AST"]
        JIT["Platform JIT Compilation"]
    end

    subgraph "Runtime Execution"
        REF["Reference Platform"]
        CPU["CPU Platform"]
        CUDA["CUDA Platform"]
        OCL["OpenCL Platform"]
        HIP["HIP Platform"]
    end

    CI --> LEPTON
    CBN --> LEPTON
    CAN --> LEPTON
    CTO --> LEPTON
    CEX --> LEPTON
    CNB --> LEPTON
    CGB --> LEPTON
    CCB --> LEPTON
    CCN --> LEPTON
    CHB --> LEPTON
    CMP --> LEPTON
    CCV --> LEPTON
    CVO --> LEPTON

    LEPTON --> AST
    AST --> JIT
    JIT --> REF
    JIT --> CPU
    JIT --> CUDA
    JIT --> OCL
    JIT --> HIP
```

The key insight is that every custom class follows the same lifecycle: you construct it with an energy expression string, register parameters (global, per-particle, per-bond, etc.), add interactions, then add it to a `System`. When a `Context` is created, the expression is parsed by Lepton and compiled into the appropriate kernel for the target platform. This means your algebraic expression is evaluated with native performance on GPU hardware without any interpreter overhead.

Sources: [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L43-L392), [CustomBondForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomBondForce.h#L40-L86), [CustomNonbondedForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomNonbondedForce.h#L44-L120)

## Shared Expression Language

All custom forces and the `CustomIntegrator` share a common expression language powered by Lepton. The language supports standard arithmetic operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`) and an extensive function library. Expressions may also define intermediate quantities using semicolons as separators, enabling clean multi-step calculations within a single expression string.

### Supported Functions and Operators

| Category | Functions / Operators |
|----------|----------------------|
| **Arithmetic** | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^` (power) |
| **Transcendental** | `sqrt`, `exp`, `log`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `sec`, `csc`, `cot`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2` |
| **Hyperbolic** | `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh` |
| **Error functions** | `erf`, `erfc` |
| **Rounding / Discontinuous** | `floor`, `ceil`, `step`, `delta`, `select`, `min`, `max`, `abs` |
| **Special (CustomExternalForce)** | `periodicdistance(x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2)` |
| **Special (CustomIntegrator vector)** | `cross(a, b)`, `dot(a, b)`, `_x(a)`, `_y(a)`, `_z(a)`, `vector(a, b, c)` |
| **Special (CustomIntegrator energy)** | `deriv(energy, param)` — derivative of energy w.r.t. context parameter |
| **Random (CustomIntegrator)** | `uniform` (U[0,1]), `gaussian` (N(0,1)) |
| **Intermediate quantities** | Separated by `;` (e.g., `"sigma=0.5*(s1+s2); 4*e*(sigma/r)^12"`) |

> [!TIP]
