> The `step(x)` function returns 0 if x < 0 and 1 otherwise, while `delta(x)` returns 1 if x = 0 and 0 otherwise. The `select(x, y, z)` function returns z if x = 0, otherwise y. These three discontinuous functions are essential for implementing conditional logic inside expressions without resorting to flow control.

All trigonometric functions operate in radians, and `log` is the natural logarithm. When `uniform` or `gaussian` appears multiple times within a single expression evaluation, the **same** random value is used at each occurrence site — this is a critical semantic for reproducible stochastic integrators.

Sources: [CustomBondForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomBondForce.h#L82-L86), [CustomExternalForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomExternalForce.h#L98-L102), [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L371-L389)

## Shared Parameter Model

Every custom force uses the same three-tier parameter hierarchy, though not all classes expose all three tiers. Understanding this model is essential because it governs how parameters flow from definition through simulation to runtime modification.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Definition Time (System creation)"
        GP["Global Parameters<br/>addGlobalParameter()"]
        PP["Per-Interaction Parameters<br/>addPerBondParameter()<br/>addPerParticleParameter()"]
    end

    subgraph "Registration Time"
        IR["Interaction Registration<br/>addBond() / addParticle()<br/>(values fixed per interaction)"]
    end

    subgraph "Runtime (Simulation)"
        CS["Context::setParameter()<br/>(modify global params live)"]
        UP["updateParametersInContext()<br/>(push per-interaction changes)"]
    end

    GP --> IR
    PP --> IR
    CS -.->|"live update"| GP
    UP -.->|"rebroadcast"| IR
```

**Global parameters** are scalar values shared across all interactions. They can be modified at runtime via `Context::setParameter()` without recreating the context — this is the mechanism behind alchemical free energy perturbation. **Per-interaction parameters** (per-bond, per-particle, etc.) are set once when registering interactions and cannot be changed without calling `updateParametersInContext()`. **Tabulated functions** provide a fourth mechanism: piecewise-defined functions (`Continuous1DFunction`, `Continuous2DFunction`, `Continuous3DFunction`, `Discrete1DFunction`, `Discrete2DFunction`, `Discrete3DFunction`) that can appear directly in expressions.

The `addEnergyParameterDerivative()` method, available on several custom forces, requests that the derivative ∂E/∂(parameter) be computed. This value can be retrieved via `getState()` and is the foundation for alchemical free energy calculations using thermodynamic integration.

Sources: [CustomBondForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomBondForce.h#L46-L52), [CustomNonbondedForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomNonbondedForce.h#L50-L60), [CustomCVForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCVForce.h#L141-L177)

## Custom Force Taxonomy

The custom forces span a design space from simple two-body bonded terms to complex multi-stage implicit solvent models. They differ in three key dimensions: **topology** (what set of particles each energy term involves), **builtin variables** (what geometric quantities the expression can reference), and **advanced features** (exclusions, cutoffs, switching functions, interaction groups, computed values).

### Complete Custom Force Matrix

| Force Class | Topology | Builtin Variables | Per-Interaction Params | Key Advanced Features |
|-------------|----------|-------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `CustomBondForce` | Pair (bonded) | `r` | per-bond | Energy derivatives |
| `CustomAngleForce` | Triple (bonded) | `theta` | per-angle | Energy derivatives |
| `CustomTorsionForce` | Quad (bonded) | `theta` (dihedral) | per-torsion | Energy derivatives |
| `CustomExternalForce` | Single particle | `x`, `y`, `z` | per-particle | `periodicdistance()` |
| `CustomNonbondedForce` | All pairs (nonbonded) | `r` | per-particle | Exclusions, cutoffs, switching, interaction groups, computed values, long-range correction |
| `CustomGBForce` | Multi-stage (GB solvation) | `r`, `I`, `B`, etc. | per-particle | Computed values, exclusions, cutoffs, particle pair vs. single particle computation types |
| `CustomCompoundBondForce` | Arbitrary N-body (bonded) | `x_i`, `y_i`, `z_i`, `distance()`, `angle()`, `dihedral()` | per-bond | Tabulated functions, energy derivatives |
| `CustomCentroidBondForce` | Centroid pairs | `x1`, `y1`, `z1`, `x2`, `y2`, `z2` | per-bond | Particle groups as "virtual" centroids |
| `CustomHbondForce` | Donor-acceptor pairs | `r`, `theta`, `dihedral` | per-donor/acceptor | Separate donor/acceptor params, exclusions, cutoffs |
| `CustomManyParticleForce` | N-body (nonbonded) | `x_i`, `y_i`, `z_i`, `distance()`, `angle()`, `dihedral()` | per-particle | Permutation modes, exclusions, cutoffs |
| `CustomCVForce` | Collective variables | User-defined CV names | N/A (global params) | CVs defined as `Force` objects, tabulated functions, energy derivatives |
| `CustomVolumeForce` | System volume | `V` | N/A (global params) | Barostat-like volume-dependent forces |

Sources: [CustomAngleForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomAngleForce.h#L1-L309), [CustomTorsionForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomTorsionForce.h#L1-L324), [CustomCentroidBondForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCentroidBondForce.h#L1-L470), [CustomHbondForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomHbondForce.h#L1-L549), [CustomVolumeForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomVolumeForce.h#L1-L157), [CustomManyParticleForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomManyParticleForce.h#L42-L100)

## Bonded Custom Forces

The three simplest custom forces follow the same pattern: they evaluate an algebraic expression once per bonded interaction, where the builtin variable (`r` for bonds, `theta` for angles/torsions) provides the geometric input. They all support per-bond parameters, global parameters, tabulated functions, and energy parameter derivatives.

`CustomBondForce` defines pairwise bonded interactions as a function of inter-particle distance `r`. The harmonic bond potential is its canonical example: `"0.5*k*(r-r0)^2"` with per-bond parameters `k` (spring constant) and `r0` (equilibrium distance). Parameters are registered via `addPerBondParameter()`, and bonds are added via `addBond(particle1, particle2, params)`. `CustomAngleForce` replaces `r` with `theta` (the angle in radians) for three-particle angular interactions, while `CustomTorsionForce` uses `theta` as the dihedral angle for four-particle interactions.

`CustomCompoundBondForce` generalizes this to arbitrary N-particle bonded interactions. It provides access to individual particle coordinates (`x1`, `y1`, `z1`, etc.) and geometric functions (`distance(p1, p2)`, `angle(p1, p2, p3)`, `dihedral(p1, p2, p3, p4)`). A Urey-Bradley potential — coupling angle and 1-3 distance terms across three particles — is its canonical use case.

Sources: [CustomBondForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomBondForce.h#L40-L86), [CustomCompoundBondForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCompoundBondForce.h#L42-L100)

## Nonbonded and Implicit Solvent Custom Forces

The nonbonded custom forces represent the most complex tier of the framework. They operate over all particle pairs (or filtered subsets) and introduce advanced features like exclusions, cutoffs, switching functions, and interaction groups.

`CustomNonbondedForce` computes pairwise interactions between all particles (or restricted interaction groups). The expression **must** be symmetric with respect to particle labeling — terms like `sigma1 - sigma2` produce undefined results because the framework makes no guarantee about which particle is "particle 1" in a given pair evaluation. The Lennard-Jones potential `"4*epsilon*((sigma/r)^12-(sigma/r)^6); sigma=0.5*(sigma1+sigma2); epsilon=sqrt(epsilon1*epsilon2)"` demonstrates the canonical combining-rule pattern. **Interaction groups** allow restricting computation to specific set-pairs (e.g., solute-solvent only), and pairs appearing in multiple groups are evaluated multiple times. **Computed values** (via `addComputedValue()`) are per-particle quantities computed once per particle rather than once per pair, providing significant optimization for soft-core or lambda-dependent parameters.

`CustomGBForce` implements the most sophisticated computation model in the framework. It defines a **multi-stage pipeline**: first, per-particle **computed values** are calculated (which may depend on particle pairs), then **energy terms** are evaluated (which may also be per-pair or per-particle). Each stage has a **computation type** — `SingleParticle` or `ParticlePair` — that determines how the expression is evaluated. Platform constraints require that the first computed value must be a `ParticlePair` computation. The OBC implementation of GB/SA implicit solvent, shown in the header documentation, demonstrates all four stages: pair-wise Born integral calculation, single-particle Born radius computation, single-particle surface area/self-energy, and pair-wise polarization screening.

Sources: [CustomNonbondedForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomNonbondedForce.h#L89-L150), [CustomGBForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomGBForce.h#L44-L150)

## Collective Variable Forces

`CustomCVForce` bridges the gap between force-field energetics and collective-variable-based methods (metadynamics, umbrella sampling, etc.). Each collective variable is itself a `Force` object whose potential energy becomes the CV's value. This means *anything computable as a potential* can serve as a CV — including distances, angles, RMSD, coordination numbers (via `RMSDForce` or custom `CustomBondForce`), or even the energy of another custom force.

The energy expression takes the CV names as variables: `"k*(cv1-cv1_0)^2 + k2*(cv2-cv2_0)^2"`. Since each CV is a `Force` object, `CustomCVForce` takes ownership of it via `addCollectiveVariable(name, force)`. This composition pattern enables deeply nested force structures. The CV forces are evaluated by their own platform kernels, and the chain rule is applied automatically to compute forces on particles.

Sources: [CustomCVForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCVForce.h#L41-L70)

## The CustomIntegrator

`CustomIntegrator` is architecturally distinct from the custom forces. Rather than defining a potential energy, it defines a **complete integration algorithm** as a sequence of computation steps. Each step belongs to one of the `ComputationType` enum values and is executed in order during every call to `step()`.

### Computation Step Types

| Computation Type | Method | Scope | Description |
|-----------------|--------|-------|-------------|
| `ComputeGlobal` | `addComputeGlobal(var, expr)` | Single scalar | Evaluates expression → global variable |
| `ComputePerDof` | `addComputePerDof(var, expr)` | Per DOF vector | Evaluates expression → per-DOF variable (vector) |
| `ComputeSum` | `addComputeSum(var, expr)` | DOF → scalar | Evaluates per-DOF, sums → global variable |
| `ConstrainPositions` | `addConstrainPositions()` | System | Applies position constraints (SETTLE/SHAKE) |
| `ConstrainVelocities` | `addConstrainVelocities()` | System | Zeroes velocity along constrained directions |
| `UpdateContextState` | `addUpdateContextState()` | System | Allows Forces to update state (thermostats, barostats) |
| `IfBlockStart` | `beginIfBlock(condition)` | Control flow | Begins conditional block (global condition only) |
| `WhileBlockStart` | `beginWhileBlock(condition)` | Control flow | Begins loop block (global condition only) |
| `BlockEnd` | `endBlock()` | Control flow | Ends innermost if/while block |

### Pre-defined Variables

The integrator provides a rich set of pre-defined variables that serve as inputs to computation steps. **Global read-only variables** include `dt` (step size) and `energy` (total potential energy, with `energy0`, `energy1`, ... for per-force-group energies). **Per-DOF variables** include `x` (position, writable), `v` (velocity, writable), `f` (force, read-only, with `f0`, `f1`, ... for per-force-group forces), and `m` (mass, read-only). The `uniform` and `gaussian` random variables can appear in either global or per-DOF expressions. A single computation step may depend on **only one** energy variable and **only one** force variable.

### User-Defined Variables

Beyond the pre-defined set, you create custom variables with `addGlobalVariable(name, initialValue)` and `addPerDofVariable(name, initialValue)`. All variables are **persistent** between time steps — once set, they retain their value until explicitly changed. This persistence is what enables the RATTLE velocity Verlet algorithm shown below, where `x1` stores pre-constraint positions for use in the velocity correction step.

> [!TIP]
> Force recomputation in `CustomIntegrator` is automatic. When a per-DOF computation references `f` (or a per-force-group variant like `f0`), the integrator checks whether particle positions have changed since the last force evaluation. If they have, forces are recomputed transparently. You never call "compute forces" explicitly — the dependency graph between computation steps and force variables handles this automatically.

Sources: [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L86-L124), [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L396-L434), [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L548-L629)

## Implementing Standard Integrators with CustomIntegrator

The following examples demonstrate how well-known integration algorithms map to `CustomIntegrator` step sequences. These serve as verified starting points for building custom algorithms.

### Velocity Verlet with Constraints (RATTLE)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["addUpdateContextState()"] --> B["v = v + 0.5*dt*f/m"]
    B --> C["x = x + dt*v"]
    C --> D["x1 = x  (save pre-constraint)"]
    D --> E["constrainPositions()"]
    E --> F["v = v + 0.5*dt*f/m + (x-x1)/dt"]
    F --> G["constrainVelocities()"]
```

The key subtlety is the correction term `(x-x1)/dt` in the final velocity update. This accounts for the position shift introduced by constraint projection, ensuring that the velocity field remains consistent with the constrained trajectory. Without this term, the integrator would accumulate energy drift in constrained systems.

### r-RESPA Multiple Time Step Integrator

The r-RESPA algorithm partitions forces into fast (force group 0) and slow (force group 1) components, evaluating the fast forces multiple times per slow force evaluation. In `CustomIntegrator`, this is expressed using per-force-group force variables `f0` and `f1`:

```
v = v + 0.5*dt*f1/m           # slow half-kick (outer step)
for i in range(4):            # 4 inner steps
    v = v + 0.5*(dt/4)*f0/m   # fast half-kick (inner step)
    x = x + (dt/4)*v           # drift
    v = v + 0.5*(dt/4)*f0/m   # fast half-kick
v = v + 0.5*dt*f1/m           # slow half-kick
```

The automatic force recomputation mechanism ensures that `f0` is recomputed every inner step (because `x` changes) while `f1` is only recomputed when it is first referenced after a position change.

### Langevin Middle Integrator

The BAOAB-style Langevin integrator splits the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process into deterministic and stochastic half-steps. The `CustomIntegrator` version pre-computes the exponential factors `a = exp(-friction*dt)` and `b = sqrt(1 - exp(-2*friction*dt))` as global variables, then applies the O (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) step via `"a*v + b*sqrt(kT/m)*gaussian"`. This demonstrates the interplay between global variable initialization, per-DOF stochastic expressions, and constraint handling in a single algorithm.

Sources: [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L126-L210), [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L264-L329)

## Flow Control and Monte Carlo Methods

`CustomIntegrator` supports `if` and `while` blocks for implementing Metropolized algorithms and iterative schemes. The condition expression must involve only **global variables** and comparison operators (`=`, `<`, `>`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`). Blocks can be nested arbitrarily.

The canonical pattern for Metropolis acceptance uses the pre-defined `uniform` random variable:

```
beginIfBlock("uniform < acceptanceProbability")
    addComputePerDof("x", "xnew")     # accept: overwrite positions
endBlock()
```

For Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with step-size adaptation, a `while` block could iteratively reject and retry until an acceptance criterion is met. However, the documentation warns that there is no guard against infinite loops — the developer must ensure that while-conditions are guaranteed to eventually become false.

Sources: [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L212-L242)

## Kinetic Energy and Energy Derivatives

Two advanced features of `CustomIntegrator` require special attention because they affect thermodynamic observables.

The **kinetic energy expression** (`setKineticEnergyExpression()`) defines how the system's kinetic energy is reported. The default `"m*v*v/2"` is correct for velocity Verlet but wrong for leapfrog integrators where velocities are offset by half a time step. The leapfrog correction is `"m*v1*v1/2; v1=v+0.5*dt*f/m"`, which advances velocities by a half-step before squaring. The kinetic energy expression may reference `x`, `v`, `f`, `m`, `dt`, and user-defined variables, but **not** energy, random numbers, or adjustable context parameters.

The **`deriv()` function** provides access to energy derivatives with respect to context parameters: `"deriv(energy, lambda)"` gives ∂E/∂λ for the total energy, and `"deriv(energy1, lambda)"` restricts it to force group 1. These derivatives are only available if the corresponding Force has been configured with `addEnergyParameterDerivative()`. This mechanism enables on-the-fly free energy gradient computation within custom integration algorithms.

Sources: [CustomIntegrator.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomIntegrator.h#L331-L389)

## Platform Implementation Notes

Each platform compiles custom expressions differently, and these differences affect both performance and feature support.

| Platform | Compilation Strategy | Key Constraints |
|----------|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Reference** | Direct Lepton evaluation | Full feature support, slowest execution |
| **CPU** | JIT compilation via Lepton + vectorized execution | Supports most features; `CustomManyParticleForce` limited |
| **CUDA** | OpenMM C++ → CUDA kernel compilation | All custom forces supported; force group indexing optimized |
| **OpenCL** | OpenMM C++ → OpenCL kernel compilation | Same feature set as CUDA |
| **HIP** | OpenMM C++ → HIP kernel compilation | Same feature set as CUDA |

The `CustomGBForce` has the tightest platform constraints: all current platforms require the first computed value to be a `ParticlePair` computation, and all subsequent computed values must be `SingleParticle`. The `CustomManyParticleForce` supports permutation modes (`UniqueCentralParticle`, `SinglePermutation`, `AllPermutations`) that control how particle orderings are enumerated — this directly affects both correctness and computational cost.

Sources: [CustomGBForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomGBForce.h#L75-L78), [CustomManyParticleForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomManyParticleForce.h#L76-L82)

## Recommended Reading Path

Having understood the custom subsystem architecture, the following pages provide deeper context on the mechanisms discussed here:

- **[Lepton Expression Engine](18-lepton-expression-engine)** — How expressions are parsed, optimized, and compiled into platform kernels
- **[Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system)** — The compilation pipeline from expression string to GPU kernel
- **[Force Classes](13-force-classes)** — The base `Force` class hierarchy that custom forces extend
- **[Integrator Hierarchy](12-integrator-hierarchy)** — The base `Integrator` class and how `CustomIntegrator` fits within it
- **[Metadynamics and Enhanced Sampling](19-metadynamics-and-enhanced-sampling)** — How `CustomCVForce` integrates with well-tempered metadynamics

# Lepton Expression Engine



Lepton is OpenMM's embedded mathematical expression parser and compiler — a self-contained library at [`libraries/lepton/`](/openmm/openmm/tree/master/libraries/lepton) that transforms human-readable mathematical strings into highly optimized, JIT-compiled evaluation kernels. Every custom force, custom integrator, and tabulated function in OpenMM passes through Lepton at some point, making it the computational backbone of OpenMM's extensibility model. This page dissects Lepton's architecture from parse to machine code, revealing how a string like `"5*k*x^2 - sigma/sqrt(r)"` becomes native assembly executing at nanosecond latency.

## Architecture Overview

Lepton implements a multi-stage compilation pipeline: **lexing → parsing → AST construction → optimization → code generation**. Each stage produces a progressively more specialized representation, culminating in either a stack-based virtual machine (`ExpressionProgram`), a JIT-compiled function pointer (`CompiledExpression`), or a SIMD-vectorized kernel (`CompiledVectorExpression`). All representations originate from a single entry point — the `Parser` — and share a common abstract syntax tree (AST) defined by `ExpressionTreeNode`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["String Expression\n\"5*k*x^2 - sigma/sqrt(r)\""] --> B["Parser\nTokenize + Recursive Descent"]
    B --> C["ParsedExpression\nAbstract Syntax Tree"]
    C --> D["optimize()\nConstant Folding + Algebraic Simplification"]
    D --> E["ExpressionProgram\nStack-Based VM"]
    D --> F["CompiledExpression\nJIT-Compiled (asmjit)"]
    D --> G["CompiledVectorExpression\nSIMD Vectorized (AVX/NEON)"]
    
    C --> H["differentiate(x)\nSymbolic Derivative AST"]
    
    style A fill:#4a5568,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e53e3e,color:#fff
    style G fill:#e53e3e,color:#fff
```

The pipeline is strictly linear in the forward direction, but the AST representation at center is fully introspectable — it supports symbolic differentiation, variable renaming, and subexpression substitution, making it as useful for code analysis as for evaluation.

Sources: [Lepton.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/Lepton.h), [ParsedExpression.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/ParsedExpression.h#L47-L141)

## Module Structure

Lepton's implementation is compact and intentionally header-oriented, with all public API surfaces in `include/lepton/` and corresponding implementations in `src/`.

```
libraries/lepton/
├── include/
│   ├── Lepton.h                          # Aggregate include (single entry point)
│   └── lepton/
│       ├── Parser.h                      # Expression parser (static methods)
│       ├── ParsedExpression.h            # AST wrapper + optimization API
│       ├── ExpressionTreeNode.h          # AST node (Operation + children)
│       ├── Operation.h                   # Operation base class + 40+ subclasses
│       ├── ExpressionProgram.h           # Stack-based VM representation
│       ├── CompiledExpression.h          # JIT-compiled scalar evaluator
│       ├── CompiledVectorExpression.h    # SIMD-vectorized evaluator (float32)
│       ├── CustomFunction.h              # User-defined function interface
│       └── Exception.h                   # Lepton exception type
└── src/
    ├── Parser.cpp                        # Recursive descent + precedence climbing
    ├── ParsedExpression.cpp              # Optimization & symbolic differentiation
    ├── ExpressionTreeNode.cpp            # Node management + tree tag assignment
    ├── Operation.cpp                     # Operation implementations + derivatives
    ├── ExpressionProgram.cpp             # AST → stack program compilation
    ├── CompiledExpression.cpp            # AST → JIT compilation (x86/ARM)
    └── CompiledVectorExpression.cpp      # AST → SIMD JIT compilation
```

Sources: [Lepton.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/Lepton.h#L1-L42), [Operation.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/Operation.h#L1-L150)

## The Operation Taxonomy

Every node in a Lepton AST is an `Operation` — a polymorphic base class with 41 concrete subclasses enumerated in `Operation::Id`. Operations are the atomic units of computation, and each carries full responsibility for evaluation, cloning, and symbolic differentiation. This design means adding a new function requires implementing exactly one class.

The full operation set, organized by semantic category:

| Category | Operations | Arity |
|----------|-----------|-------|
| **Literals** | `CONSTANT`, `VARIABLE` | 0 |
| **Arithmetic** | `ADD`, `SUBTRACT`, `MULTIPLY`, `DIVIDE`, `POWER`, `NEGATE` | 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1 |
| **Specialized Arithmetic** | `ADD_CONSTANT`, `MULTIPLY_CONSTANT`, `POWER_CONSTANT`, `SQUARE`, `CUBE`, `RECIPROCAL` | 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 |
| **Transcendental** | `SQRT`, `EXP`, `LOG` | 1 each |
| **Trigonometric** | `SIN`, `COS`, `TAN`, `SEC`, `CSC`, `COT`, `ASIN`, `ACOS`, `ATAN`, `ATAN2` | 1 each (ATAN2: 2) |
| **Hyperbolic** | `SINH`, `COSH`, `TANH` | 1 each |
| **Special Functions** | `ERF`, `ERFC`, `STEP`, `DELTA` | 1 each |
| **Rounding/Selection** | `FLOOR`, `CEIL`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `ABS`, `SELECT` | 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3 |
| **Extensibility** | `CUSTOM` | Variable |

The "specialized arithmetic" operations — `ADD_CONSTANT`, `MULTIPLY_CONSTANT`, and `POWER_CONSTANT` — are **not parseable directly**. They are generated exclusively by the optimizer as replacements for binary operations where one operand is a known constant. This distinction is critical: it allows the JIT backend to emit a single `addsd` instruction instead of loading a constant from memory and adding, eliminating an entire memory access per evaluation.

Sources: [Operation.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/Operation.h#L78-L101)

## Parsing: Recursive Descent with Precedence Climbing

The `Parser` class exposes two static overloads of `parse()` — one accepting an expression string alone, and another accepting a map of `CustomFunction*` for user-defined extensions. Internally, parsing proceeds in three phases.

**Phase 1: Subexpression extraction.** Lepton supports inline subexpression definitions via semicolons. The parser splits the input on `;` characters from right to left, extracting named subexpressions (e.g., `temp=x^2`) that become available as variables in subsequent expressions. The final segment (before the last `;`, or the entire string if no `;` exists) is the primary expression.

**Phase 2: Tokenization.** The tokenizer walks the string character-by-character, classifying each span into one of seven token types: `Number`, `Operator`, `Variable`, `Function`, `LeftParen`, `RightParen`, `Comma`, or `Whitespace`. Numbers support decimal points and scientific notation (`3.14e-2`). The key disambiguation is between variables and functions: a function is any identifier immediately followed by `(`, stripped of its trailing parenthesis before lookup.

**Phase 3: Recursive descent with precedence climbing.** `parsePrecedence()` implements a Pratt parser. The precedence table is minimal — four levels for `+`/`-` (0), `*`/`/` (1), `^` (3), with unary `-` at level 2. Power is **right-associative** (`2^3^4 = 2^(3^4)`), while all other binary operators are left-associative. This matches standard mathematical convention.

```cpp
static const int Precedence[] = {0, 0, 1, 1, 3};  // +, -, *, /, ^
static const bool LeftAssociative[] = {true, true, true, true, false};
```

The parser constructs `ExpressionTreeNode` objects bottom-up. Each node owns an `Operation*` (heap-allocated, cloned on copy) and a vector of child nodes. Variables are resolved against the subexpression definitions first, falling back to `Operation::Variable` if not found, which means user-defined subexpressions shadow built-in variable names.

Sources: [Parser.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/Parser.h#L47-L76), [Parser.cpp](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/src/Parser.cpp#L48-L53)

## ParsedExpression: The AST Gateway

`ParsedExpression` wraps an `ExpressionTreeNode` root and provides the complete surface for analysis and transformation. It is the central hub of Lepton's API — every compilation target and every symbolic operation is a method on this class.

### Evaluation

Two overloads of `evaluate()` exist: a parameterless version that requires the expression to be constant-free, and a version accepting `std::map<std::string, double>` for variable binding. Evaluation is recursive — each node evaluates its children, then invokes `Operation::evaluate()`. This is correct but slow for repeated evaluation, which is why `CompiledExpression` exists.

### Optimization

The `optimize()` method applies a multi-pass transformation pipeline:

1. **Tag assignment** — `assignTags()` assigns unique integer tags to structurally identical subtrees, enabling memoization via `nodeCache` (a `map<int, ExpressionTreeNode>` keyed by tag).
2. **Constant subexpression folding** — `precalculateConstantSubexpressions()` walks the tree bottom-up. Any subtree whose children are all `CONSTANT` operations is evaluated at compile time and replaced with a single `CONSTANT` node.
3. **Algebraic simplification** — `substituteSimplerExpression()` applies pattern-matching rewrites in a loop until convergence (fixed-point). The rewrite rules are extensive and include identity elimination (`x+0=x`, `x*1=x`), strength reduction (`x/const → x*(1/const)` via `MULTIPLY_CONSTANT`), double negation cancellation, reciprocal normalization (`a*(1/b) → a/b`), power specialization (`x^2 → SQUARE`, `x^0.5 → SQRT`, `x^-1 → RECIPROCAL`), and duplicate elimination (`x*x → SQUARE`, `x*x*x → CUBE`, `x-x → 0`).

An overloaded `optimize(map<string, double>)` variant pre-evaluates specific variables to constants before running the optimization pipeline, enabling partial evaluation when some parameters are known at setup time.

Sources: [ParsedExpression.cpp](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/src/ParsedExpression.cpp#L62-L429)

### Symbolic Differentiation

The `differentiate(variable)` method constructs a new AST representing the analytical derivative with respect to a named variable. Each `Operation` subclass implements its own chain-rule logic via the `differentiate()` virtual method, receiving both the child nodes and their already-computed derivatives. The recursion is memoized via `nodeCache` (keyed by tag), so common subexpressions are differentiated exactly once. The resulting AST can itself be optimized, creating derivative expressions suitable for JIT compilation.

This facility is how OpenMM computes forces from energy expressions in `CustomForce` subclasses — the energy expression is parsed once, differentiated symbolically with respect to each particle coordinate, and the resulting derivative expressions are compiled for inner-loop evaluation.

Sources: [ParsedExpression.cpp](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/src/ParsedExpression.cpp#L387-L408)

### Additional Transformations

- **`renameVariables(map<string, string>)`** — performs a global find-and-replace of variable names throughout the AST, used by OpenMM when mapping generic expression variables to specific particle properties.
- **`createProgram()`** — compiles the AST to a stack-based `ExpressionProgram` (see below).
- **`createCompiledExpression()`** — compiles to a `CompiledExpression` with optional JIT.
- **`createCompiledVectorExpression(width)`** — compiles to a `CompiledVectorExpression` for SIMD batch evaluation.

Sources: [ParsedExpression.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/ParsedExpression.h#L100-L131)

## ExpressionProgram: Stack-Based Virtual Machine

`ExpressionProgram` linearizes the AST into a flat sequence of `Operation*` objects executed against a stack. Each operation pops its arguments, evaluates, and pushes the result. The class tracks `maxArgs` (the maximum argument count of any operation) and `stackSize` (the maximum stack depth encountered during compilation) for pre-allocation.

This representation is portable — it works on any platform without JIT support — but introduces per-operation dispatch overhead and prevents the compiler from eliminating intermediate temporaries. In practice, `ExpressionProgram` serves as a fallback and as a debugging aid (you can inspect individual operations via `getOperation(index)`). Performance-critical paths use `CompiledExpression` instead.

Sources: [ExpressionProgram.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/ExpressionProgram.h#L36-L102)

## CompiledExpression: JIT-Compiled Scalar Evaluator

`CompiledExpression` is Lepton's primary performance target. It compiles the AST into a flat operation array with pre-assigned workspace slots, then optionally generates native machine code via the **asmjit** dynamic compiler (conditionally enabled via `LEPTON_USE_JIT`).

### Workspace Model

Unlike the stack-based `ExpressionProgram`, `CompiledExpression` allocates a contiguous `workspace` vector where each intermediate result has a fixed slot index. Variables map to dedicated workspace indices (settable by the caller via `getVariableReference()`), and every operation writes its result to a pre-determined `target` slot. This eliminates stack management overhead and allows sequential argument optimization — when arguments occupy contiguous workspace slots, the JIT emits a pointer to the first slot rather than gathering scattered values.

### Variable Binding

Two binding mechanisms exist:

- **`getVariableReference(name)`** — returns a `double&` referencing the variable's slot in the internal workspace. Setting this reference before `evaluate()` provides the variable's value.
- **`setVariableLocations(map<string, double*>)`** — redirects variable reads to external memory addresses. This is critical when multiple compiled expressions share variables (e.g., a force expression and its derivative both reading particle coordinates). On JIT builds, changing variable locations triggers `generateJitCode()` to regenerate the machine code with updated memory references.

The `variablesToCopy` vector tracks which external pointers need to be copied into the workspace before evaluation, populating a simple pre-evaluation loop.

Sources: [CompiledExpression.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/CompiledExpression.h#L63-L95)

### JIT Compilation via asmjit

When `LEPTON_USE_JIT` is defined at build time, the constructor invokes `generateJitCode()` after workspace allocation. The JIT backend is **architecture-aware**, using `asmjit::x86::Compiler` for Intel/AMD and `asmjit::a64::Compiler` for ARM64. The generated code follows a consistent pattern:

1. **Variable loading** — emit `mov`/`ldr` instructions to load variable values from their bound addresses into hardware registers.
2. **Constant loading** — pre-compute all constant values used by operations (`CONSTANT`, `ADD_CONSTANT`, `MULTIPLY_CONSTANT`, `POWER_CONSTANT`, `RECIPROCAL`, `STEP`, `DELTA`) into a `constants` vector, then load them into registers. Deduplication ensures each unique constant is loaded exactly once.
3. **Power grouping** — `findPowerGroups()` identifies clusters of `SQUARE`, `CUBE`, and `POWER_CONSTANT` operations that share the same base argument and have powers with the same sign. These are evaluated together using an exponentiation-by-squaring algorithm, reducing the number of multiplications. For example, computing x², x³, and x⁵ simultaneously requires only 3 multiplications instead of 6.
4. **Operation emission** — each remaining operation is translated to native instructions. Transcendental functions (`sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log`, etc.) use `generateSingleArgCall()` / `generateTwoArgCall()`, which emit a sequence to move arguments to the calling convention registers, execute a `call` to the libc function, and retrieve the result.

The generated function pointer is stored as `double (*jitCode)()`, and `evaluate()` simply calls `jitCode()` when available, falling back to the interpreted loop otherwise.

> [!TIP]
> **Thread safety constraint**: `CompiledExpression` is explicitly NOT thread-safe. Each instance maintains mutable workspace state (`mutable std::vector<double> workspace`). In multi-threaded contexts (which is the norm in OpenMM's force evaluation loops), each thread must have its own `CompiledExpression` instance, or external synchronization must be applied.

Sources: [CompiledExpression.cpp](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/src/CompiledExpression.cpp#L19-L80), [CompiledExpression.cpp](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/src/CompiledExpression.cpp#L201-L350)

## CompiledVectorExpression: SIMD-Vectorized Evaluator

`CompiledVectorExpression` extends the compilation model to evaluate the same expression across **multiple data points simultaneously** using the CPU's vector unit (AVX on x86, NEON on ARM). This is designed for batch scenarios such as evaluating a bonded force across many bonds in a single vector pass.

### Key Design Differences from CompiledExpression

| Aspect | CompiledExpression | CompiledVectorExpression |
|--------|-------------------|--------------------------|
| **Precision** | `double` (64-bit) | `float` (32-bit) |
| **Vector width** | Scalar (1) | Configurable: 4 (always), 8 (AVX) |
| **Variable access** | `double& getVariableReference()` | `float* getVariablePointer()` → pointer to N floats |
| **JIT backend** | `asmjit::x86::Xmm` / `arm::Vec` | `asmjit::x86::Ymm` / `arm::Vec` |
| **Output** | `double evaluate()` | `const float* evaluate()` → pointer to N results |
| **Width query** | N/A | `static getAllowedWidths()` |

The workspace uses `std::vector<float>` instead of `double`, and variables are accessed as arrays of `width` floats. The `getAllowedWidths()` static method probes CPU features at runtime via CPUID (x86) or equivalent (ARM) to determine supported vector widths.

> [!TIP]
> **Precision trade-off**: The switch to single-precision (`float`) in `CompiledVectorExpression` is deliberate — AVX2 256-bit registers hold 8 × `float` but only 4 × `double`, so the throughput advantage is 2× for single-precision vectorized evaluation. OpenMM uses `CompiledVectorExpression` primarily in nonbonded force kernels where single precision is scientifically acceptable due to the use of mixed-precision force accumulation strategies.

Sources: [CompiledVectorExpression.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/CompiledVectorExpression.h#L38-L100)

## CustomFunction: Extending the Operation Set

`CustomFunction` is an abstract interface that allows users to inject arbitrary functions into expressions. To define a custom function, you implement four methods:

```cpp
class LEPTON_EXPORT CustomFunction {
    virtual int getNumArguments() const = 0;
    virtual double evaluate(const double* arguments) const = 0;
    virtual double evaluateDerivative(const double* arguments, const int* derivOrder) const = 0;
    virtual CustomFunction* clone() const = 0;
};
```

The `evaluateDerivative()` method accepts a `derivOrder` array where `derivOrder[i]` specifies how many times the function has been differentiated with respect to argument `i`. For example, `{0, 2}` means ∂²f/∂x₂². This multi-index scheme supports mixed partial derivatives, which is essential for expressions like `custom(r, dr/dx)` where nested differentiation is needed.

Custom functions are registered with the parser via a `map<string, CustomFunction*>` passed to `Parser::parse()`. At parse time, if a function name matches a custom function key, an `Operation::Custom` node is created that wraps a cloned copy of the `CustomFunction`. This ensures each AST node owns its function instance, making the tree safe to copy and persist.

The `PlaceholderFunction` subclass is a convenience for analysis-only scenarios — it returns 0.0 for all evaluations and derivatives while correctly reporting the expected argument count, allowing parsers to accept expressions containing unknown custom functions without attempting numerical evaluation.

Sources: [CustomFunction.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/CustomFunction.h#L36-L108)

## Optimization Rules Catalog

The `substituteSimplerExpression()` method in [`ParsedExpression.cpp`](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/src/ParsedExpression.cpp#L130-L384) implements a comprehensive algebraic simplification engine. Below is the complete rule set, organized by operation:

| Source Pattern | Result | Operation |
|---------------|--------|-----------|
| `ADD(x, 0)` | `x` | Identity |
| `ADD(x, -y)` | `SUBTRACT(x, y)` | Sign normalization |
| `SUBTRACT(x, x)` | `CONSTANT(0)` | Self-cancellation |
| `MULTIPLY(x, 0)` | `CONSTANT(0)` | Zero absorption |
| `MULTIPLY(x, 1)` | `x` | Identity |
| `MULTIPLY(x, -y)` | `NEGATE(MULTIPLY(x, y))` | Sign extraction |
| `MULTIPLY(x, RECIP(y))` | `DIVIDE(x, y)` | Reciprocal normalization |
| `MULTIPLY(x, x)` | `SQUARE(x)` | Squaring detection |
| `MULTIPLY(SQUARE(x), x)` | `CUBE(x)` | Cubing detection |
| `DIVIDE(x, x)` | `CONSTANT(1)` | Self-cancellation |
| `DIVIDE(0, x)` | `CONSTANT(0)` | Zero numerator |
| `DIVIDE(1, x)` | `RECIPROCAL(x)` | Unit numerator |
| `DIVIDE(x, 1)` | `x` | Identity |
| `DIVIDE(x, RECIP(y))` | `MULTIPLY(x, y)` | Reciprocal cancellation |
| `POWER(0, n)` | `CONSTANT(0)` | Zero base |
| `POWER(1, n)` | `CONSTANT(1)` | Unit base |
| `POWER(x, 0)` | `CONSTANT(1)` | Zero exponent |
| `POWER(x, 1)` | `x` | Identity |
| `POWER(x, -1)` | `RECIPROCAL(x)` | Negative identity |
| `POWER(x, 2)` | `SQUARE(x)` | Squaring specialization |
| `POWER(x, 3)` | `CUBE(x)` | Cubing specialization |
| `POWER(x, 0.5)` | `SQRT(x)` | Square root specialization |
| `NEGATE(NEGATE(x))` | `x` | Double negation |
| `MULTIPLY_CONST(a, MULTIPLY_CONST(b, x))` | `MULTIPLY_CONST(a*b, x)` | Constant folding |
| `SQRT(SQUARE(x))` | `ABS(x)` | Inverse relationship |
| `SQUARE(SQRT(x))` | `x` | Inverse relationship |
| `SELECT(x, y, y)` | `y` | Trivial selection |

Constant-argument operations with non-specialized constants are reduced to the corresponding `*_CONSTANT` operation variants (`ADD_CONSTANT`, `MULTIPLY_CONSTANT`, `POWER_CONSTANT`), which the JIT backend handles as immediate operands rather than memory loads.

Sources: [ParsedExpression.cpp](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/src/ParsedExpression.cpp#L130-L384)

## Integration with OpenMM's Custom Forces

Lepton's design is inseparable from its role in OpenMM. The [Custom Forces and Integrators](18-lepton-expression-engine) system uses Lepton at three critical points:

1. **Expression parsing at construction time** — when a `CustomBondForce`, `CustomNonbondedForce`, or `CustomIntegrator` receives an energy/per-particle update expression, it immediately calls `Parser::parse()` to validate syntax and produce an AST.
2. **Symbolic differentiation for force computation** — the energy expression is differentiated with respect to each degree of freedom using `ParsedExpression::differentiate()`. The resulting derivative expressions are optimized and compiled.
3. **JIT compilation for inner-loop evaluation** — the compiled expressions are evaluated millions of times per simulation step (once per bond, per particle pair, per particle, depending on the force type). The combination of constant folding (per-particle parameters like charges and masses become constants), specialized constant operations, and power grouping makes this feasible.

The variable sharing mechanism (`setVariableLocations()`) is particularly important here — multiple force expressions and their derivatives can all read from the same coordinate array, avoiding data duplication and ensuring consistency without explicit synchronization.

Sources: [CompiledExpression.h](/openmm/openmm/blob/master/libraries/lepton/include/lepton/CompiledExpression.h#L63-L80)

## API Quick Reference

| Class | Key Method | Purpose |
|-------|-----------|---------|
| `Parser` | `parse(string)` / `parse(string, customFunctions)` | Entry point: string → `ParsedExpression` |
| `ParsedExpression` | `evaluate()` / `evaluate(variables)` | Direct recursive evaluation |
| `ParsedExpression` | `optimize()` / `optimize(variables)` | Constant folding + algebraic simplification |
| `ParsedExpression` | `differentiate(variable)` | Symbolic differentiation → new `ParsedExpression` |
| `ParsedExpression` | `renameVariables(replacements)` | Global variable renaming |
| `ParsedExpression` | `createProgram()` | Compile to stack VM |
| `ParsedExpression` | `createCompiledExpression()` | Compile to JIT (scalar, double) |
| `ParsedExpression` | `createCompiledVectorExpression(width)` | Compile to JIT (SIMD, float) |
| `CompiledExpression` | `getVariableReference(name)` | Bind variable → `double&` |
| `CompiledExpression` | `setVariableLocations(map)` | Redirect variables to external memory |
| `CompiledExpression` | `evaluate()` | Execute compiled expression |
| `CompiledVectorExpression` | `getVariablePointer(name)` | Bind variable → `float*` |
| `CompiledVectorExpression` | `evaluate()` | Execute vectorized expression → `float*` |
| `CompiledVectorExpression` | `getAllowedWidths()` | Query CPU SIMD capabilities |
| `CustomFunction` | `evaluate()`, `evaluateDerivative()` | Define user functions with derivative support |
| `PlaceholderFunction` | Constructor `(numArgs)` | Stub function for analysis-only parsing |


# Metadynamics and Enhanced Sampling



This page documents OpenMM's infrastructure for advanced sampling techniques—alchemical free energy methods, collective variable biasing, and path-integral nuclear quantum effects. Unlike the standard [Integrator Hierarchy](12-integrator-hierarchy) and [Force Classes](13-force-classes), these tools alter the statistical mechanics landscape to accelerate rare event sampling, crossing energy barriers, and computing free energy differences. OpenMM implements this through three complementary subsystems: the **ATMForce** for alchemical transfer, the **CustomCVForce** for arbitrary collective variable biases, and the **RPMD plugin** for ring-polymer molecular dynamics.

## Architectural Overview

The enhanced sampling subsystem occupies a distinct layer in OpenMM's force architecture. Rather than modifying integrators directly, these classes extend the `Force` base class and embed *inner evaluation contexts*—secondary `Context` objects that compute energies at perturbed configurations or along collective variable manifolds. This design preserves platform portability while enabling gradient-chain propagation through the Lepton expression engine documented in [Lepton Expression Engine](18-lepton-expression-engine).

```mermaid
classDiagram
    direction TB

    class Force {
        <<abstract>>
        +createImpl() ForceImpl*
        +usesPeriodicBoundaryConditions() bool
    }

    class ATMForce {
        -string energyExpression
        -vector~Force*~ forces
        -vector~ParticleInfo~ particles
        -vector~GlobalParameterInfo~ globalParameters
        +addForce(Force*) int
        +addParticle() int
        +addParticle(CoordinateTransformation*) int
        +addGlobalParameter(name, defaultValue) int
        +getPerturbationEnergy(Context, u1, u0, energy)
        +addEnergyParameterDerivative(name)
        +Lambda1() string
        +Lambda2() string
        +Alpha() string$
        +W0() string$
    }

    class CustomCVForce {
        -string energyExpression
        -vector~VariableInfo~ variables
        -vector~GlobalParameterInfo~ globalParameters
        -vector~FunctionInfo~ functions
        +addCollectiveVariable(name, Force*) int
        +addGlobalParameter(name, defaultValue) int
        +addTabulatedFunction(name, TabulatedFunction*) int
        +addEnergyParameterDerivative(name)
        +getCollectiveVariableValues(Context, values)
        +getInnerContext(Context) Context&
    }

    class CoordinateTransformation {
        <<abstract>>
    }

    class FixedDisplacement {
        -Vec3 displ1
        -Vec3 displ0
        +getFixedDisplacement1() Vec3
        +getFixedDisplacement0() Vec3
    }

    class ParticleOffsetDisplacement {
        -int pDestination1
        -int pOrigin1
        -int pDestination0
        -int pOrigin0
    }

    class RMSDForce {
        -vector~Vec3~ referencePositions
        -vector~int~ particles
        +setReferencePositions(positions)
    }

    class RGForce {
        -vector~int~ particles
    }

    Force <|-- ATMForce
    Force <|-- CustomCVForce
    Force <|-- RMSDForce
    Force <|-- RGForce
    CoordinateTransformation <|-- FixedDisplacement
    CoordinateTransformation <|-- ParticleOffsetDisplacement
    ATMForce o-- CoordinateTransformation
    CustomCVForce o-- Force : "collective variables"
    ATMForce o-- Force : "displacement-dependent forces"
```

## ATMForce: Alchemical Transfer Method

The `ATMForce` class implements the Alchemical Transfer Method for computing absolute and relative binding free energies, based on the soft-core softplus potential described by Azimi et al. ([J. Chem. Inf. Model. 62, 309 (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.1c01129)). It originated from the [openmm-atmmetaforce-plugin](https://github.com/Gallicchio-Lab/openmm-atmmetaforce-plugin) and was integrated into the core API ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L1-L36)).

### Core Mechanism

ATMForce works by evaluating the system's potential energy under *two* sets of coordinates simultaneously: the **reference state** (u₀, current positions) and the **target state** (u₁, displaced positions). A custom energy expression combines these into a biasing potential, and alchemical parameters are dialed to sample the transformation path. The force owns a collection of child `Force` objects whose energies depend on the displacement, and computes the energy difference Δu = u₁ − u₀ between the two coordinate sets ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L62-L76)).

Each particle in the system must be registered with the ATMForce in the same order as the parent `System`. Particles can be stationary (no displacement), fixed-displaced in lab frame, or displaced by a *variable* vector computed from other particle positions at runtime ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L274-L315)).

### Coordinate Transformation Hierarchy

ATMForce supports three modes of particle displacement through the `CoordinateTransformation` abstract base class ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L557-L567)):

| Transformation | Class | Displacement Source | State Applicability |
|---|---|---|---|
| None (stationary) | `addParticle()` (no args) | Zero vector | Both states |
| Fixed lab-frame vector | `FixedDisplacement(d1, d0)` | Static `Vec3` values | `d1` for target, `d0` for reference |
| Variable particle offset | `ParticleOffsetDisplacement(dest1, orig1, dest0, orig0)` | `pos[dest] - pos[orig]` at runtime | Separate vectors per state |

The `FixedDisplacement` class stores two displacement vectors: one for the target state and one for the reference state. When only one vector is provided, the reference-state displacement defaults to zero ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L575-L588)). The `ParticleOffsetDisplacement` class enables dynamic displacements computed from the current positions of other particles—for example, swapping two ligands by displacing each to the other's position ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L590-L617)).

### Energy Expression Interface

ATMForce provides two constructor signatures with fundamentally different energy function strategies ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L204-L229)):

**Custom expression mode** accepts an arbitrary algebraic string in variables `u0` and `u1`:
```python
# Linear alchemical interpolation
atm = ATMForce("u0 + Lambda*(u1 - u0)")
atm.addGlobalParameter("Lambda", 0.5)
```

**Default softplus mode** accepts eight numeric parameters that configure the soft-core softplus potential directly:
```python
# Soft-core alchemical transfer
atm = ATMForce(lambda1=0.1, lambda2=0.2, alpha=0.3,
               uh=0.4, w0=0.5, umax=0.7,
               ubcore=0.6, acore=0.8, direction=1.0)
```

The default energy expression ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L137-L151)) implements the full ATM potential with a Fermi-like soft-core switching function that smoothly limits large energy spikes when particles overlap during transfer.

### Global Parameters

When using the default softplus constructor, ATMForce registers eight named global parameters accessible through static methods ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L416-L494)):

| Parameter | Static Accessor | Range | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Lambda1` | `ATMForce.Lambda1()` | [0, 1] | dimensionless |
| `Lambda2` | `ATMForce.Lambda2()` | [0, 1] | dimensionless |
| `Alpha` | `ATMForce.Alpha()` | ≥ 0 | (kJ/mol)⁻¹ |
| `Uh` | `ATMForce.Uh()` | — | kJ/mol |
| `W0` | `ATMForce.W0()` | — | kJ/mol |
| `Umax` | `ATMForce.Umax()` | > Ubcore | kJ/mol |
| `Ubcore` | `ATMForce.Ubcore()` | < Umax | kJ/mol |
| `Acore` | `ATMForce.Acore()` | > 0 | dimensionless |
| `Direction` | `ATMForce.Direction()` | {−1, +1} | dimensionless |

These parameters can be modified at runtime via `Context.setParameter()`, enabling real-time alchemical control without reinitializing the context. The `Direction` parameter switches between forward (+1) and backward (−1) transfer protocols.

### Retrieving Perturbation Energies

After each evaluation step, `getPerturbationEnergy()` returns the three key quantities needed for free energy post-processing: the displaced-state energy u₁, the reference-state energy u₀, and the ATMForce's biasing energy itself ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L407-L415)).

> [!TIP]
> **ATMForce particle registration order matters.** Every particle in the System must be added to the ATMForce in the same index order as `System.addParticle()`. Failure to do so results in incorrect force application, since ATMForce maps particles by position index to compute coordinate transformations. This constraint is enforced by the test suite at [TestATMForce.h](tests/TestATMForce.h#L276-L283).

### Verified Behavior: Force Propagation and Soft-Core Switching

The test suite demonstrates the complete alchemical pipeline. In the basic two-particle case, a harmonic bond is created and one particle is displaced by a fixed vector. At λ = 0, the energy equals u₀ (undisplaced); at λ = 1, it equals u₁ (displaced); and intermediate values linearly interpolate. The forces on the displaced particle scale linearly with λ ([TestATMForce.h](tests/TestATMForce.h#L89-L142)).

The three-particle swap test validates `ParticleOffsetDisplacement` by exchanging particles 1 and 2 through mutual offset vectors. The perturbation energy correctly equals the difference in harmonic bond energies between the swapped and original configurations ([TestATMForce.h](tests/TestATMForce.h#L144-L208)).

The soft-core test activates the Fermi switching function (with `umax=10`, `ubcore=3`, `acore=0.125`) and verifies that the force on the displaced particle is attenuated by the soft-core derivative factor relative to the linear case ([TestATMForce.h](tests/TestATMForce.h#L277-L337)).

## CustomCVForce: Collective Variable Biasing

The `CustomCVForce` class provides a general-purpose framework for constructing biasing potentials that depend on arbitrary collective variables (CVs). Each CV is itself a `Force` object—its computed potential energy becomes the scalar CV value. This architecture provides enormous flexibility: any quantity expressible as a potential function can serve as a CV ([CustomCVForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCVForce.h#L42-L70)).

### Design Architecture

CustomCVForce operates through a **dual-context** model. When a `Context` is created for a `System` containing a CustomCVForce, OpenMM internally constructs a second `System` containing only the CV-defining Forces, creates a secondary `Context` for it, and uses it to evaluate the CV values. This inner context is accessible via `getInnerContext()` ([CustomCVForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCVForce.h#L232-L247)).

The energy expression can reference CV values by name, global parameters, and tabulated functions, using the same Lepton expression grammar that powers [Custom Forces and Integrators](17-custom-forces-and-integrators). This includes arithmetic operators, trigonometric functions, `step()`, `delta()`, `select()`, and standard mathematical functions ([CustomCVForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCVForce.h#L63-L66)).

### Configuration API

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `addCollectiveVariable(name, Force*)` | Register a CV defined by a Force object |
| `addGlobalParameter(name, defaultValue)` | Add a tunable parameter to the energy expression |
| `addTabulatedFunction(name, TabulatedFunction*)` | Register a lookup table for the energy expression |
| `addEnergyParameterDerivative(name)` | Request ∂E/∂(parameter) for thermodynamic integration |
| `getCollectiveVariableValues(context, values)` | Query current CV values without bias |
| `getInnerContext(context)` | Access the internal CV evaluation Context |

### Energy Parameter Derivatives

CustomCVForce supports chain-rule differentiation through nested parameter dependencies. When a global parameter appears in both the energy expression *and* in a CV-defining Force, the derivative is correctly propagated through the chain rule. The test suite verifies this with a three-parameter example where `g1` and `g2` appear in the energy expression `v1*g1+g2`, while `g3` appears in the CV force but not the outer expression—yet `∂E/∂g3` is still correctly computed as `∂E/∂v1 × ∂v1/∂g3` ([TestCustomCVForce.h](tests/TestCustomCVForce.h#L94-L131)).

### Tabulated Function Support

Arbitrary-dimensional tabulated functions (e.g., `Continuous2DFunction`) can be embedded in the energy expression, enabling metadynamics-style biasing potentials. The test creates a 2D sine-cosine table and verifies energy and force correctness across the entire domain, including table extrapolation boundaries ([TestCustomCVForce.h](tests/TestCustomCVForce.h#L133-L191)).

> [!TIP]
> **Inner Context ownership and parameter updates.** When modifying a CV-defining Force's parameters (e.g., changing `RMSDForce` reference positions), you must call `updateParametersInContext()` on the *inner* Context obtained via `getInnerContext()`, not the outer simulation Context. However, for tabulated functions, `CustomCVForce.updateParametersInContext()` handles the propagation automatically ([CustomCVForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCVForce.h#L248-L258)).

## Built-in Collective Variable Forces

OpenMM provides two dedicated Force classes designed specifically for use as collective variables inside `CustomCVForce`. Each computes a physically meaningful structural quantity as its "potential energy," enabling direct use as CV definitions.

### RMSDForce

`RMSDForce` computes the root mean squared deviation between the current particle positions and a reference structure, after optimal rigid-body alignment. It accepts the full reference position array (matching the System particle count) and an optional subset of particle indices to restrict the alignment/comparison to a specific region ([RMSDForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/RMSDForce.h#L40-L67)).

```python
rmsd = RMSDForce(reference_positions, particles=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
cv = CustomCVForce("100*rmsd^2")  # Harmonic RMSD restraint
cv.addCollectiveVariable("rmsd", rmsd)
```

The reference positions can be updated at runtime via `setReferencePositions()` followed by `updateParametersInContext()`, making it suitable for adaptive sampling schemes where the target structure evolves ([RMSDForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/RMSDForce.h#L77-L97)).

### RGForce

`RGForce` computes the radius of gyration Rg of a specified particle set—the RMS distance of particles from their center of mass. It is a 2025 addition to the core API and follows the same "energy equals scalar value" convention as RMSDForce ([RGForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/RGForce.h#L40-L57)).

```python
rg = RGForce(particles=list(range(100)))  # All 100 particles
cv = CustomCVForce("k*(rg - rg0)^2")
cv.addCollectiveVariable("rg", rg)
cv.addGlobalParameter("k", 100.0)
cv.addGlobalParameter("rg0", 2.0)
```

Both `RMSDForce` and `RGForce` return `false` for `usesPeriodicBoundaryConditions()`, meaning they compute distances in absolute coordinates without minimum-image convention ([RMSDForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/RMSDForce.h#L104-L106), [RGForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/RGForce.h#L76-L78)).

## RPMD Plugin: Nuclear Quantum Effects

The **Ring Polymer Molecular Dynamics** plugin ([plugins/rpmd/](plugins/rpmd/)) implements path-integral methods for incorporating nuclear quantum effects—zero-point energy and tunneling—into molecular dynamics simulations. This is fundamentally different from the CV-biasing approach of CustomCVForce or the alchemical approach of ATMForce; instead, it replicates the classical system into N copies ("beads") connected by harmonic springs, with the quantum partition function emerging from the classical partition function of the ring polymer.

The plugin provides its own platform implementations across CUDA, OpenCL, HIP, and Reference backends ([plugins/rpmd/platforms/](plugins/rpmd/platforms/)), following the same [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system) architecture as the core platforms.

### RPMDIntegrator

The `RPMDIntegrator` extends the standard integrator hierarchy to propagate the ring polymer using thermostatted dynamics. It resides in the `openmmrpmd` namespace ([RPMDIntegrator.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RPMDIntegrator.h)).

### RPMDMonteCarloBarostat

A specialized barostat that correctly handles the extended phase space of the ring polymer during NPT simulations ([RPMDMonteCarloBarostat.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RPMDMonteCarloBarostat.h)).

## Integration Patterns and Use Cases

The three subsystems serve distinct sampling challenges and can be combined in specific ways:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Alchemical Free Energies"
        A1["ATMForce"] --> A2["λ-schedule\nsimulation"]
        A2 --> A3["ΔG via\nTI/FEP/MBAR"]
    end

    subgraph "Enhanced Sampling"
        B1["CustomCVForce"] --> B2["CV definition\nRMSDForce / RGForce"]
        B2 --> B3["Bias potential\nWell-Tempered MetaD"]
        B3 --> B4["Free energy\nsurface reconstruction"]
    end

    subgraph "Nuclear Quantum Effects"
        C1["RPMDIntegrator"] --> C2["Ring polymer\nbeads"]
        C2 --> C3["Path integral\nMD dynamics"]
    end

    A1 -.->|"addForce()"| B2
```

**ATMForce** targets equilibrium free energy differences (binding, solvation) through thermodynamic perturbation. The `getPerturbationEnergy()` method provides the raw energy differences needed for post-processing with MBAR or similar estimators.

**CustomCVForce** targets conformational sampling along low-dimensional CV manifolds. By combining `RMSDForce` and `RGForce` with tabulated biasing potentials, it supports umbrella sampling, metadynamics, and adaptive biasing force methods. The energy parameter derivative capability enables on-the-fly thermodynamic integration.

**RPMD** targets quantum statistical mechanics. It does not compute free energy differences directly but rather modifies the dynamics to include quantum nuclear effects, producing path-integral-averaged observables.

### Force Group Interaction

The test suite demonstrates an important architectural detail: when `ATMForce` contains a `NonbondedForce`, the original System-level copy should be assigned to a non-evaluated force group (or removed entirely) to avoid double-counting. The ATMForce internally evaluates its owned copy of the force at both displaced and undisplaced configurations ([TestATMForce.h](tests/TestATMForce.h#L340-L398)). Similarly, `CustomCVForce.setForceGroup()` isolates its evaluation from the rest of the system's force groups ([TestCustomCVForce.h](tests/TestCustomCVForce.h#L193-L235)).

## Expression Grammar Reference

Both `ATMForce` and `CustomCVForce` share the same Lepton-based expression grammar for their energy functions ([ATMForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/ATMForce.h#L131-L135), [CustomCVForce.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/CustomCVForce.h#L63-L66)):

| Category | Tokens |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^` |
| Basic functions | `sqrt`, `exp`, `log`, `abs`, `floor`, `ceil` |
| Trigonometric | `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `sec`, `csc`, `cot`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2` |
| Hyperbolic | `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh` |
| Special | `erf`, `erfc`, `min`, `max` |
| Piecewise | `step(x)`, `delta(x)`, `select(x, y, z)` |

The `step` function implements the Heaviside function (0 for x < 0, 1 otherwise). The `delta` function is a Kronecker-like indicator (1 if x = 0, 0 otherwise). The `select` function acts as a ternary operator: `select(cond, a, b)` returns `b` if `cond == 0`, otherwise `a`. These piecewise functions are essential for the default ATMForce softplus expression, which uses `step(Direction)` to switch between forward and reverse transfer modes.

## Further Reading

For the expression engine underlying all custom energy functions, see [Lepton Expression Engine](18-lepton-expression-engine). For building biasing forces with the broader custom force framework, see [Custom Forces and Integrators](17-custom-forces-and-integrators). To understand how these forces integrate with the simulation loop via the [Simulation Class](14-simulation-class), and for details on building the RPMD plugin alongside the core library, see [Plugin Architecture](20-plugin-architecture).

# Plugin Architecture



OpenMM's plugin system is the mechanism by which the simulation toolkit extends its capabilities beyond the core library — adding new force fields, integrators, and hardware backends without modifying the OpenMM source itself. This architecture is rooted in a two-phase dynamic loading protocol and a factory-driven kernel dispatch system, both defined in the `olla` (OpenMM Low-Level Abstraction) layer. Understanding this system is essential for any developer intending to contribute new physics or optimize existing kernels for novel hardware.

## The Loading Contract: Two C Entry Points

Every OpenMM plugin shared library must export exactly two `extern "C"` functions declared in [PluginInitializer.h](plugins/../olla/include/openmm/PluginInitializer.h#L49-L57). These form the contractual interface between the dynamic loader and the plugin:

1. **`registerPlatforms()`** — Called first, across all plugins. This is the phase where a plugin may register entirely new `Platform` objects (hardware targets) via `Platform::registerPlatform()`. Most kernel-extension plugins leave this empty, as they target already-registered platforms like Reference, CUDA, OpenCL, or HIP.

2. **`registerKernelFactories()`** — Called second, only after *all* plugins have completed their `registerPlatforms()` pass. This ordering guarantee eliminates initialization-order problems when one plugin needs to register a `KernelFactory` on a `Platform` defined by a different plugin. Within this function, the plugin iterates over `Platform::getNumPlatforms()`, uses `dynamic_cast` to identify the target platform type, and registers its `KernelFactory` instances.

The separation into two passes is the single most critical design decision in the plugin architecture. It means a CUDA-only kernel extension for the Amoeba force field can safely assume the CUDA platform already exists when `registerKernelFactories()` is invoked, even if the Amoeba plugin library happens to be loaded before the CUDA platform library in the dynamic loading sequence.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant Loader as "Platform::loadPluginLibrary()"
    participant P1 as "Plugin A (.so/.dll)"
    participant P2 as "Plugin B (.so/.dll)"
    participant Reg as Platform Registry

    App->>Loader: loadPluginLibrary("libPluginA.so")
    Loader->>P1: registerPlatforms()
    P1-->>Loader: (optionally registers new Platforms)
    
    App->>Loader: loadPluginLibrary("libPluginB.so")
    Loader->>P2: registerPlatforms()
    P2-->>Loader: (optionally registers new Platforms)
    
    Note over Loader: Phase 2 begins only after all plugins loaded
    Loader->>P1: registerKernelFactories()
    P1->>Reg: "iterate platforms, dynamic_cast & registerKernelFactory()"
    
    Loader->>P2: registerKernelFactories()
    P2->>Reg: "iterate platforms, dynamic_cast & registerKernelFactory()"
```

Sources: [PluginInitializer.h](olla/include/openmm/PluginInitializer.h#L49-L57), [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L243-L261)

## The Kernel Dispatch Chain: Platform → Factory → Impl

The runtime kernel dispatch follows a three-layer chain that the plugin architecture plugs into at the factory and impl layers. The [Platform](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h) class acts as a named registry of `KernelFactory` objects, keyed by kernel name strings. When the simulation engine needs a computation (e.g., calculating Drude forces), it requests a kernel by name from the platform associated with the current `Context`.

The [KernelFactory](olla/include/openmm/KernelFactory.h#L43-L49) is an abstract class with a single pure-virtual method:

```cpp
virtual KernelImpl* createKernelImpl(std::string name, const Platform& platform, ContextImpl& context) const = 0;
```

Each concrete factory subclasses this and dispatches on the kernel name string to instantiate the appropriate [KernelImpl](olla/include/openmm/KernelImpl.h#L40-L42) subclass. The returned `KernelImpl` is wrapped in a [Kernel](olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h) object, which provides type-safe access via the templated `getAs<T>()` method — eliminating raw `dynamic_cast` at every call site.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Platform {
        -map~string,KernelFactory~ kernelFactories
        +registerKernelFactory(name, factory)
        +createKernel(name, context) Kernel
        +supportsKernels(kernelNames) bool
        +getSpeed() double
        +getName() string
        +loadPluginLibrary(file)$
        +loadPluginsFromDirectory(dir)$
        +findPlatform(kernelNames)$ "Platform&"
    }
    
    class KernelFactory {
        <<abstract>>
        +createKernelImpl(name, platform, context)* "KernelImpl*"
    }
    
    class Kernel {
        -"KernelImpl*" impl
        +getAs~T~() "T&"
        +getName() string
        +getImpl() "KernelImpl&"
    }
    
    class KernelImpl {
        <<abstract>>
        #string name
        #"Platform*" platform
        +getName() string
        +getPlatform() "Platform&"
    }
    
    Platform "1" --> "*" KernelFactory : owns
    KernelFactory ..> KernelImpl : creates
    Kernel "1" *--> "1" KernelImpl : wraps
    Platform ..> Kernel : creates
```

The critical insight for plugin developers: you never subclass `Platform` unless you're introducing a new hardware backend. Instead, you create a `KernelFactory` subclass and register it against an existing platform. This is the extension point used by all four current plugins.

Sources: [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L161-L178), [KernelFactory.h](olla/include/openmm/KernelFactory.h#L43-L49), [Kernel.h](olla/include/openmm/Kernel.h#L68-L81), [KernelImpl.h](olla/include/openmm/KernelImpl.h#L40-L42)

## Plugin Internal Structure

Every plugin follows a consistent internal directory layout that mirrors the core OpenMM structure. Examining the four shipped plugins reveals this shared anatomy:

```
plugins/
├── amoeba/          # 6 kernel types, 4 platform targets, serialization, Python wrappers
├── drude/           # 4 kernel types, 4 platform targets, serialization, Python wrappers
├── rpmd/            # 1 kernel type,  4 platform targets, tests only
└── cpupme/          # Minimal: include/, src/, tests/ (no full platform structure)
```

The full-structure plugins (amoeba, drude, rpmd) each contain:

| Directory | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `openmmapi/include/openmm/` | Public API headers — new Force classes, Integrator classes, and their kernel interface definitions |
| `openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/` | `ForceImpl` subclasses that mediate between the public API and the kernel system |
| `platforms/common/src/` | Platform-agnostic kernel implementations shared across CUDA, OpenCL, and HIP |
| `platforms/reference/` | Scalar C++ reference implementation with its own `KernelFactory` |
| `platforms/cuda/` | CUDA-specific `KernelFactory` delegating to common kernels |
| `platforms/opencl/` | OpenCL-specific `KernelFactory` delegating to common kernels |
| `platforms/hip/` | HIP-specific `KernelFactory` delegating to common kernels |
| `serialization/` | XML serialization support for the plugin's Force/Integrator objects |
| `wrappers/` | Python wrapper generation scripts and Doxygen configuration |

The `cpupme` plugin is a notable exception — it provides only an optimized PME implementation for the CPU platform without defining new Force or Integrator classes, and therefore has a minimal structure with just `include/`, `src/`, and `tests/`.

Sources: [plugins/ directory structure](plugins/), [amoeba platforms](plugins/amoeba/platforms), [drude platforms](plugins/drude/platforms), [rpmd platforms](plugins/rpmd/platforms)

## Kernel Interface Definition: The Abstract Contract

Each plugin defines its kernel interfaces in a dedicated header within `openmmapi/include/openmm/`. These headers declare abstract `KernelImpl` subclasses that specify the computation API. For example, the Drude plugin defines three kernel types in [DrudeKernels.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeKernels.h):

| Kernel Class | Static Name String | Purpose |
|-------------|-------------------|---------|
| `CalcDrudeForceKernel` | `"CalcDrudeForce"` | Calculate Drude particle forces and energy |
| `IntegrateDrudeLangevinStepKernel` | `"IntegrateDrudeLangevinStep"` | One integration step of the Drude Langevin thermostat |
| `IntegrateDrudeSCFStepKernel` | `"IntegrateDrudeSCFStep"` | One integration step of the Drude SCF integrator |

Each kernel interface follows a consistent pattern: a static `Name()` method returning the canonical kernel name string, a constructor forwarding to `KernelImpl(name, platform)`, and pure-virtual methods defining the computation contract (`initialize()`, `execute()`, `copyParametersToContext()`, etc.). This design enforces that every platform implementation of the same kernel must provide identical method signatures.

The Amoeba plugin defines six kernel interfaces in [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h): `CalcAmoebaTorsionTorsionForceKernel`, `CalcAmoebaVdwForceKernel`, `CalcAmoebaMultipoleForceKernel`, `CalcAmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForceKernel`, `CalcAmoebaWcaDispersionForceKernel`, and `CalcHippoNonbondedForceKernel`. The RPMD plugin defines a single kernel, `IntegrateRPMDStepKernel`, in [RpmdKernels.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RpmdKernels.h).

Sources: [DrudeKernels.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeKernels.h#L51-L144), [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h#L56-L100), [RpmdKernels.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RpmdKernels.h#L40-L50)

## Factory Registration in Practice

The concrete `KernelFactory` implementations demonstrate two distinct strategies depending on the target platform.

**Reference platform factories** use an iterative search with `dynamic_cast` to locate their platform. This pattern appears in all three reference factories — for example, [ReferenceDrudeKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/drude/platforms/reference/src/ReferenceDrudeKernelFactory.cpp#L41-L53):

```cpp
extern "C" OPENMM_EXPORT void registerKernelFactories() {
    for (int i = 0; i < Platform::getNumPlatforms(); i++) {
        Platform& platform = Platform::getPlatform(i);
        if (dynamic_cast<ReferencePlatform*>(&platform) != NULL) {
            ReferenceDrudeKernelFactory* factory = new ReferenceDrudeKernelFactory();
            platform.registerKernelFactory(CalcDrudeForceKernel::Name(), factory);
            platform.registerKernelFactory(IntegrateDrudeLangevinStepKernel::Name(), factory);
            platform.registerKernelFactory(IntegrateDrudeSCFStepKernel::Name(), factory);
        }
    }
}
```

**GPU platform factories** use `Platform::getPlatformByName()` for direct lookup, wrapped in a try-catch that silently ignores failures if the target platform is not available. This is visible in [CudaDrudeKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/drude/platforms/cuda/src/CudaDrudeKernelFactory.cpp#L41-L52):

```cpp
extern "C" OPENMM_EXPORT void registerKernelFactories() {
    try {
        Platform& platform = Platform::getPlatformByName("CUDA");
        CudaDrudeKernelFactory* factory = new CudaDrudeKernelFactory();
        platform.registerKernelFactory(CalcDrudeForceKernel::Name(), factory);
        // ...
    }
    catch (std::exception ex) {
        // Ignore — CUDA platform not available
    }
}
```

Note that a single factory instance can be registered for multiple kernel names, since the factory's `createKernelImpl()` method dispatches internally based on the name string. The platform takes ownership of all registered factories and deletes them on shutdown.

Sources: [ReferenceDrudeKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/drude/platforms/reference/src/ReferenceDrudeKernelFactory.cpp#L41-L53), [CudaDrudeKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/drude/platforms/cuda/src/CudaDrudeKernelFactory.cpp#L41-L52), [AmoebaReferenceKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/amoeba/platforms/reference/src/AmoebaReferenceKernelFactory.cpp#L55-L70), [ReferenceRpmdKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/rpmd/platforms/reference/src/ReferenceRpmdKernelFactory.cpp#L40-L47)

## Cross-Plugin Kernel Sharing via the Common Layer

A significant architectural optimization is the **common kernel layer** shared across GPU platforms. Each plugin with GPU implementations contains a `platforms/common/src/` directory with platform-agnostic kernel implementations. The CUDA, OpenCL, and HIP factories do not implement kernels directly — instead they delegate to the common layer, which abstracts the differences between GPU compute APIs through an internal abstraction.

This is evident in the Drude CUDA factory: `CudaDrudeKernelFactory::createKernelImpl()` instantiates `CommonCalcDrudeForceKernel`, `CommonIntegrateDrudeLangevinStepKernel`, and `CommonIntegrateDrudeSCFStepKernel` — not CUDA-specific classes. The common layer accesses the GPU context through platform-specific data pointers (`context.getPlatformData()`) but implements the physics once.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Plugin: Drude"
        API["DrudeForce / DrudeLangevinIntegrator"]
        KI["DrudeKernels.h<br/>(abstract interfaces)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Platform Dispatch"
        Ref["ReferenceDrudeKernelFactory"]
        Cuda["CudaDrudeKernelFactory"]
        CL["OpenCLDrudeKernelFactory"]
        HIP["HipDrudeKernelFactory"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Implementations"
        RefK["ReferenceDrudeKernels<br/>(pure C++)"]
        Common["CommonDrudeKernels<br/>(platform-agnostic GPU)"]
    end
    
    API -->|requests kernel| KI
    KI -->|Reference| Ref
    KI -->|CUDA| Cuda
    KI -->|OpenCL| CL
```
