```mermaid
    KI -->|HIP| HIP
    
    Ref -->|creates| RefK
    Cuda -->|creates| Common
    CL -->|creates| Common
    HIP -->|creates| Common
    
    style Common fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
```

Sources: [CommonDrudeKernels.cpp](plugins/drude/platforms/common/src/CommonDrudeKernels.cpp), [CudaDrudeKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/drude/platforms/cuda/src/CudaDrudeKernelFactory.cpp#L58-L67)

## Dynamic Loading at Runtime

The `Platform` class provides two static methods for loading plugins at runtime, declared in [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L243-L273):

- **`loadPluginLibrary(file)`** — Loads a single shared library by path. Invokes both `registerPlatforms()` and `registerKernelFactories()` on the loaded library. Throws on failure.
- **`loadPluginsFromDirectory(directory)`** — Scans a directory (or colon/semicolon-separated list of directories) and attempts to load every file. Failures are silently recorded and retrievable via `getPluginLoadFailures()`.
- **`getDefaultPluginsDirectory()`** — Returns the `OPENMM_PLUGIN_DIR` environment variable, or a platform-specific default.

From Python, the canonical loading pattern is:

```python
from openmm import Platform
Platform.loadPluginsFromDirectory(Platform.getDefaultPluginsDirectory())
```

This is typically called automatically by the OpenMM Python package on import, but advanced users may call it explicitly to load plugins from custom locations.

> [!TIP]
> The `OPENMM_PLUGIN_DIR` environment variable is the standard mechanism for installing third-party plugins. Set it to the directory containing your plugin shared libraries, and they will be discovered automatically by `Platform.getDefaultPluginsDirectory()`. On conda installations, this typically points to `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/openmm/plugins`.

Sources: [Platform.h](olla/include/openmm/Platform.h#L243-L273)

## Serialization Integration

Plugins that define new `Force` or `Integrator` subclasses must also integrate with OpenMM's serialization system for checkpoint/restart support. The Amoeba and Drude plugins include `serialization/` directories with `XmlSerializer` registrations that allow their objects to be written to and read from XML.

The serialization integration follows the standard OpenMM pattern: each serializable class registers itself with `XmlSerializer::registerType()` providing a tag name, type, and serialization proxy. This registration happens within the plugin's initialization code so that it occurs when the plugin is loaded.

## Static Library Build Support

The Amoeba plugin demonstrates support for static linking via the `OPENMM_BUILDING_STATIC_LIBRARY` preprocessor macro. In [AmoebaReferenceKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/amoeba/platforms/reference/src/AmoebaReferenceKernelFactory.cpp#L55-L60), the registration functions are declared as `static` rather than `extern "C"` when building as a static library:

```cpp
#ifdef OPENMM_BUILDING_STATIC_LIBRARY
static void registerPlatforms() {
#else
extern "C" OPENMM_EXPORT void registerPlatforms() {
#endif
```

This allows the same source files to be compiled into either a shared plugin library or linked statically into the OpenMM core, with the registration functions called explicitly by the host application in the static case.

Sources: [AmoebaReferenceKernelFactory.cpp](plugins/amoeba/platforms/reference/src/AmoebaReferenceKernelFactory.cpp#L55-L60)

## Summary of Current Plugins

The following table summarizes the four plugins shipped with the OpenMM repository and their kernel registrations:

| Plugin | New Force Classes | New Integrator Classes | Kernel Types Registered | GPU Common Layer | Python Wrappers | Serialization |
|--------|------------------|----------------------|------------------------|------------------|-----------------|--------------|
| **amoeba** | `AmoebaMultipoleForce`, `AmoebaVdwForce`, `AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce`, `AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce`, `AmoebaWcaDispersionForce`, `HippoNonbondedForce` | — | 6 | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **drude** | `DrudeForce` | `DrudeLangevinIntegrator`, `DrudeSCFIntegrator`, `DrudeNoseHooverIntegrator` | 4 | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **rpmd** | — | `RPMDIntegrator`, `RPMDMonteCarloBarostat` | 1 | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| **cpupme** | — | — | N/A (optimizes existing PME) | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

## Continuing the Exploration

The plugin architecture interfaces directly with the platform abstraction layer and the core API class system. To understand how plugins are consumed by the simulation engine, see [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system). For concrete examples of how the Amoeba and Drude plugins expose their physics to end users, continue to [Amoeba Polarizable Force Field](21-amoeba-polarizable-force-field) and [Drude and RPMD Plugins](22-drude-and-rpmd-plugins). For the serialization mechanisms plugins integrate with, see [Serialization and Checkpointing](23-serialization-and-checkpointing).

# Amoeba Polarizable Force Field



The AMOEBA (Atomic Multipole Optimized Energetics for Biomolecular Applications) plugin is OpenMM's GPU-accelerated implementation of Jay Ponder's polarizable force field. Unlike fixed-charge force fields, AMOEBA models electronic polarization through atomic multipoles (charge, dipole, quadrupole) and mutually induced dipoles, yielding significantly higher accuracy for electrostatic interactions at the cost of greater computational complexity. This page documents the plugin's internal architecture, force class hierarchy, platform kernel dispatch, polarization solver strategies, and serialization infrastructure — everything an advanced developer needs to extend, debug, or integrate AMOEBA simulations.

Sources: [08_amoeba_plugin.rst](docs-source/usersguide/library/08_amoeba_plugin.rst#L1-L15), [OpenMMAmoeba.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/OpenMMAmoeba.h#L1-L41)

## Architectural Overview

The AMOEBA plugin follows the same [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system) architecture as the core OpenMM library: a set of public API Force classes in `openmmapi/`, platform-specific kernel implementations in `platforms/`, a kernel abstraction layer in `amoebaKernels.h`, and serialization proxies for checkpoint/restart. The critical design difference from core OpenMM forces is the presence of **polarization solvers** — iterative or extrapolative algorithms that must converge induced dipoles self-consistently within each force evaluation. This requirement deeply influences the kernel implementation across all platforms.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Public API Layer"
        AMF["AmoebaMultipoleForce<br/>Electrostatics + Polarization"]
        AVF["AmoebaVdwForce<br/>Buffered 14-7 / LJ 12-6"]
        ATTF["AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce<br/>Coupled Torsion Grids"]
        AWDF["AmoebaWcaDispersionForce<br/>Implicit Solvent Dispersion"]
        AGKF["AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce<br/>Implicit Solvent GK"]
        HNF["HippoNonbondedForce<br/>Combined HIPPO Nonbonded"]
    end

    subgraph "Kernel Abstraction Layer"
        KAMF["CalcAmoebaMultipoleForceKernel"]
        KAVF["CalcAmoebaVdwForceKernel"]
        KATTF["CalcAmoebaTorsionTorsionForceKernel"]
        KAWDF["CalcAmoebaWcaDispersionForceKernel"]
        KAGKF["CalcAmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForceKernel"]
        KHNF["CalcHippoNonbondedForceKernel"]
    end

    subgraph "Platform Implementations"
        REF["Reference Platform"]
        CUDA["CUDA Platform"]
        HIP["HIP Platform"]
        OCL["OpenCL Platform"]
        COM["Common Kernels"]
    end

    subgraph "Serialization"
        PROXIES["Force Proxies"]
    end

    AMF --> KAMF
    AVF --> KAVF
    ATTF --> KATTF
    AWDF --> KAWDF
    AGKF --> KAGKF
    HNF --> KHNF

    KAMF --> REF & CUDA & HIP & OCL
    KAVF --> REF & CUDA & HIP & OCL & COM
    KATTF --> REF & CUDA & HIP & OCL
    KAWDF --> REF & COM
    KAGKF --> REF & COM
    KHNF --> REF & CUDA & HIP & OCL

    AMF -.-> PROXIES
    AVF -.-> PROXIES
    ATTF -.-> PROXIES
    AWDF -.-> PROXIES
    AGKF -.-> PROXIES
    HNF -.-> PROXIES
```

The plugin directory at `plugins/amoeba/` contains the following structural layout:

```
plugins/amoeba/
├── openmmapi/          # Public API: Force classes + headers
│   ├── include/openmm/ # AmoebaMultipoleForce.h, AmoebaVdwForce.h, etc.
│   └── src/            # Force implementations + Impl classes
├── platforms/          # Per-platform kernel implementations
│   ├── reference/      # Reference (double-precision) baseline
│   ├── cuda/           # CUDA GPU kernels
│   ├── hip/            # HIP GPU kernels (AMD)
│   ├── opencl/         # OpenCL GPU kernels
│   └── common/         # Shared CPU-based kernels (WCA, Vdw, GK)
├── serialization/      # XML/bytecode serialization proxies
├── tests/              # Unit test headers for each force
└── wrappers/           # SWIG wrapper generation
```

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](plugins/amoeba/CMakeLists.txt), [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h#L1-L40)

## Force Class Hierarchy

The AMOEBA plugin exposes six Force classes through the umbrella header [OpenMMAmoeba.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/OpenMMAmoeba.h#L33-L40). All inherit from the core `openmm::Force` base class and follow the established pattern of storing per-particle parameters in internal `Info` structs. Each Force class has a corresponding `ForceImpl` subclass that bridges to the kernel abstraction layer.

### Core Electrostatics: AmoebaMultipoleForce

`AmoebaMultipoleForce` is the computational heart of the AMOEBA model. It handles permanent atomic multipoles (charge, dipole, quadrupole), induced dipole polarization, and optionally PME long-range electrostatics. Each particle stores a complete multipole description defined in its **local molecular frame**, along with axis type information and reference atom indices that define the rotation from the molecular to the laboratory frame.

The class exposes three **polarization strategies** through the `PolarizationType` enum, each representing a fundamentally different trade-off between accuracy and computational cost:

| Polarization Type | Enum Value | Description | Iterative? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutual | 0 | Fully self-consistent induced dipoles, iterated until convergence | Yes |
| Direct | 1 | Induced dipoles depend only on fixed multipoles (no mutual coupling) | No |
| Extrapolated | 2 | Few iterative steps followed by analytic extrapolation to converged values | Partially |

The mutual polarization solver is controlled by two key parameters: `getMutualInducedMaxIterations()` (default iteration ceiling) and `getMutualInducedTargetEpsilon()` (convergence threshold). For the extrapolated method, `setExtrapolationCoefficients()` accepts a vector whose length determines the number of SCF iterations before extrapolation; the current default coefficients are `[-0.154, 0.017, 0.658, 0.474]`, though the API documentation warns these may change in future releases.

The `MultipoleAxisTypes` enum defines six axis conventions for rotating multipoles from the molecular to the lab frame: `ZThenX`, `Bisector`, `ZBisect`, `ThreeFold`, `ZOnly`, and `NoAxisType`. Each particle specifies its axis type along with three reference atom indices (`multipoleAtomZ`, `multipoleAtomX`, `multipoleAtomY`) that define the local coordinate system. The covalent topology is encoded via `setCovalentMap()` using `CovalentType` entries (`Covalent12` through `PolarizationCovalent14`) that control polarization group exclusion logic.

Beyond standard force/energy evaluation, the class provides diagnostic accessors for retrieving **lab-frame permanent dipoles**, **induced dipoles**, **total dipoles**, **electrostatic potential** on arbitrary grids, and **system multipole moments** — all queried post-evaluation from a live `Context`.

Sources: [AmoebaMultipoleForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaMultipoleForce.h#L55-L98), [AmoebaMultipoleForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaMultipoleForce.h#L227-L298), [AmoebaMultipoleForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaMultipoleForce.h#L308-L351), [AmoebaMultipoleForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaMultipoleForce.h#L370-L442)

### Van der Waals: AmoebaVdwForce

`AmoebaVdwForce` implements the repulsion-dispersion term, supporting two potential functions selected via the `PotentialFunction` enum: **Buffered147** (the AMOEBA default, a buffered 14-7 potential) and **LennardJones** (standard 12-6). A distinctive feature is the **hydrogen reduction factor** — each particle can place its interaction site at an offset along the bond vector toward its parent atom, typically used to shift hydrogen vdW sites closer to the heavy atom.

The class supports two parameterization modes. In the **per-particle mode**, each particle carries its own sigma and epsilon values. In the **type-based mode**, particles reference a type index, and per-type parameters are defined via `addParticleType()`, with optional pair-specific overrides via `addTypePair()` that bypass the combining rule for selected type combinations.

Since version 8.0, `AmoebaVdwForce` also supports **alchemical free energy calculations** through the `AlchemicalMethod` enum (`None`, `Decouple`, `Annihilate`). When enabled, per-particle `isAlchemical` flags mark atoms undergoing transformation, and a context parameter `"AmoebaVdwLambda"` (accessible via the static `Lambda()` method) controls the softcore state between 0.0 and 1.0. The softcore functional form follows Jiao et al. (2008) and can be tuned via softcore power (default 5) and alpha (default 0.7) parameters.

Sources: [AmoebaVdwForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaVdwForce.h#L40-L78), [AmoebaVdwForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaVdwForce.h#L109-L136), [AmoebaVdwForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaVdwForce.h#L177-L232)

### Coupled Torsions: AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce

`AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce` implements the coupled torsion-torsion (tortor) energy term, which captures the correlation between two adjacent dihedral angles — a critical correction for protein backbone energetics. The term is represented as a five-dimensional spline grid indexed by the two torsion angles (with one grid per distinct pair of atom types). This class stores per-particle grid data and maps each coupled torsion to its corresponding spline lookup.

Sources: [AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce.h), [08_amoeba_plugin.rst](docs-source/usersguide/library/08_amoeba_plugin.rst#L55-L57)

### Implicit Solvent: AmoebaWcaDispersionForce and AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce

Implicit solvent in the AMOEBA plugin is split across two complementary Force classes. **AmoebaWcaDispersionForce** computes the WCA (Weeks-Chandler-Andersen) dispersion correction and the ACE-based solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) cavity term, which replaces TINKER's GPU-unfriendly SASA algorithm with the Analytical Continuum Electrostatics approximation. **AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce** implements the Generalized Kirkwood polar solvation model, computing the reaction field using Grycuk Born radii. Both are implemented as **common kernels** shared across the Reference and CPU platforms rather than having per-platform GPU implementations.

Sources: [AmoebaWcaDispersionForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaWcaDispersionForce.h), [AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce.h), [08_amoeba_plugin.rst](docs-source/usersguide/library/08_amoeba_plugin.rst#L96-L105)

### HIPPO Nonbonded: HippoNonbondedForce

`HippoNonbondedForce` is a monolithic force class that consolidates **all** nonbonded interactions in the HIPPO (Hydrogen-like Intermolecular Polarizable Potential) successor to AMOEBA: electrostatics, induction, charge transfer, dispersion, and Pauli repulsion. The design rationale for merging these into a single Force is efficiency — the terms share multipole definitions and are most naturally computed together on GPUs. The class manages separate PME parameters for electrostatics (`getPMEParameters`) and dispersion (`getDPMEParameters`), supports the same extrapolation coefficient scheme for induced dipoles, and provides a switching function to smooth repulsion and charge-transfer interactions near the cutoff boundary.

Sources: [HippoNonbondedForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/HippoNonbondedForce.h#L42-L55), [HippoNonbondedForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/HippoNonbondedForce.h#L113-L175), [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h#L256-L309)

## Kernel Abstraction and Platform Dispatch

The kernel interface is defined in [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h) with six abstract kernel classes. Each follows the standard OpenMM kernel pattern: a `Name()` static factory identifier, an `initialize()` method that receives the System and Force objects, an `execute()` method that performs force/energy computation, and optional query methods for dipole retrieval and parameter introspection.

| Kernel Class | Force | Platform Implementations | GPU Kernel Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CalcAmoebaMultipoleForceKernel` | AmoebaMultipoleForce | Reference, CUDA, HIP, OpenCL | `kernels/` subdirectory |
| `CalcAmoebaVdwForceKernel` | AmoebaVdwForce | Reference, CUDA, HIP, OpenCL, Common | `kernels/` subdirectory |
| `CalcAmoebaTorsionTorsionForceKernel` | AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce | Reference, CUDA, HIP, OpenCL | Inline |
| `CalcAmoebaWcaDispersionForceKernel` | AmoebaWcaDispersionForce | Reference, Common | N/A (CPU) |
| `CalcAmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForceKernel` | AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce | Reference, Common | N/A (CPU) |
| `CalcHippoNonbondedForceKernel` | HippoNonbondedForce | Reference, CUDA, HIP, OpenCL | `kernels/` subdirectory |

The GPU platforms (CUDA, HIP, OpenCL) store their kernel source strings in generated files like `CudaAmoebaKernelSources.cpp.in` / `CudaAmoebaKernelSources.h.in`, which embed the actual kernel source code as C++ string constants. This follows the same pattern as the core OpenMM platforms described in [CUDA Platform Implementation](9-cuda-platform-implementation). The **common** platform provides CPU-optimized implementations for forces that don't benefit from GPU parallelism (WCA dispersion and GK solvation).

Sources: [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h#L44-L134), [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h#L176-L254), [CudaAmoebaKernelSources.cpp.in](plugins/amoeba/platforms/cuda/src/CudaAmoebaKernelSources.cpp.in)

## Polarization Solver Internals

The polarization solver is the most architecturally distinctive component of the AMOEBA plugin. In **Mutual** mode, the solver iterates the induced dipole equation:

```
μ_induced = α · E_fixed + α · T · μ_induced
```

where α is the atomic polarizability, E_fixed is the electric field from permanent multipoles, and T is the dipole-dipole interaction tensor. The iteration continues until the change in induced dipoles falls below `mutualInducedTargetEpsilon` or `mutualInducedMaxIterations` is reached.

In **Extrapolated** mode, the solver performs a small number of SCF iterations (determined by the length of the extrapolation coefficient vector), then applies an analytic extrapolation:

```
μ_final = c_0·μ_0 + c_1·μ_1 + c_2·μ_2 + ... + c_n·μ_n
```

where μ_i is the induced dipole vector after iteration i and c_i are the extrapolation coefficients. This approach can achieve near-mutual accuracy at a fraction of the cost, making it particularly attractive for GPU implementations where iterative convergence is expensive due to global synchronization requirements. The default 4-term coefficient set `[-0.154, 0.017, 0.658, 0.474]` was calibrated to minimize energy error relative to fully converged mutual polarization.

> [!TIP]
> The extrapolated polarization mode is not merely a performance optimization — it fundamentally changes the integration landscape. Because the induced dipoles at each timestep are a deterministic function of the current coordinates (no iterative solver state to carry over), the extrapolated method produces smoother potential energy surfaces and can improve integrator stability in some regimes. However, the coefficients are release-dependent and may change.

The `getInducedDipoles()`, `getLabFramePermanentDipoles()`, and `getTotalDipoles()` methods on `AmoebaMultipoleForce` allow real-time inspection of the polarization state, which is invaluable for debugging convergence issues or validating that polarization groups are correctly configured.

Sources: [AmoebaMultipoleForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaMultipoleForce.h#L70-L92), [AmoebaMultipoleForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaMultipoleForce.h#L336-L351), [AmoebaMultipoleForce.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/AmoebaMultipoleForce.h#L371-L392)

## TINKER Compatibility and Unit Conversions

A critical concern for developers working with the AMOEBA plugin is the **unit system mismatch** between TINKER and OpenMM. TINKER parameter files use kcal/mol for energy, Ångströms for distance, and atomic charge units, while OpenMM uses kJ/mol, nanometers, and elementary charges. The mapping requires systematic conversion of all force-field parameters. Standard bonded terms (bonds mapped to `HarmonicBondForce`, angles to `HarmonicAngleForce`, Urey-Bradley to `HarmonicBondForce`) are handled by the TINKER-OpenMM conversion layer. The following table documents the complete TINKER-to-OpenMM force mapping with support status:

| TINKER Force Term | OpenMM Force Class | Supported Options | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ebond1` (bond) | `HarmonicBondForce` | HARMONIC only | MORSE not implemented |
| `Eangle71` (angle) | `HarmonicAngleForce` | HARMONIC, IN-PLANE | LINEAR, FOURIER not implemented |
| `etors1a` (torsion) | `PeriodicTorsionForce` | All | Smoothing (etors1b) not supported |
| `etortor1` (tortor) | `AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce` | All | — |
| `eopbend1` (opbend) | `AmoebaOutOfPlaneBendForce` | ALLINGER only | W-D-C not implemented |
| `epitors1` (pitor) | `AmoebaPiTorsionForce` | All | — |
| `estrbnd1` (strbnd) | `AmoebaStretchBendForce` | All | — |
| `ehal1a` (vdw) | `AmoebaVdwForce` | All | LIGHTS (ehal1b) not supported |
| `empole1a` (mpole) | `AmoebaMultipoleForce` | MUTUAL, DIRECT | — |
| `empole1c` (PME) | `AmoebaMultipoleForce` | MUTUAL, DIRECT + PME | VACUUM boundary unsupported |
| `esolv1` (solvate) | AmoebaWcaDisp + AmoebaGK | GK + grycuk only | ASP, SASA, ONION, pb unsupported |
| `eurey1` (urey) | `HarmonicBondForce` | All | — |

Sources: [08_amoeba_plugin.rst](docs-source/usersguide/library/08_amoeba_plugin.rst#L47-L82)

## Serialization Infrastructure

Every AMOEBA Force class has a corresponding **serialization proxy** in `plugins/amoeba/serialization/src/` that enables the [Serialization and Checkpointing](23-serialization-and-checkpointing) workflow. The proxy registration is centralized in [AmoebaSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp](plugins/amoeba/serialization/src/AmoebaSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp). Each proxy implements `getProxyTypeName()` for XML type identification and manages the marshaling/unmarshaling of per-particle parameters, covalent maps, PME settings, and polarization configuration.

| Proxy Class | Force | Serialization File |
|---|---|---|
| `AmoebaMultipoleForceProxy` | AmoebaMultipoleForce | `AmoebaMultipoleForceProxy.cpp` |
| `AmoebaVdwForceProxy` | AmoebaVdwForce | `AmoebaVdwForceProxy.cpp` |
| `AmoebaTorsionTorsionForceProxy` | AmoebaTorsionTorsionForce | `AmoebaTorsionTorsionForceProxy.cpp` |
| `AmoebaWcaDispersionForceProxy` | AmoebaWcaDispersionForce | `AmoebaWcaDispersionForceProxy.cpp` |
| `AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForceProxy` | AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForce | `AmoebaGeneralizedKirkwoodForceProxy.cpp` |
| `HippoNonbondedForceProxy` | HippoNonbondedForce | `HippoNonbondedForceProxy.cpp` |

Corresponding serialization test files (`TestSerialize*.cpp`) validate round-trip correctness for each force. When building custom workflows that create AMOEBA systems, ensure the plugin is loaded before deserializing — the proxy registration is triggered by the shared library's static initialization.

> [!TIP]
> AMOEBA serialization includes the extrapolation coefficients and polarization type. If you serialize a System using Extrapolated polarization and later load it with an older plugin version that has different default coefficients, the stored coefficients will be used correctly. However, the warning in the API that "default coefficients may change in a future release" applies to programmatically created forces, not deserialized ones — serialized Systems capture their coefficients explicitly.

Sources: [AmoebaSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp](plugins/amoeba/serialization/src/AmoebaSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp), [serialization tests](plugins/amoeba/serialization/tests/)

## Validation and Numerical Accuracy

The plugin has been validated against TINKER 6.1.01 using dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) in both implicit and explicit solvent. The validation metric is the per-atom relative force difference: `2·|F_MM - F_T| / (|F_MM| + |F_T|)`, and the reported value is the **median** across all atoms. The results demonstrate that the dominant source of discrepancy in implicit solvent is the SASA cavity term (different algorithms in TINKER vs. OpenMM), not the core electrostatics:

| Solvent Model | CUDA Single Precision | CUDA Double Precision |
|---|---|---|
| Implicit (full) | 1.04 × 10⁻² | 1.04 × 10⁻² |
| Implicit (no cavity) | 9.23 × 10⁻⁶ | 1.17 × 10⁻⁶ |
| Explicit | 3.73 × 10⁻⁵ | 1.83 × 10⁻⁷ |

For developers implementing new AMOEBA features, the explicit-solvent double-precision benchmark (1.83 × 10⁻⁷ median relative difference) represents the achievable accuracy floor. The single-precision explicit result (3.73 × 10⁻⁵) is typical for GPU single-precision electrostatics. The plugin supports both Verlet and Stochastic integrators — the TINKER Beeman integrator has no OpenMM equivalent.

Sources: [08_amoeba_plugin.rst](docs-source/usersguide/library/08_amoeba_plugin.rst#L107-L124)

## Extending the AMOEBA Plugin

Developers wishing to extend the AMOEBA plugin should follow this pattern:

1. **Define the Force class** in `plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/` with per-particle parameter storage in an internal `Info` struct
2. **Create the ForceImpl** in `plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/src/` that calls `ForceImpl::registerKernel()` with the appropriate kernel name
3. **Add the abstract kernel** to [amoebaKernels.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/openmm/amoebaKernels.h) following the existing naming convention
4. **Implement per-platform kernels** in each `platforms/*/src/` directory, registering them via each platform's kernel factory
5. **Create the serialization proxy** in `plugins/amoeba/serialization/src/` and register it in [AmoebaSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp](plugins/amoeba/serialization/src/AmoebaSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp)
6. **Register the header** in [OpenMMAmoeba.h](plugins/amoeba/openmmapi/include/OpenMMAmoeba.h) and update the wrapper generation script [generateAmoebaWrappers.py](plugins/amoeba/wrappers/generateAmoebaWrappers.py)

For GPU kernel development, the CUDA platform's `kernels/` subdirectory contains the AMOEBA-specific kernel source strings. HIP and OpenCL implementations are direct translations of the same algorithms with platform-specific syntax.

## Next Steps

- For a deeper understanding of the platform abstraction that dispatches AMOEBA kernels, see [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system)
- To learn how AMOEBA forces integrate with the broader force-field generation pipeline, see [ForceField and System Generation](15-forcefield-and-system-generation)
- To explore the Drude polarizable force field — an alternative polarization approach — see [Drude and RPMD Plugins](22-drude-and-rpmd-plugins)
- For the core OpenMM serialization mechanisms that AMOEBA proxies build upon, see [Serialization and Checkpointing](23-serialization-and-checkpointing)
- To build the plugin from source, consult [Building from Source](24-building-from-source)

# Drude and RPMD Plugins



OpenMM's plugin architecture extends the core simulation engine with domain-specific capabilities that would bloat the main library if bundled natively. Two of the most scientifically significant plugins are the **Drude polarizable force field plugin** and the **Ring Polymer Molecular Dynamics (RPMD) plugin**, each addressing fundamentally different physical phenomena—electronic polarization and nuclear quantum effects—through specialized Force and Integrator classes that integrate seamlessly with the existing [System and Context](11-system-and-context) and [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system).

## Architectural Overview

Both plugins follow the same architectural blueprint established by the core OpenMM framework: a public API layer defines domain-specific `Force` and `Integrator` classes, abstract kernel interfaces declare platform-agnostic operations, and concrete platform implementations (Reference, CUDA, OpenCL, HIP) provide hardware-accelerated execution. This separation ensures that new platforms automatically gain support for plugin features without modification to the plugin's public API.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Drude Plugin"
        DF[DrudeForce] --> DFI[DrudeForceImpl]
        DI[DrudeIntegrator] --> DLI[DrudeLangevinIntegrator]
        DI --> DNI[DrudeNoseHooverIntegrator]
        DI --> DSI[DrudeSCFIntegrator]
        DFI --> CDFK[CalcDrudeForceKernel]
        DLI --> IDLSK[IntegrateDrudeLangevinStepKernel]
        DSI --> IDSSK[IntegrateDrudeSCFStepKernel]
    end

    subgraph "RPMD Plugin"
        RI[RPMDIntegrator] --> IRPK[IntegrateRPMDStepKernel]
        RMB[RPMDMonteCarloBarostat] --> RMBI[RPMDMonteCarloBarostatImpl]
    end

    subgraph "Platform Implementations"
        CDFK --> REF[Reference]
        CDFK --> CUDA[CUDA]
        CDFK --> OCL[OpenCL]
        CDFK --> HIP[HIP]
        IDLSK --> REF
        IDLSK --> CUDA
        IDLSK --> OCL
        IDLSK --> HIP
        IRPK --> REF
        IRPK --> CUDA
        IRPK --> OCL
        IRPK --> HIP
    end

    DFI -.->|delegates to| DH[DrudeHelpers]
    DNI -.->|extends| NHI[NoseHooverIntegrator]
```

Both plugins reside under `plugins/` and share an identical internal layout: `openmmapi/` for the public C++ API, `platforms/` for per-platform kernel implementations, `serialization/` for checkpoint/proxy support (Drude only), and `tests/` for validation suites. A notable structural asymmetry is that the Drude plugin includes a `wrappers/` directory and full serialization proxies, while the RPMD plugin omits these—reflecting its more specialized usage pattern.

Sources: [DrudeForce.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeForce.h#L53-L53), [RPMDIntegrator.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RPMDIntegrator.h#L67-L67), [DrudeKernels.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeKernels.h#L47-L139), [RpmdKernels.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RpmdKernels.h#L46-L85)

## Drude Polarizable Force Field Plugin

The Drude plugin implements the Drude oscillator model for electronic polarization, a computationally efficient alternative to fully self-consistent polarizable force fields like [Amoeba](21-amoeba-polarizable-force-field). In this model, each polarizable atom is augmented with an attached massless (or very low mass) "Drude particle" carrying a partial charge, connected to its parent by an anisotropic harmonic spring. The induced dipole emerges from the displacement of the Drude particle under the local electric field—avoiding the iterative self-consistent field convergence required by induced dipole methods.

### DrudeForce: The Core Force Class

`DrudeForce` is the central class that defines two distinct energetic contributions. First, an **anisotropic harmonic bond** connects each Drude particle to its parent atom, with spring constants derived from the specified polarizability and optional anisotropy scale factors along user-defined molecular axes. Second, a **screened Coulomb (Thole) interaction** between specific dipole pairs replaces the standard Coulomb interaction for 1-2 and 1-3 bonded interactions, preventing unphysical charge penetration that would otherwise occur when Drude pairs approach each other closely.

The `addParticle()` method registers each Drude particle with up to five particle indices and four physical parameters. The particle and particle1 fields define the Drude-parent pair (required), while particle2 through particle4 define auxiliary atoms that establish the local frame for anisotropic polarizability (optional, via -1 sentinel values). The `charge` parameter specifies the Drude particle's charge, `polarizability` sets the isotropic polarizability α (converted internally to a spring constant k = q²/α), and `aniso12`/`aniso34` are scale factors that modulate the spring constant along specific molecular directions.

Sources: [DrudeForce.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeForce.h#L72-L88), [DrudeForce.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeForce.cpp#L42-L49)

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `particle` | `int` | System index of the Drude particle |
| `particle1` | `int` | System index of the parent atom |
| `particle2` | `int` | Second atom defining anisotropy axis 1-2 (-1 to disable) |
| `particle3` | `int` | Third atom defining anisotropy axis 3-4 (-1 to disable) |
| `particle4` | `int` | Fourth atom defining anisotropy axis 3-4 (-1 to disable) |
| `charge` | `double` | Charge on the Drude particle (e or elementary charge units) |
| `polarizability` | `double` | Isotropic polarizability α (must be > 0) |
| `aniso12` | `double` | Scale factor along particle1→particle2 axis (must be > 0 if particle2 set) |
| `aniso34` | `double` | Scale factor along particle3→particle4 axis (must be > 0 if particle3/4 set) |

Screened pairs are added via `addScreenedPair()`, which takes indices into the DrudeForce's particle list (not system indices) and a Thole damping factor. The `DrudeForceImpl` validates at initialization that particle indices are within bounds, no particle participates in multiple Drude pairs, and no duplicate screened pairs exist—providing early error detection before simulation begins.

Sources: [DrudeForce.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeForce.h#L126-L133), [DrudeForceImpl.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeForceImpl.cpp#L51-L113)

### Drude Helper Utilities

The `DrudeHelpers` module provides three critical utility functions shared across all Drude integrator implementations. The `getDrudeForce()` function locates the `DrudeForce` in a `ContextImpl` by iterating over the system's forces and, if not found directly, searching within contained forces of other force implementations—a design that accommodates scenarios where the DrudeForce is embedded within a composite force. The `findParticlesAndPairs()` function partitions all system particles into "normal" (non-Drude) particles and Drude-parent pair tuples, which every Drude integrator needs to apply separate thermostats. The `assignDrudeVelocities()` function generates Maxwell-Boltzmann distributed velocities with a critical distinction: normal particles and center-of-mass modes of Drude pairs are thermalized at the system temperature, while internal (relative) motions of Drude pairs are thermalized at the much lower Drude temperature using the reduced mass of each pair.

Sources: [DrudeHelpers.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeHelpers.cpp#L48-L153)

### DrudeIntegrator Hierarchy

All Drude-specific integrators extend `DrudeIntegrator`, which itself extends the base `Integrator` class. The base class provides shared infrastructure: Drude temperature management via `getDrudeTemperature()`/`setDrudeTemperature()`, a hard-wall distance constraint via `getMaxDrudeDistance()`/`setMaxDrudeDistance()` (default 0.02 nm), and the `getVelocitiesForTemperature()` override that dispatches to the helper's velocity assignment logic. This design avoids code duplication across integrator implementations while enforcing a consistent initialization contract.

Sources: [DrudeIntegrator.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeIntegrator.h#L43-L135)

| Integrator | Thermostat | Base Class | Strategy |
|------------|-----------|------------|----------|
| `DrudeLangevinIntegrator` | Dual Langevin | `DrudeIntegrator` | Stochastic, velocity-dependent friction on COM and relative modes |
| `DrudeNoseHooverIntegrator` | Dual Nose-Hoover chains | `NoseHooverIntegrator` | Deterministic, MTS with Yoshida-Suzuki decomposition |
| `DrudeSCFIntegrator` | None | `DrudeIntegrator` | Energy minimization of Drude positions each step |

**DrudeLangevinIntegrator** applies two independent Langevin thermostats: one at the system temperature for ordinary particles and the center-of-mass motion of Drude pairs, and a second at the Drude temperature for the relative internal displacement of each pair. The constructor requires five parameters: `temperature`, `frictionCoeff`, `drudeTemperature`, `drudeFrictionCoeff`, and `stepSize`. It exposes `computeSystemTemperature()` and `computeDrudeTemperature()` for monitoring, delegating to the shared `computeTemperaturesFromVelocities()` helper which correctly accounts for constraints and center-of-mass motion removal when computing degrees of freedom.

Sources: [DrudeLangevinIntegrator.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeLangevinIntegrator.h#L54-L156), [DrudeHelpers.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeHelpers.cpp#L159-L217)

**DrudeNoseHooverIntegrator** provides a deterministic alternative by extending `NoseHooverIntegrator` directly (bypassing `DrudeIntegrator`'s `Integrator` inheritance path). It maintains separate Nose-Hoover chains for the real and Drude subsystems, with support for multiple time stepping (MTS) through Yoshida-Suzuki decomposition. The constructor signature includes `chainLength` (default 3), `numMTS` (default 3), and `numYoshidaSuzuki` (default 7), giving fine-grained control over integration accuracy. Like the Langevin variant, it provides `computeSystemTemperature()`, `computeDrudeTemperature()`, `computeDrudeKineticEnergy()`, and `computeTotalKineticEnergy()`, along with the hard-wall Drude distance constraint.

Sources: [DrudeNoseHooverIntegrator.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeNoseHooverIntegrator.h#L54-L125)

**DrudeSCFIntegrator** takes a fundamentally different approach: rather than dynamically integrating Drude particle motion with a thermostat, it performs a self-consistent minimization of Drude positions at every time step using a leap-frog Verlet scheme for the real atoms. The `getMinimizationErrorTolerance()`/`setMinimizationErrorTolerance()` methods control the convergence criterion (in kJ/mol/nm) for this energy minimization. This integrator is suitable when the Drude degrees of freedom are well-separated in timescale from the nuclear motion and can be treated as adiabatic.

Sources: [DrudeSCFIntegrator.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeSCFIntegrator.h#L48-L101)

> [!TIP]
> The `computeTemperaturesFromVelocities()` helper in [DrudeHelpers.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeHelpers.cpp#L159-L217) computes Drude temperature from the **relative** velocity between pair members using the reduced mass, while system temperature uses the **center-of-mass** velocity and the total pair mass. This decomposition is critical for correctly dual-thermostatted simulations and properly handles constraints and CMMotionRemover when counting degrees of freedom.

### Drude Kernel Interface and Platform Coverage

The `DrudeKernels.h` header defines three abstract kernel classes that bridge the public API to platform-specific implementations. `CalcDrudeForceKernel` handles force/energy evaluation for `DrudeForce`, `IntegrateDrudeLangevinStepKernel` handles the dual-thermostatted Langevin time step, and `IntegrateDrudeSCFStepKernel` handles the SCF minimization loop. Each kernel declares `initialize()`, `execute()`, and (where applicable) `copyParametersToContext()` methods that platforms must implement. The Drude plugin provides implementations across all five OpenMM platforms: Reference, CUDA, OpenCL, HIP, and Common (shared utility code).

Sources: [DrudeKernels.h](plugins/drude/openmmapi/include/openmm/DrudeKernels.h#L47-L139)

## RPMD Plugin

The Ring Polymer Molecular Dynamics plugin implements path-integral-based quantum dynamics through the ring polymer representation. Where the Drude plugin adds extra particles to model electronic polarization, the RPMD plugin replicates the *entire* system across multiple "beads" (copies) connected by harmonic springs, with the number of beads determining the level of quantum effects captured.

### RPMDIntegrator

`RPMDIntegrator` extends the base `Integrator` class and manages N copies of the system arranged in a ring (copy *i* connected to copies *i−1* and *i+1* with periodic boundary conditions). By default, it applies a PILE (Pile-Langevin-Estimator) thermostat to maintain canonical sampling across the ring polymer. The constructor accepts `numCopies`, `temperature`, `frictionCoeff`, and `stepSize`, with an optional `contractions` map that enables **ring polymer contraction**—a critical optimization where different force groups are evaluated on different numbers of beads. For example, bonded forces may be computed on all 32 beads while PME reciprocal space is computed on a single centroid bead, dramatically reducing computational cost while preserving accuracy.

Sources: [RPMDIntegrator.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RPMDIntegrator.h#L67-L91)

A fundamental API difference from standard integrators is that state management occurs through the integrator, not the context. The `setPositions(copy, positions)`, `setVelocities(copy, velocities)`, and `getState(copy, types, ...)` methods operate on individual copies, while `getTotalEnergy()` returns the aggregate ring polymer energy including all spring potentials. Direct calls to `Context.setPositions()` or `Context.getState()` should be avoided; the integrator internally manages which copy's state is loaded into the context at any given time.

Sources: [RPMDIntegrator.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RPMDIntegrator.h#L174-L204)

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `numCopies` | `int` | Number of system replicas (beads) in the ring polymer |
| `temperature` | `double` | Heat bath temperature (K) |
| `frictionCoeff` | `double` | Langevin friction coefficient (1/ps) |
| `stepSize` | `double` | Integration time step (ps) |
| `contractions` | `map<int,int>` | Force group → bead count mapping for ring polymer contraction |

### RPMDMonteCarloBarostat

`RPMDMonteCarloBarostat` extends `Force` (not `Barostat`) and provides pressure control specifically designed for the ring polymer ensemble. Unlike the standard `MonteCarloBarostat` which scales a single copy, this barostat scales **all copies uniformly** and accepts or rejects the volume change based on the total ring polymer energy returned by `RPMDIntegrator.getTotalEnergy()`. The constructor takes `defaultPressure` (in bar) and `frequency` (default 25 steps). It uses the string key `"RPMDMonteCarloPressure"` for context parameter storage and always reports periodic boundary condition usage.

Sources: [RPMDMonteCarloBarostat.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RPMDMonteCarloBarostat.h#L46-L124)

### RPMD Kernel and Platform Architecture

The `IntegrateRPMDStepKernel` defined in `RpmdKernels.h` declares the full contract for platform implementations: `initialize()`, `execute()` (with a `forcesAreValid` flag to support selective recalculation), `setPositions()`, `setVelocities()`, `copyToContext()` (loading a specific copy into the active context), and `computeKineticEnergy()`. The RPMD plugin mirrors the Drude plugin's platform coverage with implementations for Reference, CUDA, OpenCL, and HIP, but notably lacks a Common shared-code layer and serialization support, indicating a narrower deployment scope.

Sources: [RpmdKernels.h](plugins/rpmd/openmmapi/include/openmm/RpmdKernels.h#L46-L85)

## Comparative Analysis: Drude vs. RPMD

Despite sharing the plugin architecture, the two plugins address fundamentally different physical regimes and impose different constraints on simulation setup. The table below highlights the key structural and functional distinctions relevant to developers integrating either plugin into custom workflows.

| Dimension | Drude Plugin | RPMD Plugin |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| **Physical model** | Electronic polarization via classical Drude oscillators | Nuclear quantum effects via path-integral ring polymer |
| **System modification** | Adds individual Drude particles (lightweight) | Replicates entire system N× (heavyweight) |
| **Force classes** | `DrudeForce` (spring + Thole screening) | `RPMDMonteCarloBarostat` |
| **Integrator classes** | 3: Langevin, NoseHoover, SCF | 1: RPMDIntegrator |
| **Thermostat strategy** | Dual-temperature (system + Drude internal) | Single PILE thermostat across all beads |
| **State management** | Standard Context API | Integrator-scoped per-copy API |
| **Serialization** | Full proxy support (Force + Integrators) | None |
| **Python wrappers** | Generated via `generateDrudeWrappers.py` | None dedicated |
| **Key optimization** | Hard-wall distance constraint | Ring polymer contraction by force group |

> [!TIP]
> When using `RPMDIntegrator` with ring polymer contraction, the `contractions` map keys are **force group indices** (not force group bitmasks). A force assigned to group 2 should use key `2`, not `4`. The contracted bead count must divide the total `numCopies` evenly for correct normal mode transformation.

## Integration Patterns and Practical Considerations

Both plugins are loaded at runtime through OpenMM's plugin discovery mechanism and require linking against their respective shared libraries. The Drude plugin demands that exactly one `DrudeForce` be present in the System—`getDrudeForce()` in [DrudeHelpers.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeHelpers.cpp#L48-L74) throws if none or multiple are found. This constraint is enforced during integrator initialization, meaning any simulation using a Drude integrator will fail fast with a clear error message if the system is misconfigured.

The serialization subsystem provides checkpoint/restart for Drude simulations through proxy classes: `DrudeForceProxy`, `DrudeLangevinIntegratorProxy`, and `DrudeNoseHooverIntegratorProxy`. These are registered via `DrudeSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp`, enabling full state serialization through OpenMM's standard `XmlSerializer` interface. The RPMD plugin lacks this infrastructure, meaning RPMD simulations cannot be serialized through the standard checkpoint mechanism—a significant consideration for long-running production simulations.

For developers extending the Drude plugin, the `updateParametersInContext()` pathway on `DrudeForce` supports modifying numeric parameters (polarizability, Thole factors) without reinitializing the context, but cannot change particle identities or add/remove particles. This is implemented by delegating to `CalcDrudeForceKernel.copyParametersToContext()` followed by a `context.systemChanged()` call, as seen in [DrudeForceImpl.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeForceImpl.cpp#L126-L129).

Sources: [DrudeForceImpl.cpp](plugins/drude/openmmapi/src/DrudeForceImpl.cpp#L126-L129), [DrudeSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp](plugins/drude/serialization/src/DrudeSerializationProxyRegistration.cpp)

## Further Reading

Having examined both plugin implementations, the natural progression for understanding OpenMM's extension mechanisms leads to the broader [Plugin Architecture](20-plugin-architecture) overview, which describes how plugins are discovered, loaded, and registered at runtime. For comparison with another polarizable force field implementation that shares the same plugin infrastructure, see [Amoeba Polarizable Force Field](21-amoeba-polarizable-force-field). To understand how the kernel abstraction layer enables these platform-specific implementations, revisit the [Platform and Kernel System](8-platform-and-kernel-system) discussion.

# Serialization and Checkpointing



OpenMM provides two complementary mechanisms for persisting simulation state: an **XML-based serialization framework** for portable object reconstruction, and a **binary checkpointing system** for exact Context-level state restoration. Understanding the boundary between these systems—and the architectural decisions that separate them—is essential for building reliable, reproducible simulation workflows. This page dissects both subsystems from the proxy registration layer down to the XML encoding primitives.

## Architectural Overview

The serialization subsystem is organized as a classic **Proxy pattern** with a global type registry. Every serializable type (System, State, Force, Integrator, TabulatedFunction) has a corresponding `SerializationProxy` subclass that knows how to encode that type into a `SerializationNode` tree and decode it back again. `XmlSerializer` acts as the I/O bridge, converting node trees to/from XML text streams. Context-level checkpointing operates on an entirely separate code path within `ContextImpl`, producing opaque binary data.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Application Layer"
        APP[User Code]
    end
    
    subgraph "XML Serialization Path"
        XS[XmlSerializer<br/>serialize / deserialize / clone]
        SN[SerializationNode<br/>tree of properties + children]
        SP[SerializationProxy<br/>abstract: serialize + deserialize]
        
        subgraph "Concrete Proxies"
            SPr[SystemProxy]
            StPr[StateProxy]
            FPr[Force Proxies<br/>Nonbonded, Custom, ...]
            IPr[Integrator Proxies<br/>Verlet, Langevin, ...]
            TPr[TabulatedFunction Proxies]
        end
        
        REG[Global Proxy Registry<br/>typeid → Proxy map<br/>name → Proxy map]
    end
    
    subgraph "Binary Checkpoint Path"
        CTX[Context]
        CP[ContextImpl<br/>createCheckpoint / loadCheckpoint]
        BIN[Opaque Binary Stream]
    end
    
    APP -->|"XmlSerializer::serialize&lt;T&gt;"| XS
    APP -->|"XmlSerializer::deserialize&lt;T&gt;"| XS
    APP -->|"Context::createCheckpoint"| CP
    APP -->|"Context::loadCheckpoint"| CP
    
    XS -->|"encodeNode / decodeNode"| SN
    XS -->|"proxy.serialize / proxy.deserialize"| SP
    SP -->|"typeid lookup"| REG
    SP --> SPr & StPr & FPr & IPr & TPr
    SPr & StPr & FPr & IPr & TPr --> SN
    
    CTX -->|"delegates"| CP
    CP --> BIN
```

## The Proxy Registration System

All serialization capability is bootstrapped through a single entry point: the `registerSerializationProxies()` function defined in [SerializationProxyRegistration.cpp](serialization/src/SerializationProxyRegistration.cpp#L121-L191). This function is invoked automatically when the shared library loads—via `DllMain` on Windows or `__attribute__((constructor))` on POSIX systems—ensuring every proxy is registered before any user code executes.

The `SerializationProxy` base class ([SerializationProxy.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SerializationProxy.h#L54-L113)) maintains two parallel lookup maps: one keyed by `std::type_info` (used during serialization to find the correct proxy for a concrete C++ object) and another keyed by type name string (used during deserialization to reconstruct an object when only the XML `type` attribute is known). Each concrete proxy constructor passes its type name string—typically the class name—to the `SerializationProxy` constructor. The table below shows the complete set of registered types:

| Category | Registered Types |
|----------|-----------------|
| **Core Objects** | `System`, `State` |
| **Standard Forces** | `NonbondedForce`, `HarmonicBondForce`, `HarmonicAngleForce`, `PeriodicTorsionForce`, `RBTorsionForce`, `CMAPTorsionForce`, `GBSAOBCForce`, `GayBerneForce`, `LCPOForce`, `ATMForce`, `ConstantPotentialForce`, `OrientationRestraintForce`, `RGForce`, `RMSDForce` |
| **Custom Forces** | `CustomBondForce`, `CustomAngleForce`, `CustomTorsionForce`, `CustomNonbondedForce`, `CustomHbondForce`, `CustomGBForce`, `CustomExternalForce`, `CustomManyParticleForce`, `CustomCentroidBondForce`, `CustomCompoundBondForce`, `CustomCVForce`, `CustomVolumeForce` |
| **Integrators** | `VerletIntegrator`, `LangevinIntegrator`, `LangevinMiddleIntegrator`, `BrownianIntegrator`, `VariableLangevinIntegrator`, `VariableVerletIntegrator`, `CustomIntegrator`, `CompoundIntegrator`, `DPDIntegrator`, `NoseHooverIntegrator`, `QTBIntegrator` |
| **Thermostats & Barostats** | `AndersenThermostat`, `MonteCarloBarostat`, `MonteCarloAnisotropicBarostat`, `MonteCarloFlexibleBarostat`, `MonteCarloMembraneBarostat`, `CMMotionRemover` |
| **Tabulated Functions** | `Continuous1DFunction`, `Continuous2DFunction`, `Continuous3DFunction`, `Discrete1DFunction`, `Discrete2DFunction`, `Discrete3DFunction` |

Sources: [SerializationProxyRegistration.cpp](serialization/src/SerializationProxyRegistration.cpp#L121-L191), [SerializationProxy.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SerializationProxy.h#L88-L104)

## SerializationNode: The Intermediate Representation

`SerializationNode` ([SerializationNode.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SerializationNode.h#L50-L273)) is the tree-structured intermediate representation that decouples object serialization logic from XML encoding. Each node carries a name, an ordered list of child nodes, and a property map where keys are always strings and values are stored as strings internally but accessible through typed accessors (`getIntProperty()`, `getDoubleProperty()`, `getBoolProperty()`, `getLongProperty()`). Type coercion is implicit: setting a property via `setIntProperty()` and reading it via `getStringProperty()` produces the decimal string representation, while reading via `getDoubleProperty()` performs the numeric conversion. If the original string is non-numeric, the behavior is undefined—this is a deliberate performance trade-off that avoids validation overhead in the deserialization hot path.

The node tree is deliberately flexible. While there is typically a one-to-one correspondence between serializable objects and nodes, proxies are free to create arbitrary child structures. The `SystemProxy`, for example, creates nested `<Particles>`, `<Constraints>`, and `<Forces>` child containers, each holding per-element nodes. During deserialization, `getChildNode(name)` throws if the expected child is absent, providing fail-fast semantics for malformed input.

Sources: [SerializationNode.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SerializationNode.h#L50-L100), [SerializationNode.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SerializationNode.h#L105-L190)

## XmlSerializer: The I/O Bridge

`XmlSerializer` ([XmlSerializer.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/XmlSerializer.h#L43-L97)) is a fully static class providing three templated entry points. The **serialize** method resolves the proxy via `typeid(*object)`, invokes `proxy.serialize()` to populate a `SerializationNode`, stamps the node with a `type` property (guarding against proxies that accidentally use the reserved name `type`), and then recursively encodes the tree to XML using tab-indented formatting. The **deserialize** method reverses this: it parses XML via irrXML into a root `SerializationNode`, reads the `type` property to locate the correct proxy by name, and calls `proxy.deserialize()` to reconstruct the object. The **clone** method is an optimization that bypasses XML entirely—serializing to a `SerializationNode` and immediately deserializing—for deep-copying objects without the overhead of string encoding.

The XML encoding in [XmlSerializer.cpp](serialization/src/XmlSerializer.cpp#L107-L158) applies standard entity escaping (`&amp;`, `&lt;`, `&gt;`, `&quot;`, `&apos;`) and represents control characters below ASCII 32 as hexadecimal character references (e.g., `&#x0A;`). Leaf nodes (those with no children) are emitted as self-closing XML elements. The `StreamReader` adapter class wraps a C++ `std::istream` behind irrXML's `IFileReadCallBack` interface, enabling the parser to read from any standard stream source.

Sources: [XmlSerializer.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/XmlSerializer.h#L43-L80), [XmlSerializer.cpp](serialization/src/XmlSerializer.cpp#L107-L196)

## System Serialization

The `SystemProxy` ([SystemProxy.cpp](serialization/src/SystemProxy.cpp#L44-L179)) serializes the complete definition of a molecular system. The encoded XML includes a `version` property (currently always `1`) and an `openmmVersion` property for provenance tracking. The body contains three principal child containers:

- **`<PeriodicBoxVectors>`** — Three child nodes (`A`, `B`, `C`) each with `x`, `y`, `z` double properties encoding the default periodic box. This captures the `System.setDefaultPeriodicBoxVectors()` configuration.
- **`<Particles>`** — One `<Particle>` child per particle, each carrying a `mass` property. Particles that are virtual sites include an additional child node whose name identifies the virtual site type: `TwoParticleAverageSite`, `ThreeParticleAverageSite`, `OutOfPlaneSite`, `LocalCoordinatesSite`, or `SymmetrySite`. Each variant encodes its construction parameters (particle indices, weights, rotation matrices, offset vectors) as properties.
- **`<Constraints>`** — One `<Constraint>` child per constraint, with `p1`, `p2` (particle indices) and `d` (distance) properties.
- **`<Forces>`** — One `<Force>` child per force, each serialized by its own proxy. The `SerializationNode` constructor overload `createChildNode("Force", &system.getForce(i))` automatically delegates to the appropriate force proxy, creating nested subtrees.

During deserialization, the proxy reconstructs particles, virtual sites, constraints, and forces in order. A `try/catch` block ensures that a partially-constructed `System*` is deleted if deserialization fails partway through, preventing memory leaks from allocation errors in later stages.

Sources: [SystemProxy.cpp](serialization/src/SystemProxy.cpp#L44-L115), [SystemProxy.cpp](serialization/src/SystemProxy.cpp#L117-L179)

## State Serialization

The `StateProxy` ([StateProxy.cpp](serialization/src/StateProxy.cpp#L43-L157)) serializes a simulation snapshot. Unlike `SystemProxy` which captures structural definition, `StateProxy` captures instantaneous dynamical data. The serialized form is conditional on the `State.getDataTypes()` bitmask—the proxy only includes child nodes for data that was actually requested when `Context.getState()` was called.

| Child Node | Data Types Flag | Content |
|------------|----------------|---------|
| `<PeriodicBoxVectors>` | Always present | `A`, `B`, `C` with `x`, `y`, `z` double properties |
| `<Parameters>` | `State::Parameters` | Key-value double properties from `State.getParameters()` |
| `<Energies>` | `State::Energy` | `PotentialEnergy` and `KineticEnergy` double properties |
| `<Positions>` | `State::Positions` | One `<Position>` child per particle with `x`, `y`, `z` |
| `<Velocities>` | `State::Velocities` | One `<Velocity>` child per particle with `x`, `y`, `z` |
| `<Forces>` | `State::Forces` | One `<Force>` child per particle with `x`, `y`, `z` |
| `<IntegratorParameters>` | `State::IntegratorParameters` | A raw `SerializationNode` pushed directly from `State.getIntegratorParameters()` |

The deserialization path uses `State::StateBuilder` to incrementally assemble the `State` object. A critical validation step at [line 151](serialization/src/StateProxy.cpp#L151-L155) checks that all array-type data (positions, velocities, forces) have identical sizes, throwing `OpenMMException("State Deserialization Particle Size Mismatch")` if they disagree. This guard prevents subtle corruption from truncated or partially-written state files.

Sources: [StateProxy.cpp](serialization/src/StateProxy.cpp#L43-L95), [StateProxy.cpp](serialization/src/StateProxy.cpp#L96-L157)

## Checkpointing: Binary Context State

Context-level checkpointing via `Context::createCheckpoint()` and `Context::loadCheckpoint()` ([Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L274-L294)) is architecturally distinct from XML serialization. While XML serialization operates at the object level (System, State) and produces portable, human-readable text, checkpointing captures the **complete internal state of a Context**—including platform-specific GPU memory, random number generator seeds, constraint solver state, and any other internal data that the platform implementation maintains. The checkpoint stream is an **opaque binary blob** with no guaranteed format stability across OpenMM versions, hardware configurations, or even platform backends.

The official API documentation in [Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L281-L293) makes this specificity explicit: *"A checkpoint contains data that is highly specific to the Context from which it was created. It depends on the details of the System, the Platform being used, and the hardware and software of the computer it was created on."* Loading a checkpoint on different hardware or with a different OpenMM version will likely throw an exception. Even when it succeeds, deterministic trajectory reproducibility is described as not *"strictly guaranteed."*

The checkpoint system also underpins `Context::reinitialize(bool preserveState)` ([Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L267-L273)). When `preserveState` is `true`, the reimplementation internally creates a checkpoint before destroying the Context's internal state, then loads it after reconstruction. This means `reinitialize(true)` will throw if the System has changed incompatibly (e.g., particle count change) because the checkpoint cannot be loaded.

The test suite in [TestCheckpoints.h](tests/TestCheckpoints.h#L140-L288) exercises three critical checkpoint properties. First, `testSetState()` verifies that `Context.setState()` correctly restores positions, velocities, and parameters from a `State` object, and that partial states (positions-only) leave other fields untouched. Second, `testMultipleDevices()` confirms that a checkpoint created on one Context can be loaded into a different Context, and that subsequent simulation steps produce identical trajectories. Third, `testLangevin()` validates checkpoint behavior with stochastic integrators where random number generator state is critical for reproducibility.

Sources: [Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L274-L294), [TestCheckpoints.h](tests/TestCheckpoints.h#L73-L139), [TestCheckpoints.h](tests/TestCheckpoints.h#L140-L288)

## setState vs. loadCheckpoint: Choosing the Right Mechanism

The table below captures the critical distinctions between the two state restoration mechanisms, based directly on the API contract documented in [Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L120-L135) and [Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h#L281-L293).

| Dimension | `Context.setState(State)` | `Context.loadCheckpoint(stream)` |
|-----------|---------------------------|----------------------------------|
| **Data restored** | Positions, velocities, energies, parameters, forces, time, step count | All of the above plus RNG state, constraint solver state, platform internal state |
| **Portability** | Fully portable across platforms, hardware, and OpenMM versions | Tied to specific System, Platform, hardware, and OpenMM version |
| **Format** | `State` object (optionally XML-serialized via `XmlSerializer`) | Opaque binary stream |
| **Partial state** | Supported—only specified data types are applied | Always full state restoration |
| **Trajectory reproducibility** | Not guaranteed (RNG state is lost) | Nearly deterministic (same hardware/software) |
| **Failure mode** | Silent loss of RNG-related state | Explicit exception on incompatibility |
| **Use case** | Cross-platform state transfer, analysis workflows, human-readable archives | Exact simulation restart, debugging, `reinitialize(true)` |

> [!TIP]
> The `loadCheckpoint()` guarantee is intentionally weaker than binary equivalence. The API documentation states *"the internal state should be close enough to be reasonably considered equivalent"* rather than guaranteeing bit-identical trajectories. For workflows requiring strict reproducibility, you must use the same hardware, platform, and OpenMM build—and even then, validate empirically rather than relying on the contract alone.

> [!TIP]
> When using `Context.setState()` with a `State` that was deserialized from XML, be aware that the `State` must have been created with the appropriate data type flags. A State serialized without `State::Velocities` will leave velocities unchanged in the target Context—even if the original Context had well-defined velocities. Always check `State.getDataTypes()` before relying on a deserialized State for state restoration.

## Plugin Serialization Extensibility

The proxy registry is a global, flat namespace. Plugin libraries (such as the AMOEBA, Drude, and RPMD force field plugins) register their own serialization proxies when their shared libraries are loaded, using the same `SerializationProxy::registerProxy()` mechanism. This means plugin-specific types (e.g., `AmoebaMultipoleForce`) become transparently serializable once the plugin is loaded—the XML output will contain the plugin type's `type` attribute, and deserialization will resolve to the plugin's proxy at load time.

The implication for checkpointing is important: a Context using plugin forces can only be checkpointed and restored in an environment where the same plugins are loaded. A checkpoint from an AMOEBA simulation is useless without the AMOEBA plugin library present. This coupling does not exist for XML-based System serialization (the System XML is self-describing), but it does affect Context checkpoints because the binary format may encode plugin-specific platform kernel state.

## Summary of Key Source Locations

| Component | Header | Implementation |
|-----------|--------|----------------|
| SerializationProxy (abstract) | [SerializationProxy.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SerializationProxy.h) | [SerializationProxy.cpp](serialization/src/SerializationProxy.cpp) |
| SerializationNode | [SerializationNode.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SerializationNode.h) | [SerializationNode.cpp](serialization/src/SerializationNode.cpp) |
| XmlSerializer | [XmlSerializer.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/XmlSerializer.h) | [XmlSerializer.cpp](serialization/src/XmlSerializer.cpp) |
| SystemProxy | [SystemProxy.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/SystemProxy.h) | [SystemProxy.cpp](serialization/src/SystemProxy.cpp) |
| StateProxy | [StateProxy.h](serialization/include/openmm/serialization/StateProxy.h) | [StateProxy.cpp](serialization/src/StateProxy.cpp) |
| Proxy Registration | — | [SerializationProxyRegistration.cpp](serialization/src/SerializationProxyRegistration.cpp) |
| Context Checkpoint API | [Context.h](openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h) | Platform-specific `ContextImpl` |
| Checkpoint Tests | [TestCheckpoints.h](tests/TestCheckpoints.h) | Platform test suites |

For broader context on how serialized Systems feed into simulation construction, see [System and Context](11-system-and-context). For details on the specific Force and Integrator classes that the proxy system serializes, see [Force Classes](13-force-classes) and [Integrator Hierarchy](12-integrator-hierarchy). To understand how plugins extend the serialization registry, see [Plugin Architecture](20-plugin-architecture). For the practical workflow of building simulations from serialized systems, proceed to [Building from Source](24-building-from-source).

# Building from Source



Building OpenMM from source gives you full control over platform targets, compiler optimizations, and plugin selection. This guide covers the complete build pipeline — from prerequisites through verification — based on the actual CMake configuration used by the project's own CI infrastructure. It is written for developers who need to produce custom builds, integrate OpenMM into larger CMake projects, or contribute platform-specific code.

## Build Architecture Overview

OpenMM's build system follows a **monorepo aggregation pattern**: a single root `CMakeLists.txt` orchestrates the compilation of the core library, all hardware platforms, every plugin, the Python bindings, the test suite, and the documentation into one unified build tree. There is no separate build step per component — everything is resolved in a single `cmake --build` invocation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["cmake -B build<br/>-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release<br/>-DOPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB=ON ..."] --> B["CMake Configure Phase"]
    B --> C{Architecture Detection}
    C -->|x86_64| D["X86=ON<br/>vecmath + asmjit + SSE2"]
    C -->|ARM64| E["ARM=ON<br/>vecmath + asmjit + __ARM64__"]
    C -->|PPC| F["PPC=ON<br/>__PPC__"]
    C -->|LoongArch64| G["LOONGARCH64=ON<br/>__LOONGARCH64__ -mlsx"]

    B --> H["Core Library<br/>(OpenMM / OpenMM_static)"]
    B --> I["CUDA Platform<br/>(OpenMMCuda)"]
    B --> J["OpenCL Platform<br/>(OpenMMOpenCL)"]
    B --> K["HIP Platform<br/>(OpenMMHIP)"]
    B --> L["CPU Platform<br/>(OpenMMCPU)"]
    B --> M["Plugins<br/>(Amoeba, RPMD, Drude, CPUPME)"]
    B --> N["Python Wrappers<br/>(SWIG + Doxygen)"]
    B --> O["Serialization + Tests + Examples"]

    I --> P["EncodeKernelFiles.cmake<br/>CudaKernelSources.cpp/.h"]
    J --> Q["EncodeKernelFiles.cmake<br/>OpenCLKernelSources.cpp/.h"]
    K --> R["EncodeKernelFiles.cmake<br/>HipKernelSources.cpp/.h"]

    H & I & J & K & L & M --> S["cmake --build build"]
    S --> T["ctest --test-dir build"]
```

The key architectural insight is the **kernel encoding system**: GPU platforms (CUDA, OpenCL, HIP) do not compile kernel source files directly into the binary. Instead, `EncodeKernelFiles.cmake` reads the kernel sources from `platforms/*/src/kernels/`, escapes them into C string literals, and generates a `*KernelSources.cpp` file at configure time. These kernels are then JIT-compiled at runtime. This is why you will find `.cu.in`, `.cl.in`, and `.hip.in` template files rather than pre-compiled kernels in the source tree.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L1-L13), [cmake_modules/EncodeKernelFiles.cmake](cmake_modules/EncodeKernelFiles.cmake#L1-L30), [cmake_modules/TargetArch.cmake](cmake_modules/TargetArch.cmake#L100-L187)

## Prerequisites and Toolchain Requirements

The minimum CMake version is **3.17**, enforced at configure time. Beyond CMake, requirements vary by which platforms and components you intend to build.

### Core Build Dependencies

| Dependency | Minimum Version | Required For | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| CMake | 3.17 | All builds | Enforced via `CMAKE_MINIMUM_REQUIRED` |
| C++ Compiler | C++11 standard | All builds | GCC, Clang, or MSVC |
| Python | 3.x | Python wrappers, SWIG input generation | Found via `find_package(PythonInterp)` |
| SWIG | ≥ 3.0.5 | Python wrappers | Build fails with `SEND_ERROR` if older |
| Doxygen | Any recent | Python wrappers | Required for parsing headers into SWIG input |
| NumPy | Any | Python wrappers | Needed at build time for Cython |
| Cython | Any | Python wrappers | Listed in CI environment |

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L24-L24), [wrappers/python/CMakeLists.txt](wrappers/python/CMakeLists.txt#L105-L122), [wrappers/python/CMakeLists.txt](wrappers/python/CMakeLists.txt#L124-L125)

### GPU Platform Dependencies

| Platform | SDK/Library | Detection Method | CMake Cache Variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CUDA** | CUDA Toolkit | `find_package(CUDAToolkit QUIET)` | `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB` |
| **OpenCL** | OpenCL ICD / SDK | Custom `FindOpenCL.cmake` (checks `OPENCL_DIR`, `CUDA_PATH`, `AMDAPPSDKROOT`, macOS framework) | `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB` |
| **HIP** | ROCm (hip, hiprtc) | `find_package(HIP CONFIG QUIET)` with `$ROCM_PATH` and `/opt/rocm` prefix | `OPENMM_BUILD_HIP_LIB` |

A critical design decision: **GPU platform detection is automatic and opt-out, not opt-in**. If `CUDAToolkit_FOUND` is true, `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB` defaults to `ON`. If `OPENCL_FOUND` is true, `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB` defaults to `ON`. If `HIP_FOUND` is true, `OPENMM_BUILD_HIP_LIB` defaults to `ON`. To build *only* the Reference and CPU platforms, you must explicitly set these to `OFF`.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L324-L357), [cmake_modules/FindOpenCL.cmake](cmake_modules/FindOpenCL.cmake#L1-L96), [platforms/hip/CMakeLists.txt](platforms/hip/CMakeLists.txt#L15-L15)

### Architecture-Specific Compiler Flags

The build system detects the target architecture via `TargetArch.cmake`, which uses a clever preprocessor trick: it compiles a C file containing nested `#ifdef`/`#error` directives, and parses the architecture name from the compiler's error output. This works correctly even when cross-compiling because the code is never executed, only preprocessed.

| Architecture | Flag | Special Libraries |
|---|---|---|
| x86_64 / i386 | `-msse2 -pthread` (Linux), `-msse2 -stdlib=libc++` (macOS) | `vecmath`, `asmjit` (with `-DLEPTON_USE_JIT`) |
| ARM64 | `-pthread` | `vecmath`, `asmjit` (with `-DLEPTON_USE_JIT`) |
| PPC | `-pthread` | No vecmath/asmjit |
| LoongArch64 | `-pthread -mlsx` | No vecmath/asmjit |
| MSVC (any) | `/W2 /wd4305 /wd4244` | No extra flags for SSE (handled differently) |

The `asmjit` JIT compiler library is conditionally included only for x86 and ARM architectures, and only when building the shared library (it is explicitly excluded on Windows static builds). When present, it enables Lepton expression JIT compilation via the `-DLEPTON_USE_JIT` define.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L36-L53), [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L97-L132), [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L237-L250)

## Source Subdirectory Composition

Understanding which source directories are aggregated into each build target is essential for debugging compilation issues and adding new code.

### Core Library Source Subdirectories

The core `OpenMM` library is built from these source directories, all handled from the root `CMakeLists.txt` rather than as CMake subdirectories:

```
.  openmmapi  olla  libraries/jama  libraries/quern  libraries/lepton
libraries/sfmt  libraries/lbfgs  libraries/hilbert  libraries/csha1
libraries/pocketfft  libraries/vkfft  platforms/reference  serialization
libraries/irrxml  [+ libraries/vecmath if X86 or ARM]
```

This means the core library already includes the Reference platform implementation, the serialization subsystem, and all vendored math libraries. The GPU platforms and CPU platform are **not** part of the core library — they are separate shared libraries loaded at runtime.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L90-L95)

### Plugin Source Subdirectories

Plugins mirror the core pattern but add their own platform implementations:

| Plugin | Source Subdirs | GPU Platform Links |
|---|---|---|
| **Amoeba** | `.`, `openmmapi`, `serialization` | Conditionally adds `platforms/cuda`, `platforms/opencl`, `platforms/hip` |
| **RPMD** | Follows same pattern | Conditional GPU platforms |
| **Drude** | Follows same pattern | Conditional GPU platforms |
| **CPU PME** | Standalone | Links against `OpenMM` core |

Each plugin links against the core `OpenMM` shared library. The Amoeba plugin, in particular, has its own CUDA, OpenCL, and HIP sub-platforms (producing `OpenMMAmoebaCuda`, `OpenMMAmoebaOpenCL`, `OpenMMAmoebaHIP`) which are only built if the corresponding core platform is also being built.

Sources: [plugins/amoeba/CMakeLists.txt](plugins/amoeba/CMakeLists.txt#L17-L17), [plugins/amoeba/CMakeLists.txt](plugins/amoeba/CMakeLists.txt#L126-L166)

## Complete Build Procedure

### Step 1: Configure

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/openmm/openmm.git
cd openmm

# Create a build directory (out-of-source build is required)
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
```

The default install prefix is `/usr/local/openmm` on Unix and `$ENV{ProgramFiles}/OpenMM` on Windows. Override with `-DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/your/path`.

### Step 2: Customize Build Targets

All build customization happens through CMake cache variables. Here are the most important ones for advanced use:

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB` | Auto-detected | Build CUDA platform (`libOpenMMCuda.so`) |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB` | Auto-detected | Build OpenCL platform (`libOpenMMOpenCL.so`) |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_HIP_LIB` | Auto-detected | Build HIP platform (`libOpenMMHIP.so`) |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CPU_LIB` | `ON` | Build optimized CPU platform (`libOpenMMCPU.so`) |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_SHARED_LIB` | `ON` | Build shared libraries |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_STATIC_LIB` | `OFF` | Build static libraries |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_PYTHON_WRAPPERS` | `ON` | Build SWIG-based Python wrappers |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_C_AND_FORTRAN_WRAPPERS` | `ON` | Build C/Fortran API wrappers |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_AMOEBA_PLUGIN` | `ON` | Build Amoeba polarizable FF plugin |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_RPMD_PLUGIN` | `ON` | Build RPMD plugin |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_DRUDE_PLUGIN` | `ON` | Build Drude polarizable plugin |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_PME_PLUGIN` | `ON` | Build CPU PME plugin |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_EXAMPLES` | `ON` | Build example executables |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_COMMON` | `OFF` | Build common compute files without GPU platforms |
| `BUILD_TESTING` | `ON` | Build test suite |

**Important constraint**: The Python wrappers require all three plugins (Amoeba, RPMD, Drude) to be built — CMake will emit a `SEND_ERROR` and halt configuration if any is disabled. Similarly, CPU platform tests require the CPU PME plugin. If you want a minimal build without Python wrappers, you must also set `OPENMM_BUILD_PYTHON_WRAPPERS=OFF`.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L316-L474), [wrappers/python/CMakeLists.txt](wrappers/python/CMakeLists.txt#L437-L448)

### Step 3: Build and Install

```bash
# Build everything
cmake --build build -j$(nproc)

# Run the test suite
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure -j$(nproc)

# Install to the configured prefix
cmake --install build
```

On Linux, the default build type is `Release` if `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` is not explicitly set. Release builds use `-O3 -DNDEBUG`. Debug builds use `-g` with no optimization flags.

> [!TIP]
> **Kernel encoding is a configure-time operation, not a build-time operation.** If you modify a `.cu`, `.cl`, or `.hip` kernel file under `platforms/*/src/kernels/`, you must re-run CMake configuration (not just the build) to regenerate the encoded kernel source files. CMake tracks this via `DEPENDS` on the `GLOB`-discovered kernel files, but incremental builds may miss changes if files are added or removed — always reconfigure after kernel file additions.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L134-L150), [platforms/hip/CMakeLists.txt](platforms/hip/CMakeLists.txt#L91-L97)

## Platform-Specific Build Configurations

### CUDA Platform (NVIDIA GPUs)

When `CUDAToolkit_FOUND` is true, the CUDA platform produces `libOpenMMCuda.so` (or `OpenMMCUDA.dll`). The platform includes its own test suite, controlled by `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_TESTS` (default `ON`). On MSVC, kernel `.cu` files are compiled directly; on Unix, they are encoded into C++ strings at configure time.
